pages.title: HI-PRO

props.v: Extended low-dose apixaban after provoked VTE with an enduring risk factor

pages.html:
Findings

After ≥3 months of treatment, 12 more months of apixaban 2.5 mg BD cut recurrent VTE from 10% to 1.3% with no excess major bleeding

PopulationProvoked DVT/PE after ≥3 months anticoagulation with ≥1 persistent provoking factor; N=600
InterventionApixaban 2.5 mg BD for 12 months
ComparatorPlacebo
OutcomeRecurrent VTE 1.3% vs 10.0% (HR 0.13, 0.04–0.36; NNT 11); major bleeding 0.3% vs 0%

Notes

Piazza, NEJM 2025; single-centre (Boston), double-blind. Enduring factors: immobility, BMI ≥30, heart failure, chronic lung disease, eGFR <60, autoimmune/inflammatory disease, ASCVD. Few events; CRNM bleeding 4.8% vs 1.7% (NS). Definitions differ from ASH 'provoked, chronic'

pages.title: O'Malley et al.

props.v: LR vs saline in kidney transplantation

pages.html:
Findings

LR caused less hyperkalaemia and less acidosis than saline; study stopped early for metabolic complications in the saline arm

PopulationAdult kidney transplant recipients; N=51 (25 LR, 26 saline)
InterventionLactated Ringer's
Comparator0.9% saline
OutcomeK+ >6 mmol/L requiring treatment 0/25 (0%) vs 5/26 (19%); metabolic acidosis requiring treatment 0% vs 31%

Notes

Prospective randomised double-blind trial. No signal that LR worsened potassium in this high-risk renal population. Small, single-centre.

pages.title: Procalcitonin Antibiotic Consensus Trial (ProACT)
pages.html:
Findings

Procalcitonin guidance did not reduce antibiotic use or improve outcomes

PopulationED/inpatient adults with suspected lower respiratory tract infection; N=1664
InterventionProcalcitonin-guided antibiotic prescribing
ComparatorUsual care
OutcomeAntibiotic days 4.2 vs 4.3 (no difference); 30-day adverse outcomes similar

Notes

US ED patients; low-risk population; clinician adherence to guidance poor. Safe but no stewardship gain

pages.title: ADOPT

props.v: Oral vs extended-release injectable naltrexone started at hospital discharge for AUD

pages.html:
Findings

Both formulations reduced heavy drinking days by roughly 40 percentage points; no significant difference between them

PopulationInpatients with AUD and ≥1 heavy drinking day in prior 30 days; N=248
InterventionXR-naltrexone 380 mg IM at discharge, 1 and 2 months
ComparatorOral naltrexone 50–100 mg daily
OutcomeChange in % heavy drinking days −46.4 vs −38.4 points; adjusted difference −8.2 (−19.0 to 2.6), NS; ED/admission 61% vs 54%, NS

Notes

Magane, JAMA Intern Med 2025; single US urban hospital, open-label, N=248, 80% male. Injectable had better adherence (OR 1.89) but cost ~3× more ($5,208 vs $1,630 over 3 months). Hospitalisation is the moment to start AUD pharmacotherapy

pages.title: PLUS

props.v: Balanced crystalloid (Plasma-Lyte 148) vs saline in ICU

pages.html:
Findings

No difference in 90-day mortality between balanced solution and saline

PopulationCritically ill adults needing ICU crystalloid; N=5037
InterventionPlasma-Lyte 148 (balanced multielectrolyte solution)
Comparator0.9% saline
Outcome90-day mortality 21.8% vs 22.0%; no significant difference

Notes

Large blinded RCT (ANZICS CTG). Supports either fluid; saline not clearly harmful. Pre-specified TBI subgroup showed a signal favouring saline.

pages.title: 6S

props.v: HES 130/0.42 vs Ringer's acetate in severe sepsis

pages.html:
Findings

HES increased 90-day mortality and need for RRT

PopulationSevere sepsis needing fluid; N=804
InterventionHES 130/0.42
ComparatorRinger's acetate
OutcomeDeath or dialysis dependence at 90 days 51% vs 43%; RRT 22% vs 16%

Notes

Perner, NEJM 2012; N=804, Scandinavian. With CHEST, ended starch use in sepsis

pages.title: SODa-BIC (NEJM 2026)

props.v: Sodium bicarbonate for metabolic acidosis in vasopressor-dependent ICU patients

pages.html:
Findings

Routine 8.4% bicarbonate for mild–moderate metabolic acidosis in shock did not reduce MAKE30, death, RRT or persistent renal dysfunction, though it halved recurrent acidosis

Population498 ICU adults on continuous vasopressors with metabolic acidosis within 2 h (pH <7.30, BE ≤−4, PaCO2 ≤45 non-intubated/≤50 intubated); DKA, eGFR <30, current/imminent RRT, severe dysnatraemia, K <2.5 excluded; 46% had AKI, median pH 7.26, APACHE 21–22; 55 ICUs in 7 countries (ANZ, Japan, India, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Brazil) 2023–25; double-blind placebo-controlled RCT; 2422 of 3060 screened were excluded
Intervention8.4% sodium bicarbonate infusion over 5 h titrated to pH 7.30–7.35 and BE ≥0
Comparator5% dextrose placebo; open-label bicarbonate allowed if pH <7.10, HCO3 <8, BE <−15 or K >7 with pH <7.10
OutcomePrimary: MAKE30 (death, RRT or persistent renal dysfunction at 30 d) 40.2% vs 39.4%, adjusted difference 1.2% (95% CI −7.1 to 9.4), p=0.78; in-hospital death by 30 d 25.4% vs 24.0%; RRT 16.8% vs 20.9%; persistent renal dysfunction 14.0% vs 18.3%; RRT dependence at 30 d 5.7% vs 9.1% (all NS); recurrent acidosis 32.0% vs 55.7%; AKI 64.5% vs 64.8%; adverse events 1.6% vs 0 (all hypokalaemia <3.0)

Notes

Double-blind, multinational, included mild-moderate acidosis (pH <7.30). Massive exclusion rate (2,422 of 3,060 screened) limits generalisability; non-shock patients excluded. Not a universal protocol: selective, clinician-directed use; strict potassium monitoring mandatory. TBL critique (Rockie Kang, May 2026): strengths — pH <7.30 inclusion unlike BICAR-ICU 1/2 (pH <7.20), double-blinded, international. Weaknesses — vasopressor requirement excluded non-shock patients; high exclusion rate. TBL verdict: in ICU patients with pH <7.30, bicarbonate does not reduce death, RRT or persistent renal dysfunction at 30 days; keep it as a clinician-directed, selective therapy aimed at specific haemodynamic/metabolic goals. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/uncategorized/sodium-bicarbonate-for-metabolic-acidosis-in-the-intensive-care-unit-soda-bic-trial/

pages.title: ABC trial — Girard (Lancet 2008)

props.v: Daily spontaneous awakening trial paired with spontaneous breathing trial

pages.html:
Findings

Pairing a daily sedation interruption (SAT) with an SBT increased ventilator-free days and reduced 1-year mortality vs usual sedation plus SBT

PopulationMechanically ventilated adults on sedative infusions; N=336
InterventionDaily SAT followed by SBT if passed
ComparatorSedation per usual care plus daily SBT
OutcomeVentilator-free days 14.7 vs 11.6 (p=0.02); 1-year mortality 44% vs 58% (HR 0.68, NNT ≈7); ICU and hospital LOS shorter; self-extubation 10% vs 4%, reintubation no difference

Notes

Awakening and Breathing Controlled trial; 4 US centres. SAT = stop sedatives, observe, restart at half dose if failed; if SAT passed → SBT. More self-extubations in the intervention arm but no more reintubations. This trial is the 'B' (Both SAT and SBT) of today's ABCDEF bundle — it was the 'A' and 'B' (Awakening and Breathing Coordination) of the original ABCDE bundle. 1-year mortality was a secondary outcome.

pages.title: ABCDEF Bundle
pages.html:
Findings

Higher bundle compliance reduced delirium (62%→49%) and reduced mortality and LOS

PopulationMechanically ventilated ICU patients
InterventionHigher ABCDEF bundle compliance
ComparatorLower compliance
OutcomeDelirium ↓; mortality and LOS ↓

Notes

Now standard of care in most ICUs. Pun et al, Crit Care Med 2019 — observational, 15,000+ patients; dose-response with bundle completion

pages.title: Parlati et al. – ANOCA, INOCA, MINOCA review
pages.html:
Findings

Narrative review: ANOCA/INOCA/MINOCA are not benign; linked to serious CV events and long-term disability

PopulationPatients with angina, ischaemia or MI and non-obstructive coronary arteries
InterventionReview of pathogenic mechanisms, risk factors, diagnostic work-up and treatment
ComparatorNot applicable (narrative review)
OutcomeNo trial outcome data; IHD affects >250 million people and caused ~9.4 million deaths in 2021

Notes

Non-obstructive CAD may be more prevalent than obstructive CAD. Review covers mechanisms, risk factors, diagnostic steps, interventional and pharmacological management. J Cardiovasc Dev Dis 2025.

pages.title: ACCORD
pages.html:
Findings

Intensive control increased mortality

PopulationT2DM high CV risk; N=10,251
InterventionHbA1c <6.0%
ComparatorHbA1c 7.0–7.9%
OutcomeMortality 5.0% vs 4.0%

Notes

More treatment ≠ better

pages.title: ACURASYS
pages.html:
Findings

Early cisatracurium improved 90-day survival and increased ventilator-free days

PopulationSevere ARDS
InterventionEarly cisatracurium
ComparatorPlacebo
Outcome90-day survival 31% vs 40%

Notes

In part superseded by ROSE

pages.title: ADAPT-Sepsis (JAMA 2024)
pages.html:
Findings

A daily PCT-guided stop prompt safely shortened total antibiotic exposure by about a day in ICU sepsis; a CRP-guided prompt did not

Population2760 adults in 41 UK ICUs with suspected sepsis (acute organ dysfunction + suspected infection) on IV antibiotics started <24 h and expected ≥72 h; 1:1:1 RCT, clinicians blinded to biomarker values (received only protocol advice)
InterventionDaily PCT-guided (<0.25 µg/L 'strongly supports stopping'; >80% fall or 0.25–0.5 'supports stopping') or daily CRP-guided (<25 mg/L strongly supports; 50% fall supports) written discontinuation advice
ComparatorStandard care — daily advice always 'protocol supports usual care' (no PCT/CRP tested for trial)
OutcomeTotal antibiotic days to day 28: PCT 9.8 vs standard 10.7 d (difference 0.19–1.58 d, p=0.01); CRP 10.6 vs 10.7 d (NS). 28-d mortality (non-inferiority margin 5.4%): PCT 20.9% vs 19.4% (abs diff 1.57%, 95% CI −2.18 to 5.32 — non-inferior); CRP 21.1% vs 19.4% (CI −2.07 to 5.45 — inconclusive). 90-d mortality 25.6 vs 26.4 vs 25.5%. Initial-episode antibiotic duration 7.0 (PCT) vs 7.4 (CRP) vs 8.1 d

Notes

Large, pragmatic, well-run UK trial with blinded protocol advice. Weaknesses: alert-based advice stops clinicians personalising thresholds; clinicians still continued antibiotics ~3.5 days beyond the first 'strong stop' so real-world adherence may differ; wide 5.4% non-inferiority margin for mortality (reassured by 90-day data and prior PCT trials). TBL verdict: further evidence that PCT-guided discontinuation is a safe way to shorten antibiotics in suspected sepsis, but implementation needs process evaluation. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/adapt-sepsis/

pages.title: ADRENAL
pages.html:
Findings

Faster shock resolution; no mortality benefit

PopulationSeptic shock; N=3658
InterventionHydrocortisone
ComparatorPlacebo
Outcome90-day mortality 27.9% vs 28.8%

Notes

Useful in refractory shock

pages.title: ADVANCE
pages.html:
Findings

Reduced nephropathy, not mortality

PopulationT2DM; N=11,140
InterventionHbA1c ≤6.5%
ComparatorStandard control
OutcomeMajor macro/microvascular 18.1% vs 20.0%

Notes

Less alarming than ACCORD

pages.title: AFFIRM
pages.html:
Findings

Rate and rhythm control had similar survival

PopulationAF + stroke risk; N=4060
InterventionRhythm control
ComparatorRate control
Outcome5-year mortality 23.8% vs 21.3%, NS

Notes

Rhythm useful for symptoms, not mortality

pages.title: AID-ICU (NEJM 2022)

props.v: Haloperidol vs placebo for ICU delirium

pages.html:
Findings

Haloperidol did not increase days alive and out of hospital in ICU delirium; the secondary mortality reduction is intriguing but fragile

Population1000 adults with ICU delirium (CAM-ICU or ICDSC positive; 55% hypoactive, 64% ventilated, median age 70); 16 European ICUs; double-blind placebo-controlled RCT
InterventionHaloperidol 2.5 mg IV TDS, extra doses to max 20 mg/day (median 8.3 mg/day for 3.6 days), until delirium-free, ICU discharge or day 90
ComparatorPlacebo; rescue propofol/benzodiazepine/α2-agonist allowed in both arms
OutcomePrimary days alive and out of hospital at 90 d: 35.8 vs 32.9, adjusted difference 2.9 (95% CI −1.2 to 7, p=0.22). 90-d mortality 36.3% vs 43.3%, adjusted difference −6.9% (−13 to −0.6; fragility index 4, 24 missing). Days alive without delirium/coma 57.7 vs 52.6 (NS); SAEs 2.2% vs 1.9%; QTc-related stop 2.4% vs 1.4%; rescue medication 57.5% vs 62.1%

Notes

TBL critique (David Slessor): blinded multicentre RCT with validated delirium tools; weaknesses include a composite primary outcome, an optimistic power assumption (15% mortality reduction), ~20% major protocol violations, 13% open-label antipsychotic use, selection bias from excluding prior antipsychotic users, and heavy treatment of hypoactive delirium (not standard practice). Verdict: treat the mortality signal with caution (secondary outcome, missing data exceeds fragility index); still reasonable to use haloperidol for symptom control in hyperactive delirium despite minimal evidence for longer-term benefit. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/aid-icu/

pages.title: AKIKI
pages.html:
Findings

Delayed RRT avoided dialysis in many

PopulationSevere AKI ICU; N=620
InterventionEarly RRT
ComparatorDelayed RRT
Outcome60-day mortality 48.5% vs 49.7%

Notes

Supports waiting if safe

pages.title: ALBICS-AKI (JAMA Surgery 2025)

props.v: 20% albumin to prevent AKI after cardiac surgery

pages.html:
Findings

Post-operative 20% albumin infusion after high-risk cardiac surgery increased rather than reduced AKI, especially in pre-existing renal impairment, and increased transfusion

Population621 adults after high-risk on-pump cardiac surgery (combined procedures, thoracic aortic surgery, or any cardiac surgery with eGFR <60); 7 centres (6 Australia, 1 Italy) 2019–2024; open-label RCT, stratified by eGFR <60
Intervention300 mL of 20% albumin at 20 mL/h over 15 h started within 6 h of ICU admission
ComparatorUsual care; no 20% albumin for 24 h (4–5% albumin permitted)
OutcomeKDIGO stage 1–3 AKI within 7 d: 48.9% vs 43.4%, adjusted RR 1.12 (95% CI 1.04–1.21, p=0.003) — harm concentrated in eGFR <60 (66.2% vs 57.6%, RR 1.14, 1.07–1.22); eGFR ≥60 no difference. No difference in MAKE-28, sustained stage 2–3 AKI, RRT, mortality (2% vs 0.7%), LOS. More transfusion by day 2 (38% vs 30%, p=0.04); albumin at 24 h 37.4 vs 32.1 g/L

Notes

Pragmatic, well-balanced RCT with consistent sensitivity/subgroup analyses and a supporting meta-analysis. Limits: open-label; creatinine-only, biomarker primary outcome; one centre contributed a third of patients; control group got more 4–5% albumin. TBL verdict: do not use 20% albumin for AKI prevention after cardiac surgery; the transfusion signal raises concerns about albumin and haemostasis in this group. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/albics-aki-draft/

pages.title: ALBIOS

props.v: Albumin replacement in severe sepsis/septic shock

pages.html:
Findings

Albumin targeting ≥30 g/L plus crystalloid did not improve 28- or 90-day mortality

PopulationSevere sepsis/septic shock; N=1818
Intervention20% albumin to target ≥30 g/L + crystalloid
ComparatorCrystalloid alone
Outcome28-day mortality 31.8% vs 32.0%; 90-day 41.1% vs 43.6%, NS

Notes

Caironi, NEJM 2014; N=1818, Italy, open-label. Post hoc septic-shock subgroup (n=1121) hinted at lower 90-day mortality — hypothesis only

pages.title: ALVEOLI
pages.html:
Findings

No difference in mortality or ventilator-free days

PopulationALI/ARDS
InterventionHigher PEEP
ComparatorLower PEEP
OutcomeNo difference in mortality or vent-free days

Notes

Higher vs lower PEEP

pages.title: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK 2 (JAMA 2025)
pages.html:
Findings

CRT-targeted personalised resuscitation beat usual care on the composite, almost entirely via shorter duration of organ support — no mortality difference. Builds on ANDROMEDA-SHOCK (CRT vs lactate) and informed 2026 Surviving Sepsis guidance to use CRT as an adjunct resuscitation target

Population1467 adults with early septic shock (Sepsis-3: lactate ≥2 mmol/L, noradrenaline needed after ≥1 L fluid, ≤4 h from meeting criteria); 86 ICUs in 19 countries (mostly Spain/Latin America), 2022–25; multicentre open-label RCT, 1:1
InterventionCRT-PHR: tiered 6-h protocol targeting CRT normalisation (glass-slide CRT >3 s abnormal, hourly). Tier 1: fluid-responsiveness-tested fluid (max 1 L) / noradrenaline guided by pulse pressure and DBP. Tier 2: bedside echo; MAP 80–85 trial for 1 h if prior hypertension; dobutamine 5 mcg/kg/min trial for 1 h; rescue therapies if all fail
ComparatorUsual care per local/international guidelines (CRT measured only at baseline and 6 h)
OutcomePrimary hierarchical composite (28-d mortality > vital-support days > hospital LOS, win ratio): 48.9% vs 42.1% wins, stratified win ratio 1.16 (95% CI 1.02–1.33) — effect driven by APACHE II >19. 28-d mortality 26.5% vs 26.6% (HR 0.99, 0.81–1.21). Vital-support-free days 16.5 vs 15.4 (pOR 1.28, 1.06–1.54). Hospital LOS 15.3 vs 16.2 d (NS). At 6 h CRT-PHR group had less fluid (600 vs 850 mL), more dobutamine (12 vs 5%), lower lactate (3.2 vs 3.5)

Notes

doi:10.1001/jama.2025.20402. The Bottom Line critique (Tim Law, Dec 2025): unblinded; CRT has inter-observer variability and fluid-responsiveness testing was not standardised; stopping organ support was at intensivist discretion. Primary difference rests on <1 day less support/LOS — is that worth a complex protocol? Bundle effect: cannot separate CRT from dedicated expert-driven hourly reassessment (Hawthorne effect). Feasibility and adherence may not transfer to less-resourced settings; predicted mortality 39% much higher than UK/Australian septic shock. TBL verdict: supports CRT as a useful target; favour a multimodal approach (CRT + lactate clearance + MAP + urine output). See also Castro et al (microcirculatory flow). Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/blog/ebm/andromeda-shock2-personalized-hemodynamic-resuscitation/

pages.title: Annane 2002

props.v: Low-dose hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone in septic shock

pages.html:
Findings

Hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone reduced 28-day mortality in non-responders to a short corticotropin test

PopulationSeptic shock with vasopressors; N=300
InterventionHydrocortisone 50 mg 6-hourly + fludrocortisone 50 mcg ×7 days
ComparatorPlacebo
Outcome28-day mortality in non-responders 53% vs 63% (p=0.02)

Notes

JAMA 2002; N=300, French, very sick cohort (control mortality ~60%). Started the modern steroids-in-shock debate; corticotropin testing later abandoned (CORTICUS)

pages.title: ANNEXA-I (NEJM 2024)

props.v: Reversal of factor Xa inhibitors in intracerebral haemorrhage

pages.html:
Findings

Andexanet improved a 12-hour haemostatic/haematoma-expansion endpoint over usual care (mostly PCC) but doubled thrombotic events, with no sign of better functional outcome

Population530 adults (median age 79, GCS 15, haematoma ~10 mL) with ICH within 6 h of symptoms (later criteria: 0.5–60 mL, NIHSS ≤35, GCS ≥7) who had taken a factor Xa inhibitor within 15 h (apixaban 60%, rivaroxaban 29%); 131 sites, 23 countries 2019–23; open-label RCT with blinded adjudication, stopped early for efficacy at 452
InterventionAndexanet alfa (low or high dose by inhibitor dose/timing): bolus then 2-h infusion
ComparatorUsual care — 85.5% received PCC (92% 4-factor)
OutcomeHaemostatic efficacy at 12 h (haematoma expansion ≤35%, NIHSS rise <7, no rescue therapy): 67.0% vs 53.1%, adjusted difference 13.4% (95% CI 4.6–22.2, p=0.003). Thrombotic events 10.3% vs 5.6% (ischaemic stroke 6.5% vs 1.5%). 30-d mortality 27.8% vs 25.5%; mRS 0–3 at 30 d 28.0% vs 31.0% (post hoc, NS)

Notes

International RCT, minimal crossover, anti-Xa activity measured. Weaknesses: unblinded; not powered for mortality or function, and the only functional data are post hoc and unfavourable; primary outcome driven by small-volume haematoma change; industry-sponsored with design involvement; many protocol amendments; excludes severe ICH (GCS <7) and slow presenters; usual care poorly described; cost unaddressed. TBL verdict: reduces haematoma expansion but no patient-important benefit and clear harm (thrombosis, ischaemic stroke) — not enough evidence to use andexanet; PCC remains the pragmatic choice. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/annexa-i/

pages.title: ANSWER
pages.html:
Findings

Long-term albumin improved survival

PopulationCirrhosis + ascites; N=431
InterventionWeekly albumin
ComparatorStandard care
Outcome18-month survival 77% vs 66%

Notes

Outpatient ascites context

pages.title: APROCCHSS
pages.html:
Findings

Hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone reduced mortality

PopulationSeptic shock; N=1241
InterventionHydro + fludro
ComparatorPlacebo
Outcome90-day mortality 43.0% vs 49.1% (p=0.03)

Notes

Annane, NEJM 2018. Hydrocortisone 50 mg q6h + fludrocortisone 50 mcg daily × 7 days. More positive than ADRENAL — a sicker population with higher baseline mortality (~49% control vs ~29% in ADRENAL) is one reason the results differ. Faster wean off pressors, more vasopressor-free and organ-failure-free days, but more hyperglycaemia

pages.title: ARDSNet LaSRS (late steroids)
pages.html:
Findings

Late methylprednisolone did not reduce 60-day mortality; more ventilator-free days early but higher mortality when started >14 days after onset

PopulationPersistent ARDS ≥7 days; N=180
InterventionMethylprednisolone 2 mg/kg then taper
ComparatorPlacebo
Outcome60-day mortality 29.2% vs 28.6%, NS; started >14 days: 35% vs 8%

Notes

Steinberg, NEJM 2006; N=180. More neuromyopathy; rebound after taper. Why guidelines say avoid starting steroids after day 14

pages.title: ARiE (Am J Gastroenterol 2024)

props.v: Rifaximin added to broad-spectrum antibiotics for acute hepatic encephalopathy in ICU

pages.html:
Findings

Adding rifaximin to broad-spectrum antibiotics did not hasten HE resolution in critically ill cirrhotics; possible mortality benefit only in the decompensated-cirrhosis (non-ACLF) subgroup

Population184 adults (18–75) with cirrhosis and overt HE (West Haven ≥2) admitted to ICU; single centre, Hyderabad, India; mostly alcohol-related, MELD ~29, ~30% ventilated; open-label (no placebo) RCT
InterventionRifaximin 550 mg BD (PO/NG) + broad-spectrum antimicrobials
ComparatorBroad-spectrum antimicrobials alone (all received lactulose)
OutcomePrimary ≥2-grade reduction/resolution of HE: 46.7% vs 44.6% (p=0.84), over 4.1 vs 3.6 days (p=0.27). In-hospital mortality 50% vs 62% (HR 0.7, p=0.06); nosocomial infection 13% vs 6.5% (NS). Subgroup decompensated cirrhosis without ACLF (n=88): mortality 33.3% vs 56.5% (p=0.003); no effect in ACLF

Notes

TBL critique: pragmatic question in a relevant ICU population with protocolised infection work-up; but single centre, no placebo, muddled 'non-inferiority' framing not supported by methods, HE scored only once daily, LOLA co-treatment imbalance, and the subgroup mortality signal lacks a plausible mechanism. Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics for all HE is not established practice outside India/variceal bleeding. Verdict: lactulose stays first line; rifaximin is a safe adjunct where lactulose is not tolerated or HE is refractory, particularly in decompensated cirrhosis. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/arie-trial-rifaximin-for-encephalopathy/

pages.title: ARISE FLUIDS

props.v: Restrictive vs liberal fluids in septic shock

pages.html:
Findings

Restricted fluid with early vasopressors did not improve days alive and out of hospital at 90 days vs a liberal strategy; less pulmonary oedema but more ICU admissions

PopulationED adults with suspected infection, hypotension after ≥1 L fluid and lactate >2; N=1000
InterventionStop fluids, start vasopressors immediately (250 mL boluses if needed)
ComparatorFurther boluses towards 30 mL/kg, later vasopressors
OutcomeDays alive and out of hospital to day 90: 76 vs 76 (difference 0.0, −2.7 to 2.7); 90-day death 16.4% vs 14.4%; pulmonary oedema 0.6% vs 5.0%; ICU admission 76.5% vs 67.8%

Notes

NEJM 2026; 51 ED sites in Australia, NZ and Ireland, open-label, N=1000. Fluid 0–24 h: 1140 vs 2248 mL. Death at 90 days 16.4% vs 14.4% (RR 1.14, 0.85–1.54). Third neutral trial after CLASSIC and CLOVERS

pages.title: ARISE

props.v: Early goal-directed therapy in septic shock (Australasia)

pages.html:
Findings

EGDT did not reduce 90-day mortality vs usual care; more fluids, pressors, dobutamine and transfusion for no gain

PopulationED patients with early septic shock (hypotension after ≥1 L or lactate ≥4); N=1600
Intervention6-h EGDT (CVC with ScvO2, fluids, pressors, dobutamine, transfusion to targets)
ComparatorUsual care (no ScvO2 monitoring)
Outcome90-day mortality 18.6% vs 18.8% (RR 0.98, 0.80–1.21); ICU LOS and organ support — no difference

Notes

ANZICS CTG, NEJM 2014; 51 centres in Australia, NZ, Finland, Hong Kong, Ireland. Low control mortality (18.8%) reflects good usual care. ScvO2 catheter in 90% of EGDT arm vs 0% control. One of the trio (ProCESS, ARISE, ProMISe) that retired protocolised EGDT; MAP 65 target was common to all arms

pages.title: ARISS
pages.html:
Findings

Albumin added to crystalloid did not reduce 90-day mortality; trial stopped early and underpowered

PopulationSeptic shock within 24 h; N=440
InterventionAlbumin 60 g/day to target ≥30 g/L
ComparatorCrystalloid alone
Outcome90-day mortality — no significant difference

Notes

Stopped at 440 of planned 1412; over half of albumin arm never reached target albumin. Neutral but inconclusive — not a clear negative

pages.title: ARISTOTLE
pages.html:
Findings

Apixaban better than warfarin with less bleeding

PopulationAF; N=18,201
InterventionApixaban
ComparatorWarfarin
OutcomeStroke/SEE 1.27%/yr vs 1.60%/yr; major bleed 2.13%/yr vs 3.09%/yr

Notes

Why apixaban is popular

pages.title: ARMA (ARDSNet)
pages.html:
Findings

Low tidal volume reduced mortality

PopulationARDS; N=861
InterventionVT 6 ml/kg
ComparatorVT 12 ml/kg
OutcomeMortality 31.0% vs 39.8%

Notes

Core ICU practice

pages.title: ARREST — cardiac arrest centre transfer (Lancet 2023)

props.v: Expedited transfer to a cardiac arrest centre vs nearest ED after non-STEMI OHCA

pages.html:
Findings

Routing all non-ST-elevation OHCA survivors to a cardiac arrest centre did not reduce 30-day mortality compared with the nearest ED

Population862 adults with ROSC after OHCA of presumed cardiac cause and no ST elevation on post-ROSC ECG (55% shockable, 24 min to ROSC); London Ambulance Service and 35 hospitals, 2018–22; open-label RCT randomised at dispatch
InterventionDirect transport to a cardiac arrest centre with delivery to the cath lab and combined cardiology/ICU assessment (angiography 56% at 2.3 h)
ComparatorTransport to the geographically closest ED (angiography 37% at 5.7 h)
OutcomePrimary 30-d all-cause mortality: 63% vs 63%, RR 1.00 (95% CI 0.90–1.11). 3-month mortality 65% vs 64%; favourable mRS at 3 months 30% vs 31%. Survivors at 3 months had worse mRS at discharge in the CAC arm (OR 1.55, 1.00–2.41). Age subgroups: <57 y RR 0.76 (0.60–0.97) favouring CAC; 57–71 y RR 1.28 (1.05–1.56) favouring ED. More ICU admission (80% vs 69%) and organ support in CAC arm

Notes

TBL critique (Andrew Achilleos): first RCT of its kind, remarkable execution, central randomisation, few crossovers, patient-centred outcome, broad inclusion; it challenges resource-intensive professional-body recommendations built on confounded observational data and continues the TOMAHAWK/COACT message that early stabilisation beats early angiography in non-STEMI OHCA. Limitations: open-label, dense urban setting (transit-time differences small, may not generalise to rural areas), patients without ROSC or with STEMI not tested, younger-age subgroup benefit hypothesis-generating. Verdict: does not support pre-hospital transfer of all resuscitated non-STEMI OHCA to a cardiac arrest centre. NB distinct from ARREST 2020 (ECPR). Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/arrest-2/

pages.title: ARREST
pages.html:
Findings

ECPR improved neurologic survival vs standard ACLS in refractory VT/VF (43% vs 7%)

PopulationRefractory VT/VF out-of-hospital arrest
InterventionECPR
ComparatorStandard ACLS
OutcomeSurvival to discharge with good neuro outcome 43% vs 7%

Notes

Single-centre; hypothesis-generating

pages.title: ART
pages.html:
Findings

Aggressive recruitment with high PEEP titration increased mortality

PopulationModerate-severe ARDS
InterventionRecruitment + high PEEP titration
ComparatorLow PEEP (ARDSNet)
Outcome28-day mortality ↑ with recruitment strategy

Notes

Cautions against aggressive recruitment manoeuvres; ↑ barotrauma

pages.title: ASTER (JAMA 2024)

props.v: IV paracetamol for organ dysfunction in sepsis

pages.html:
Findings

Scheduled IV paracetamol was safe in sepsis but did not increase organ-support-free days; secondary signals (less ARDS, lower mortality) were unadjusted and hypothesis-generating

Population447 adults with sepsis plus vasopressor-dependent hypotension or respiratory failure (ventilation/NIV/O2 >6 L/min), randomised within 36 h; 40 US academic ICUs 2021–23; phase 2b double-blind placebo-controlled RCT (vitamin C arm dropped)
InterventionIV acetaminophen 1 g 6-hourly for 5 days (20 doses; mean ~12 received)
ComparatorMatched IV placebo (5% dextrose) 6-hourly for 5 days
OutcomeDays alive and free of organ support to day 28: 20.2 vs 19.6 (MD 0.6, 95% CI −1.4 to 2.6, p=0.56). 28-d mortality 16.5% vs 21.6% (NS); 90-d mortality, MAKE-28, SOFA change NS. ARDS within 7 d 2.2% vs 8.5% (secondary, unadjusted). No excess hepatotoxicity or hypotension. No benefit in high cell-free haemoglobin (>10 mg/dL) subgroup

Notes

Well-run blinded multicentre trial with high adherence. Weaknesses: dropped vitamin C arm, secondary outcomes unadjusted for multiplicity, drug only given in ICU (mean 12 of 20 doses), high pre-randomisation paracetamol use, single country. TBL verdict: with HEAT, no case for routine paracetamol in sepsis; a mortality-powered trial in high cell-free haemoglobin patients could be justified. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/aster/

pages.title: ATACAS
pages.html:
Findings

TXA reduced bleeding, transfusion and reoperation without more thrombotic events; more seizures

PopulationOn-pump CABG at increased risk; N=4662
InterventionTXA (initially 100 mg/kg, later 50 mg/kg)
ComparatorPlacebo
OutcomeDeath/thrombotic events 16.7% vs 18.1%, NS; reoperation for bleeding 1.4% vs 2.8%; seizures 0.7% vs 0.1%

Notes

Myles, NEJM 2017; N=4662. Seizure signal dose-related — supports lower doses in cardiac surgery

pages.title: ATHOS-3
pages.html:
Findings

Reduced background vasopressor use in ~60% of patients

PopulationVasodilatory shock
InterventionAngiotensin II
ComparatorPlacebo
OutcomeVasopressor requirement reduced in ~60%

Notes

Prospective study; angiotensin II now used in refractory shock

pages.title: ATTIRE
pages.html:
Findings

Routine albumin targeting did not improve outcomes

PopulationDecompensated cirrhosis; N=777
InterventionAlbumin to target ≥30g/L
ComparatorStandard care
OutcomeInfection/renal dysfunction/death no reduction

Notes

Challenged “more albumin” approach

pages.title: AQUATIC

props.v: Aspirin added to oral anticoagulation in high-risk stable CAD after stenting

pages.html:
Findings

Adding aspirin to anticoagulation increased major CV events, major bleeding and all-cause death; trial stopped early

PopulationChronic coronary syndrome, prior PCI >6 months, high risk, on long-term OAC; N=872
InterventionAspirin 100 mg daily + OAC
ComparatorPlacebo + OAC
OutcomeCV death/MI/stroke/embolism/revascularisation/limb ischaemia 16.9% vs 12.1%; major bleeding 10.2% vs 3.4%; all-cause death 13.4% vs 8.4%

Notes

NEJM 2025 (ESC Hot Line); French, placebo-controlled, N=872, stents >6 months old, high atherothrombotic risk. Median 2 years. Drop the aspirin — anticoagulant alone

pages.title: BALANCE (NEJM 2024)
pages.html:
Findings

Seven days of antibiotics was non-inferior to 14 days for 90-day mortality in bloodstream infection, with fewer antibiotic days and shorter hospital stay

Population3631 hospitalised adults (55% ICU) with a pathogenic bacteraemia — 44% E. coli, 15% Klebsiella, 7% Enterococcus; source UTI 42%, abdominal 19%, lung 13%; S. aureus, S. lugdunensis, fungaemia, endocarditis/osteomyelitis/undrained abscess, prosthetic valves and severe immunosuppression excluded; 74 sites in 7 countries (75% Canada) 2014–23; open-label non-inferiority RCT (4% margin)
Intervention7 days of adequate antibiotics (median received 8)
Comparator14 days (median received 14)
OutcomePrimary: 90-day mortality difference −1.6% (95% CI −4.0 to 0.8) — 7 days non-inferior; no subgroup differed (source, ICU, gram stain, vasopressors, APACHE). 7-day group: hospital LOS 10 vs 11 days, hospital-free days 17 vs 15, antibiotic-free days 19 vs 14; relapse 2.6% vs 2.2%, C. difficile 1.7% vs 2.0%, resistant organisms 9.5% vs 8.5% — all NS

Notes

TBL critique: largest antibiotic-duration trial, international, ward and ICU patients, minimal attrition, allocation concealed until day 7, blinded adjudication of relapse; ITT, mITT and per-protocol all concordant. Weaknesses: predominantly Canadian; 4% margin may be too generous for some; not powered by source (40% UTI, where short courses are already usual); 24% non-adherence in the 7-day arm; S. aureus excluded; unclear pre-culture antibiotic exposure. TBL verdict: solid evidence that 7 days of appropriate antibiotics suffices for most bacteraemias. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/balance-7-vs-14-days-of-antibiotics/

pages.title: Soliman et al. — balanced crystalloids vs saline in DKA (SR/MA)

props.v: Choice of initial fluids in DKA

pages.html:
Findings

No clinical differences in time to resolution of DKA

PopulationDKA, initial fluid resuscitation
InterventionBalanced crystalloids
Comparator0.9% saline
OutcomeTime to DKA resolution — no difference

Notes

Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (PMC13403006). Evidence base weak: mostly open-label, underpowered, inconsistent DKA-resolution criteria; authors call for blinded trials powered for patient-important outcomes in homogeneous groups. (Merged from three screenshots)

pages.title: BaSICS

props.v: Balanced crystalloid (Plasma-Lyte) vs saline, and slow vs fast bolus, in ICU

pages.html:
Findings

No difference in 90-day mortality between balanced solution and saline, nor between slow and fast bolus rates; pre-specified TBI subgroup had higher mortality with balanced fluid

PopulationCritically ill adults expected to need fluid and stay >1 day; N=11,052
InterventionPlasma-Lyte 148 (balanced); separately, slow bolus 333 ml/h
Comparator0.9% saline; separately, fast bolus 999 ml/h
Outcome90-day mortality 26.4% vs 27.2% (HR 0.97, 0.90–1.05); SMART-type kidney outcomes no difference; slow vs fast bolus 26.6% vs 27.0% (NS); TBI subgroup 31.3% vs 21.1% favouring saline

Notes

Zampieri, JAMA 2021; 75 Brazilian ICUs, 2×2 factorial (fluid type × infusion rate 333 vs 999 ml/h). Low-volume trial — median ~1.5 L study fluid in first days, so limited separation. TBI subgroup (n≈450): 90-day mortality 31.3% balanced vs 21.1% saline — the signal that keeps saline as the default in brain injury. With SMART and PLUS, completes the balanced-vs-saline trio: balanced fluids are a reasonable default, the benefit is small.

pages.title: BICARICU-2 (JAMA 2025)

props.v: Bicarbonate in severe acidaemia with moderate–severe AKI

pages.html:
Findings

Targeted 4.2% bicarbonate in severe metabolic acidaemia with moderate–severe AKI did not reduce 90-day mortality (62% vs 62%), but reduced and delayed KRT

Population640 ICU adults (627 analysed) within 48 h of admission with pH ≤7.20, HCO3 ≤20, PaCO2 ≤45 and KDIGO stage 2–3 AKI, SOFA >4 or lactate ≥2; 55% septic shock, 14% haemorrhagic shock, 80% on vasopressors, 75% ventilated; 43 French ICUs 2019–23; open-label RCT powered for 10% ARR in 90-day mortality
Intervention4.2% sodium bicarbonate 125–250 mL over 30 min targeting pH ≥7.30, max 1 L (500 mEq)/24 h, for 28 days or ICU discharge; median 750 mL in first 48 h
ComparatorNo bicarbonate; standardised KRT indications in both arms
OutcomePrimary: 90-day mortality 62.1% vs 61.7%, absolute difference 0.4% (95% CI −7.2 to 8.0), no subgroup effect; 28-day mortality 54% vs 54%, 180-day 65% vs 63%; KRT by day 28 35% vs 50% (less with bicarbonate), time to KRT 31 vs 16 h; vasopressor use 97% vs 94%, day-2 fluid balance 2.8 vs 2.2 L (more with bicarbonate); no difference in KRT-free days, ventilation, ICU/hospital LOS, SOFA

Notes

Follow-on to BICAR-ICU (2018). Tested the hypothesis from BICAR-ICU's AKI subgroup prospectively — largely neutral. TBL critique (George Walker, Nov 2025): multicentre, standardised KRT criteria, low protocol violations, clear pH/bicarbonate separation. Weaknesses: single country, 4.2% rather than 1.26%/8.4% used elsewhere, open-label (objective endpoint), 15% crossover, possible heterogeneity by acidosis type (HAGMA vs mixed), observed mortality lower than the 80% assumed and powered only for a 10% difference. TBL verdict: no mortality effect but a reduction in KRT, which may still matter given dialysis-related harms; SODa-BIC and MOSAICC to follow. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/bicaricu-2/

pages.title: BigpAK-2 (Lancet 2025)

props.v: KDIGO bundle to prevent post-operative AKI

pages.html:
Findings

A KDIGO-based supportive-care bundle cut moderate/severe AKI after major surgery by ~8% absolute, but shifted patients to stage 1 AKI rather than preventing AKI, and did not change RRT, mortality or MAKE90

Population1176 adults after major surgery (>2 h, ICU/HDU, cardiac 33%, general 34%, vascular 15%) at high AKI risk — biomarker-enriched (urinary TIMP-2×IGFBP7 >0.3) plus ≥1 clinical risk factor; 34 European hospitals 2020–24; open-label adaptive RCT
InterventionKDIGO-recommended preventive bundle for ≥12 h: 3-hourly passive leg raise with 0.5–1 L crystalloid if responsive, MAP >65 with vasopressors, advanced haemodynamic monitoring targeting CI >2.5 (dobutamine/adrenaline if needed), ACEi/ARB withheld ≥48 h and other nephrotoxins 72 h, glucose 5.5–8.3 mmol/L
ComparatorStandard institutional care
OutcomePrimary: moderate/severe (KDIGO 2–3) AKI within 72 h 14.4% vs 22.3%, OR 0.57 (95% CI 0.40–0.79), p=0.0002; stage 2 AKI 23.5% vs 38.8% but stage 1 AKI higher (60.6% vs 45.4%); any AKI 36.5% vs 40.8% (NS); stage 3 AKI 16.0% vs 15.8%; RRT to day 90 5.1% vs 5.9%; 90-day mortality 7.0% vs 7.0%; MAKE90 11.0% vs 10.6% — all NS

Notes

TBL critique: multicentre, adaptive, blinded outcome assessment, result held on ITT and per-protocol. But unblinded; full bundle adherence <50% (62% without the glucose component) with ~10% crossover; haemodynamic differences actually small (+200 mL fluid, more dobutamine) so benefit may reflect frequent clinician review; exploratory analysis points to avoiding MAP <65 (OR 0.19) and stopping ACEi/ARB (OR 0.36) as the key components. Biomarker-negative and CKD 4–5 patients excluded, so effect in everyday patients is likely smaller. TBL verdict: adherence to KDIGO guidance reduces moderate/severe AKI at 72 h, but no difference in longer-term patient-centred outcomes — AKI risk can be reduced with high-quality supportive care and frequent assessment. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/bigpak-2-preventive-care-strategy-to-reduce-acute-kidney-injury-after-major-surgery/

pages.title: BLING III (JAMA 2024)

props.v: Continuous vs intermittent beta-lactam infusion in sepsis

pages.html:
Findings

Continuous beta-lactam infusion did not significantly reduce 90-day mortality (primary), but the interval is compatible with meaningful benefit, clinical cure improved, and there was no signal of harm

Population7202 adults in 104 ICUs (7 countries, 55 UK) with sepsis (infection + organ dysfunction) started on piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem within 24 h, not on RRT; open-label RCT 2018–23
InterventionContinuous 24-h infusion of the beta-lactam (after a loading bolus) for the prescribed course or until ICU discharge; median 5.8 d
ComparatorIntermittent infusion over 30 min; median 5.7 d (same total daily dose)
Outcome90-d all-cause mortality: 24.9% vs 26.8%, absolute difference −1.9% (95% CI −4.9 to 1.1), OR 0.91 (0.81–1.01), p=0.08; adjusted OR 0.89 (0.79–0.99), p=0.04. Clinical cure by day 14: 55.7% vs 50.0% (diff 5.7%, 2.4–9.1). No difference in MRO/C. difficile acquisition (7.2% vs 7.5%), ICU or hospital mortality, organ-support-free days. Adverse events 0.3% vs 0.2%

Notes

Very large, well-balanced RCT with excellent follow-up. Weaknesses: unblinded; reverted to intermittent dosing outside ICU (bias to null); 'clinical cure' definition debatable; ~1/3 protocol violations (mostly >1 h infusion pauses); no TDM or susceptibility data. TBL verdict: start continuous infusions in ICU sepsis when IV access allows — potential benefit, no evidence of harm; meta-analysis with BLING III supports a mortality reduction. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/bling-iii/

pages.title: Bourdeaux 2011 (bicarbonate vs 5% saline for ICP)

props.v: Hypertonic sodium bicarbonate vs equimolar hypertonic saline for raised ICP in TBI

pages.html:
Findings

Both lowered ICP equally over the first hour; bicarbonate's effect lasted longer (ICP higher in the saline group at 150 min, 2 saline patients needed re-dosing)

PopulationRaised ICP after traumatic brain injury; 20 episodes, 11 patients
Intervention85 ml 8.4% sodium bicarbonate
Comparator100 ml 5% NaCl (equimolar)
OutcomeICP fall at 60 min — no difference; at 150 min lower with bicarbonate; repeat dosing 0 vs 2

Notes

Bourdeaux & Brown, Neurocrit Care 2011; crossover-style RCT, 20 episodes in 11 TBI patients. Companion 2010 observational study: 85 ml 8.4% bicarbonate over 30 min dropped ICP 28 → 10 mmHg without significant pH change. 8.4% bicarbonate ≈ 6% NaCl osmotically

pages.title: BOX — blood pressure arm (NEJM 2022)

props.v: MAP target after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest

pages.html:
Findings

A MAP target of 77 vs 63 mmHg after OHCA made no difference to death or poor neurological outcome

Population789 comatose (GCS <9) adults with OHCA of presumed cardiac cause and sustained ROSC; 2 Danish tertiary centres, 2017–21; double-blind (monitor calibration offset ±10%) 2×2 factorial RCT with oxygen arm; 85% shockable rhythm
InterventionHigher MAP target 77 mmHg for duration of invasive BP monitoring
ComparatorStandard MAP target 63 mmHg
OutcomePrimary (death or discharge with CPC 3–4 by day 90): no significant difference; 90-d mortality HR ~1.0 with no subgroup signal. Separation achieved: ~10 mmHg MAP and noradrenaline 0.038 mcg/kg/min higher in high-target group. No difference in bleeding, infection, MoCA or CPC

Notes

TBL critique: ingenious blinding of a haemodynamic trial, good separation, event rate as predicted, minimal loss to follow-up. Weaknesses: 2 centres in 1 country, dopamine as second-line, 10 mmHg difference may be too small, powered for a large (10% absolute) effect, MoCA only in 359 patients. Verdict: author will keep targeting MAP >65 mmHg after OHCA — anything in this range appears safe. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/box-trial-bloodpressure/

pages.title: BOX — oxygen arm (NEJM 2022)

props.v: Restrictive vs liberal oxygenation after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest

pages.html:
Findings

Restrictive (9–10 kPa) vs liberal (13–14 kPa) PaO2 targets after OHCA did not change mortality or neurological outcome

Population789 comatose adults with OHCA of presumed cardiac cause and sustained ROSC, randomised within 4 h of ROSC; 2 Danish cardiac arrest centres, 2017–21; open-label 2×2 factorial RCT (with MAP arm); TTM 36 °C for 24 h in all
InterventionRestrictive oxygenation: PaO2 9–10 kPa (initial FiO2 0.3) until extubation
ComparatorLiberal oxygenation: PaO2 13–14 kPa (initial FiO2 0.6)
OutcomePrimary (death or discharge with CPC 3–4 within 90 d): 32.0% vs 33.9%, HR 0.95 (0.75–1.21), p=0.69. 90-d death 28.7% vs 31.1% (HR 0.93, 0.72–1.20); AKI needing RRT 8.6% vs 11.9% (NS); median CPC 1 vs 1, MoCA 27 vs 27, NSE 17 vs 18. Adverse events similar

Notes

TBL critique: RCT with ITT, balanced groups, PaO2 measured at set times with clear separation. But open-label, 2 centres, liberal group had more PEEP, restrictive group sat at the top of its range (~10 kPa) and both groups were ~16–17 kPa at randomisation (~2.5 h post arrest) — consistent with EXACT (pre-hospital SpO2 90–94 vs 98–100, no difference); powered for an implausible 10% absolute reduction. Verdict: targeting PaO2 9–10 vs 13–14 kPa after OHCA does not affect mortality or neurological outcome. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/box-oxygen/

pages.title: API-CAT

props.v: Extended low-dose apixaban for cancer-associated VTE

pages.html:
Findings

Reduced-dose apixaban was non-inferior for recurrent VTE in extended treatment, with less bleeding

PopulationCancer-associated VTE, after 6 months of anticoagulation
InterventionApixaban 2.5 mg BD
ComparatorApixaban 5 mg BD
Outcome

Notes

Extended therapy beyond 6 months; reduced dose 2.5 mg BD

pages.title: CandiSep (Intensive Care Med 2022)
pages.html:
Findings

BDG-guided early antifungal therapy doubled antifungal use without improving 28-day mortality in at-risk septic patients

Population339 adults with sepsis within 24 h of onset and ≥1 risk factor for invasive candidiasis (TPN, abdominal surgery, >48 h antibiotics, CRRT); 18 German ICUs, 2016–19; open-label RCT; ~90% septic shock, APACHE II ~20, only ~14% had invasive candida infection
Intervention(1→3)-β-D-glucan (Fungitell) at enrolment and 24 h, results phoned within 24 h; antifungals started if any BDG ≥80 pg/mL
ComparatorStandard care — antifungals on culture-based diagnosis only (BDG taken but not reported)
Outcome28-d mortality 33.7% vs 30.5%, RR 1.10 (0.80–1.51), p=0.53; no subgroup benefit. Antifungal use 57.6% vs 27.5%, time to antifungal 1.1 vs 4.4 d; no difference in hospital/ICU LOS, ventilator- or vasopressor-free days; cost €4451 vs €2800

Notes

TBL critique: multicentre RCT, balanced groups, ITT, good separation in antifungal timing. But German-only, mortality far below the 49% assumed (underpowered), many protocol violations (per-protocol trend to benefit, NS), ~85% screened not enrolled, and only 15% had invasive candidiasis — so not a truly high-risk cohort. Verdict: author will not use BDG alone to trigger empirical antifungals within 24 h of sepsis; a higher cut-off (median BDG 170 in confirmed ICI vs 62 without) deserves study. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/candisep/

pages.title: CANVAS
pages.html:
Findings

Reduced CV events

PopulationT2DM high CV risk; N=10,142
InterventionCanagliflozin
ComparatorPlacebo
OutcomeMACE 26.9 vs 31.5/1000 pt-years

Notes

Amputation signal noted

pages.title: CAPE COD (NEJM 2023)
pages.html:
Findings

Hydrocortisone reduced 28-day mortality in severe community-acquired pneumonia

Population800 adults admitted to ICU with severe CAP (PSI >130, or mechanical ventilation, or HFNC FiO2 >0.5 with P/F <300, or high-flow mask); excluded septic shock on vasopressors at inclusion, influenza PCR+, aspiration, chronic steroids; 31 French ICUs, 2015–20; double-blind placebo-controlled RCT, stopped early (planned 1146)
InterventionHydrocortisone 200 mg/day IV started within ~20 h of admission, 4 days then 8- or 14-day taper by response (median 5 days)
ComparatorPlacebo, same schedule
Outcome28-d mortality 6.2% vs 11.9%, difference −5.6% (95% CI −9.6 to −1.7, p=0.006). 90-d mortality 9.3% vs 14.7%; intubation by day 28 in those not ventilated at baseline 19.5% vs 27.7%; new vasopressors 15.3% vs 25.0%. No increase in hospital-acquired infection (9.8% vs 11.1%) or GI bleeding; more insulin needed (35.5 vs 20 IU/day)

Notes

Adds to the steroid-in-pneumonia evidence base. TBL critique (George Walker): well-conducted blinded multicentre RCT, early initiation, severe cohort, minimal selection bias and only 6% open-label steroids; weaknesses are single country, only 72 deaths (fragility index 6), unstandardised microbiology (~45% no pathogen; that subgroup trended to more benefit), and the optimal steroid/regimen is unsettled. Verdict: strongly consider hydrocortisone in severe CAP admitted to ICU (started early, without shock, excluding influenza); REMAP-CAP steroid domain awaited. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/cape-cod/

pages.title: CESAR
pages.html:
Findings

ECMO referral improved survival without disability

PopulationSevere respiratory failure; N=180
InterventionECMO centre referral
ComparatorConventional care
OutcomeSurvival without disability 63% vs 47%

Notes

Referral trial, not pure ECMO trial

pages.title: CHEST
pages.html:
Findings

HES increased RRT requirement

PopulationICU patients; N=7000
InterventionHES
ComparatorSaline
OutcomeRRT 7.0% vs 5.8%

Notes

Helped kill starch fluids

pages.title: CLASSIC (NEJM 2022)

props.v: Restrictive vs standard IV fluids in septic shock

pages.html:
Findings

Restricting IV fluid after initial resuscitation did not change 90-day mortality in septic shock — but standard care was already fairly restrictive

Population1554 adults with septic shock (Sepsis-3, lactate >2, vasopressors) within 12 h of onset who had received ≥1 L fluid in the prior 24 h (median ~3 L); 31 ICUs in 8 European countries, 2018–21; open-label RCT; predicted mortality 40%, noradrenaline ~0.25 mcg/kg/min, GI source most common (~37%)
InterventionRestrictive IV fluid: 250–500 mL boluses only for severe hypoperfusion (lactate >4, MAP <50, mottling beyond kneecap, UO <0.1 mL/kg/h in first 2 h), replacement of overt losses, or to ensure 1 L/day intake if enteral route unavailable
ComparatorStandard care — no upper limit, fluids per SSC guidance, for losses and as maintenance
Outcome90-d mortality 42.3% vs 42.1%, adjusted difference 0.1% (−4.7 to 4.9), p=0.96. No difference in serious adverse events, days alive without life support, or days alive out of hospital. Cumulative day-5 fluid 8.8 vs 10.8 L (only ~2 L separation; ~800 mL difference in balance)

Notes

Meyhoff, NEJM 2022; N=1554, European. Median fluid difference ~2 L. TBL critique: multicentre, pre-published SAP, ITT, 0.6% loss to follow-up, a sick cohort. But unblinded, powered for a 7% absolute reduction, ~3 L given before randomisation and only ~2 L separation by day 5 (European standard care is already restrictive — bias to the null), GI-source predominance may have needed replacement fluid, and protocol violations in 21.5% vs 13% (no effect in per-protocol). Verdict: restriction is not superior for 90-d mortality, but the small standard-care balance means every patient still needs a deliberate fluid strategy including de-escalation/evacuation. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/classic-trial/

pages.title: CLIP-II (JAMA 2025)

props.v: Cryopreserved vs liquid-stored platelets for cardiac surgical bleeding

pages.html:
Findings

Cryopreserved platelets could not be shown non-inferior to liquid-stored platelets for bleeding after cardiac surgery and were associated with more blood loss, more transfusion and longer ICU stay

Population202 adults undergoing cardiac surgery at high bleeding risk (ACSePT ≥1) who actually received study platelets (388 randomised); 11 Australian hospitals 2021–24; double-blind non-inferiority RCT, 20% margin
InterventionCryopreserved (DMSO, −80 °C, up to 2-year shelf life) group O apheresis platelets reconstituted in ABO-matched plasma; median 2 units
ComparatorConventional liquid-stored platelets (22 °C, 5–7 day shelf life); median 1 unit
OutcomePrimary: 24-h chest-drain loss geometric mean 605 vs 535 mL, ratio 1.13 (95% CI 0.96–1.34), p=0.07 — upper CI exceeded 20% margin so non-inferiority NOT shown. Cryopreserved group: more total postoperative blood loss (ratio 1.31, 1.07–1.60), more BARC-4 bleeding (31.7% vs 12.3%), more RBC/FFP/cryo transfusion, longer time to drain removal, extubation, ICU and hospital stay, lower 24-h platelet count (103 vs 140); no difference in thrombosis, adverse events or survival

Notes

TBL critique: well-blinded, pragmatic, objective outcome, pre-specified SAP, per-protocol analysis concordant. Weaknesses: max 3 study units limits dose-response; more open-label platelets in cryo group (possible unblinding from DMSO smell); 'unit' equivalence questionable as cryo platelets differ in phenotype/recovery; cardiac surgery and Australia only. TBL verdict: where liquid-stored platelets are available they remain first line for cardiac surgical bleeding; cryopreserved platelets may still have a role where supply is limited (remote, military) but need further evaluation. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/clipii/

pages.title: CLOVERS (NEJM 2023)

props.v: Restrictive fluids + early vasopressors vs liberal fluids in sepsis

pages.html:
Findings

No difference in 90-day mortality between restrictive (early pressor) and liberal fluid strategies

Population1563 adults with sepsis-induced hypotension (SBP <100 or MAP <65 after ≥1 L IV fluid, <4 h from criteria, <3 L given; median 2 L pre-randomisation, SOFA 3.4, lactate 2.9); 60 US centres, mostly ED, 2018–22; open-label RCT stopped for futility at second interim (planned 2320)
InterventionRestrictive: no further fluid after 1–3 L (rescue 500 mL boluses for defined triggers), early noradrenaline ± second pressor to MAP ≥65 (peripheral infusion allowed, 40%) for 24 h
ComparatorLiberal: 2 L crystalloid at randomisation then 500 mL boluses for hypotension, lactate >4, UO <30 mL/h, HR >110; rescue vasopressors for defined triggers
OutcomeDeath before discharge home by day 90: 14.0% vs 14.9%, difference −0.9% (95% CI −4.4 to 2.6, p=0.61). No difference in organ-support-free, ventilator-free or ICU-free days, new intubation or ARDS; 3 vs 0 pressor extravasations (conservatively managed). Post hoc: more ICU admission in restrictive arm (70% vs 62% by day 7)

Notes

NEJM 2023; N=1563, US EDs, stopped for futility. Either approach acceptable in the first 24 h. TBL critique (George Walker): high internal validity, 97% protocol adherence, clear separation in first-24-h fluid, excellent safety reporting including peripheral pressors; but unblinded, single country, early cessation, ~25% eligible not enrolled (consent/MD refusal — selection bias), patients not that sick (SBP >90, low lactate, ~60% needed pressors), no dynamic fluid-responsiveness assessment and fixed volumes not weight-adjusted. Dovetails with CLASSIC (ICU-phase restriction). Verdict: both strategies safe — continue a multimodal, individualised assessment of fluid need vs vasopressor start; ARISE-FLUIDS and ANDROMEDA-SHOCK 2 to add more. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/clovers/

pages.title: Cochrane: doxapram for ventilatory failure in COPD exacerbations

props.v: Respiratory stimulants in hypercapnic COPD exacerbation

pages.html:
Findings

Doxapram marginally improved blood gases over the first few hours vs placebo; evidence vs NIV conflicting and no mortality difference — NIV has since superseded it

PopulationVentilatory failure from acute COPD exacerbation; 4 RCTs, N=176
InterventionDoxapram infusion
ComparatorPlacebo or NIV
OutcomeBlood gas deterioration marginally less vs placebo; vs NIV — conflicting; mortality no difference

Notes

Greenstone & Lasserson, Cochrane 1997 (search updated 2003, no new trials). 4 trials, N=176, variable quality. Early small study favoured NIV; a larger study in severe patients found doxapram equally effective on gases with frequent treatment failure. Place today: short-term bridge when NIV is unavailable or not tolerated

pages.title: Collaborative VLS (JAMA 2024)

props.v: Video vs direct laryngoscopy for intubation in theatre

pages.html:
Findings

Hyperangulated video laryngoscopy markedly reduced the number of intubation attempts and intubation failure compared with direct laryngoscopy in a high-acuity surgical population

Population8429 adults undergoing cardiac (75%), thoracic or vascular surgery needing single-lumen intubation; 80% ASA 4; 70% of first attempts by nurse anaesthetists/residents; single US centre (Cleveland Clinic) 2021–22; cluster-randomised multiple-crossover (22 theatres, weekly blocks), stopped early at 50% for efficacy
InterventionFirst attempt with hyperangulated GlideScope 3/4 blade with stylet
ComparatorFirst attempt with Macintosh direct laryngoscopy
OutcomePrimary: fewer intubation attempts with VL — proportional OR 0.20 (95% CI 0.14–0.28), p<0.001; first-pass success 98.3% vs 92.4%; intubation failure (device switch or >3 attempts) 0.27% vs 4.0%, RR 0.06 (0.03–0.14); dental/airway injury no difference RR 0.87 (0.48–1.58)

Notes

TBL critique: by far the largest VL vs DL trial, pragmatic, mix of operator experience, high-acuity (80% ASA 4) population. But single centre; three variables confounded (hyperangulated geometry, stylet, video) so may not generalise to standard-geometry VL or bougie use; training provided only for VL; number of attempts is not patient-centred and severe outcomes (aspiration, death) not assessed; stopped early for efficacy; devices supplied by manufacturer. TBL verdict: reaffirms video laryngoscopy as the default device where available. Sits alongside DEVICE (ED/ICU, first-pass 85% vs 70%). Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/collaborative-vls-video-vs-direct-laryngoscopy-for-endotracheal-intubation-in-the-ot/

pages.title: CRYOSTAT-2 (JAMA 2023)

props.v: Early empiric high-dose cryoprecipitate in major traumatic haemorrhage

pages.html:
Findings

Empiric early high-dose cryoprecipitate did not reduce 28-day mortality in major traumatic haemorrhage, with a possible harm signal in penetrating trauma

Population1604 trauma patients with active haemorrhage requiring major haemorrhage protocol activation, within 3 h of injury (ISS 29, 37% penetrating, 80% pre-hospital TXA); 26 major trauma centres UK (plus 49 US patients); open-label RCT, 1531 in ITT
Intervention3 pools cryoprecipitate (6 g fibrinogen) as early as possible (target <90 min; median 68 min, 85% received) plus standard MHP
ComparatorStandard MHP (1:1:1 with 2 pools cryo in later packs; 32% received cryo, median 120 min)
OutcomePrimary 28-d all-cause mortality: 25.3% vs 26.1%, OR 0.96 (95% CI 0.75–1.23, p=0.74). No difference at 6 h, 24 h, 6 or 12 months, transfusion needs, ICU/hospital LOS, or thrombotic events. Penetrating subgroup worse with cryo: 28-d mortality 16.2% vs 10%, OR 1.74 (1.2–2.51); blunt 30.4% vs 34.8%, OR 0.82 (0.62–1.09). Exploratory: cryo at 61–90 min OR 0.57 (0.38–0.87)

Notes

TBL critique (Celia Bradford): strong internal validity, severe-injury cohort, clinically meaningful outcome, but unblinded, 15% of intervention arm got no cryo and 9% of controls got early cryo, and empiric dosing means many without hypofibrinogenaemia were treated (potentially pro-inflammatory). Subgroup signals (blunt benefit/penetrating harm; '61–90 min Goldilocks window') are underpowered and hypothesis-generating. Verdict: does not support empiric cryo; use ROTEM/viscoelastic testing to guide product administration. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/early-and-empirical-high-dose-cryoprecipitate-for-hemorrhage-after-traumatic-injury/

pages.title: DEVICE (NEJM 2023)

props.v: Video vs direct laryngoscopy for emergency tracheal intubation of critically ill adults

pages.html:
Findings

Videolaryngoscopy markedly improved first-pass intubation success for critically ill adults, especially with less experienced operators, without changing peri-intubation complications

Population1417 critically ill adults intubated in 7 EDs and 10 ICUs in the USA (70% ED; mostly resident operators with median 50 prior intubations; 96% paralysed); pragmatic unblinded RCT stopped at first interim analysis for efficacy (planned 2000)
InterventionVideolaryngoscope on first attempt (brand/blade at operator discretion; 14% hyperangulated)
ComparatorDirect laryngoscope on first attempt
OutcomePrimary first-attempt success: 85.1% vs 70.8%, absolute difference 14.3% (95% CI 9.9–18.7, p<0.001). Severe complications (SpO2 <80%, SBP <65, new/increased pressors, arrest, death) 21.4% vs 20.9% (difference 0.5, −3.9 to 4.9). Benefit in all subgroups except operators with >100 prior intubations or <25% prior VL use

Notes

TBL critique (Jan Hansel): robust, pragmatic, minimal crossover; but open-label with a gameable non-patient-centred primary outcome, heterogeneous blade choice, and a skill mix skewed to VL-trained juniors (low overall first-pass success ~71–85%) — the effect trended to null in operators with >100 intubations, so findings may not transfer to anaesthetist-led systems. Verdict: VL improves first-pass success in the critically ill when intubated by relatively inexperienced operators; reinforces default VL (Macintosh-style or hyperangulated by patient) in ED/ICU. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/device/

InterventionDexamethasone 20 mg/d ×5 then 10 mg/d ×5
ComparatorStandard care
OutcomeVentilator-free days 12.3 vs 7.5; 60-day mortality 21% vs 36%

Notes

pages.title: DOSE VF (NEJM 2022)

props.v: Double sequential external defibrillation or vector-change defibrillation for refractory VF

pages.html:
Findings

DSED (and to a lesser extent vector change) doubled survival to discharge in refractory VF, but the trial stopped early with few events and the as-treated analysis was not significant

Population405 adults with out-of-hospital refractory VF/VT (persisting after 3 consecutive standard shocks), presumed cardiac cause; 6 paramedic services (~4000 paramedics) in Ontario, Canada; 3-arm cluster-randomised crossover trial (clusters switched every 6 months), stopped early for paramedic staffing shortages (planned 930)
InterventionVector-change (VC) defibrillation: all further shocks with anterior-posterior pads; or Double sequential external defibrillation (DSED): second defibrillator AP, anterior-lateral shock followed <1 s later by AP shock
ComparatorStandard anterior-lateral defibrillation for all shocks
OutcomePrimary survival to hospital discharge: DSED 30.4% vs standard 13.3%, RR 2.21 (95% CI 1.33–3.67, fragility index 9); VC 21.7% vs 13.3%, RR 1.71 (1.01–2.88, fragility index 1). DSED vs standard: VF termination 84.0% vs 67.6%, ROSC 46.4% vs 26.5% (aRR 1.72), mRS ≤2 27.4% vs 11.2% (aRR 2.21). VC: VF termination 79.9% vs 67.6%; ROSC and good neuro outcome NS. Treatment-received analysis: no significant difference for either (DSED RR 1.38, 0.90–2.11)

Notes

TBL critique (David Slessor): randomised cluster crossover with blinded outcome assessment and CPR quality monitoring; but stopped early with low event numbers (likely overestimates effect), pilot data pooled without pre-registration, outcomes only to discharge, possible bias from extra crews attending DSED arrests, baseline imbalances, and 10-min call-to-shock times may not generalise. Verdict: interpret with caution, further trials needed; if you cannot randomise, DSED or VC defibrillation is a reasonable option for refractory VF knowing the evidence is not definitive. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/dosevf/

Findings

ComparatorPlacebo
OutcomeHead-injury death 18.5% vs 19.8% (RR 0.94, 0.86–1.02); mild–moderate TBI RR 0.78

pages.title: EFFORT Protein (Lancet 2023)

props.v: High-dose vs usual-dose protein in critically ill patients at high nutritional risk

pages.html:
Findings

Higher protein dosing did not improve hospital discharge alive by 60 days and may have harmed patients with AKI or greater illness severity

Population1301 ventilated adults within 96 h of ICU admission with ≥1 nutritional risk factor (BMI ≤25 or ≥35, malnutrition, frailty CFS ≥5, sarcopenia); 85 ICUs in 16 countries; pragmatic registry-based RCT, clinicians unblinded, modified ITT
InterventionHigh protein ≥2.2 g/kg/day prescribed (delivered 1.6 g/kg/day) for up to 28 days
ComparatorUsual protein ≤1.2 g/kg/day prescribed (delivered 0.9 g/kg/day); energy not controlled
OutcomePrimary discharge alive from hospital by 60 d: 46.1% vs 50.2%, RR 0.91 (95% CI 0.77–1.07). 60-d mortality 34.6% vs 32.1%, RR 1.08 (0.92–1.26). No difference in MV duration, ICU or hospital LOS. Subgroups: high protein worse with baseline AKI (time-to-discharge HR 0.5, p=0.001; 60-d mortality HR 1.4, p=0.02) and SOFA ≥9 (HR 0.8, p=0.05)

Notes

TBL critique (Andrew Achilleos): large pragmatic multinational RCT with good separation, concealed allocation and objective primary outcome; limitations are unblinded clinicians, protocol/primary outcome amended during COVID (underpowered for original 60-d mortality), fixed dosing not adapted to illness phase, under-representation of trauma/surgery/burns, no functional/QoL outcomes, and AKI/SOFA harm signals from subgroups. Verdict: high-protein delivery for all ICU comers with nutritional risk is not warranted and may worsen outcomes in sicker patients or those with AKI; supports ESPEN's progressive 1.3 g/kg/day. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/effort/

pages.title: Continued enteral nutrition until extubation vs fasting — Ambroisie (Lancet Respir Med 2023)
pages.html:
Findings

Continuing enteral feeding right up to extubation is non-inferior to 6 h fasting with gastric suctioning for extubation failure, and shortens time from SBT to extubation and ICU discharge

Population1130 adults ventilated ≥48 h on prepyloric enteral feed ≥24 h at extubation decision; 22 French ICUs; open-label cluster-randomised (unit level) non-inferiority trial, margin 10%
InterventionContinue enteral nutrition unchanged until extubation; no gastric suctioning (median 375 mL feed in the 6 h before)
ComparatorStop feed 6 h before extubation with continuous gastric suctioning (maximal gastric vacuity)
OutcomeExtubation failure (reintubation or death) within 7 days: 17.2% vs 17.5%, absolute difference −0.4% (95% CI −5.2 to 4.5) — non-inferior; per-protocol 17.0% vs 17.9%. Pneumonia within 14 d 1.6% vs 2.5% (NS). SBT-to-extubation 2.0 h vs 17.6 h; SBT-to-ICU discharge 4.0 vs 6.6 d (HR 1.45, 1.19–1.77); ICU mortality 3.9% vs 6.8% (RR 0.56, 0.32–0.99); fewer hyper/hypoglycaemic episodes around extubation

Notes

Open-label; cluster design without crossover so centre practice differences are baked in (fasting-arm patients were older with weaker cough but got far more pre-extubation steroids, 48% vs 17%); reintubation and post-extubation nutrition left to clinicians; many excluded. TBL verdict: feed patients like these continuously up to extubation, but be cautious with ileus, high aspirates, prolonged ventilation or high risk of post-extubation oropharyngeal dysfunction. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/continued-enteral-nutrition-until-extubation-compared-with-fasting-before-extubation/

pages.title: FAKT (Acad Emerg Med 2021)

props.v: Fentanyl as co-induction with ketamine for ED RSI

pages.html:
Findings

Adding fixed-ratio fentanyl to ketamine/rocuronium for ED RSI did not improve haemodynamic stability overall — it traded hypertension for a near-doubling of post-induction hypotension

Population290 adults undergoing RSI in 5 EDs in New South Wales, Australia, 2018–20; double-blind placebo-controlled RCT; ~88% medical indications, 12% on vasopressors, baseline SBP ≥151 in ~27%
InterventionFentanyl 1 mcg per 1 mg ketamine (median 0.14 mg/kg) before ketamine (~1.3 mg/kg) and rocuronium 1.5 mg/kg
ComparatorEqual-volume saline placebo before the same ketamine/rocuronium
OutcomePrimary SBP outside 100–150 mmHg (or >10% change) within 10 min: 66% vs 65%, difference 1% (−10 to 12), p=0.86. Fentanyl: more hypotension SBP <100 (29% vs 16%, diff 13%, 3–23) but less hypertension >150 (55% vs 69%) and less tachycardia (48% vs 61%). First-pass success 92% both; hypoxia, cardiac arrest, ventilator-free days and 30-d mortality (19% vs 24%) NS

Notes

TBL critique: well-designed double-blind trial in the real ED setting, 96% primary-outcome data, standardised pre-intubation optimisation, biologically plausible separation. But a surrogate author-defined outcome, fixed fentanyl:ketamine ratio, additional sedation discouraged for 10 min, 82 patients excluded for clinician preference (equipoise), one region, night-time recruitment gaps. Verdict: fentanyl given in fixed ratio with ketamine may increase peri-intubation hypotension; dose induction and co-induction agents to the individual patient and their haemodynamic target. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/fakt/

pages.title: FAVoR — family voice recordings for delirium (Am J Crit Care 2025)

props.v: Non-pharmacological delirium prevention in ventilated patients

pages.html:
Findings

Scripted family-recorded voice messages were associated with slightly more delirium-free days in ventilated patients, but only after adjusted analysis — a cheap, low-risk adjunct that needs confirmation

Population178 mechanically ventilated adults within 48 h of intubation (dementia, imminent death, auditory hallucinations, profound deafness excluded); 9 ICUs in 2 US hospitals 2018–20; blinded-assessor RCT
InterventionFAVoR: 10 scripted 2-minute re-orientation messages recorded by a family member, played hourly by bedside speaker during waking hours (up to 8/day) for 5 days or until ICU discharge
ComparatorUsual care with an identical silent bedside speaker (to preserve blinding)
OutcomePrimary: delirium-free days (twice-daily CAM-ICU) 34.8% vs 33.7% — unadjusted p=0.07 (NS); Poisson regression adjusted for ICU LOS and dose heard p<0.001, SMD 0.354 (95% CI 0.182–0.608); dose–response r=0.62

Notes

TBL critique: simple, reproducible, low-cost intervention; published protocol, blinded CAM-ICU assessors, met recruitment target, dose–response signal. But significance emerged only in the adjusted model (unadjusted p=0.07) with just a 1.1% absolute difference; two US hospitals; small baseline imbalances (e.g. trauma ICU 17% vs 12%) could matter given the tiny effect; unclear whether the content or the familiar voice drives any benefit. TBL verdict: practical, low-cost addition to delirium prevention, but wants further data before widespread adoption. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/delirium-reduction-via-scripted-family-voice-recordings-in-critically-ill-patients-receiving-mechanical-ventilation/

pages.title: Ferrari — diuretics vs volume expansion in intermediate-high-risk PE (Lung 2022)

props.v: Fluid vs diuretic in acute PE with RV strain

pages.html:
Findings

A single 40 mg furosemide bolus was safe in intermediate-high-risk PE and sped BNP/sPAP/IVC improvement but did not change troponin kinetics or RV echo function

Population60 adults with CT-confirmed acute PE, RV dilatation (RV:LV >0.9) and dysfunction (TAPSE <16 mm, RV S' <10), troponin >70 ng/L and BNP >100 pg/mL, IVC ≥21 mm, no shock/thrombolysis/pressors; French centres (Cannes/Nice), 2016–19; unblinded phase 2 RCT
InterventionIV furosemide 40 mg bolus, repeated at 4 h if urine output <500 mL
ComparatorVolume expansion: 500 mL saline over 4 h then 1000 mL over 24 h
OutcomePrimary: time to troponin normalisation 76 vs 72 h, p=0.74 (no difference). Diuretics: faster BNP normalisation (56 vs 108 h, p=0.05), BNP fallen at 12 h in 47% vs 13%, greater fall in sPAP (−7 vs 0 mmHg) and IVC diameter at 4 h only; no difference in TAPSE or RV S'

Notes

TBL critique: addresses a real gap (ESC 2019 suggests 'cautious fluid' if CVP low) with detailed echo/biomarker data and no loss to follow-up, but methodology is thinly reported, it is a hypothesis-generating phase 2 trial with surrogate endpoints, and the claim that diuretics improve RV function isn't supported by the data; no cardiac output measured. Verdict: RV dysfunction is common in PE (33% here); diuretics will lower RA/PA pressure but outcome benefit unknown — author tailors preload (fluid or diuretic), contractility and afterload individually. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/ferrari/

pages.title: FLUID — hospital-wide Lactated Ringer's vs normal saline (NEJM 2025)

props.v: Balanced crystalloid vs saline across the whole hospital

pages.html:
Findings

Switching an entire hospital from saline to Lactated Ringer's did not significantly reduce 90-day death or readmission, though every point estimate favoured LR

Population43,626 index admissions (all-comers: 40% medicine, 42% surgery, 17% obstetrics; ~15% ICU) in 7 Ontario hospitals 2016–20; cluster-randomised crossover (two 12-week periods), administrative data, stopped early at 7 of 16 planned sites (COVID)
InterventionLactated Ringer's as default fluid hospital-wide (78% inventory adherence)
Comparator0.9% saline as default (94% adherence); >330,000 L used in total
OutcomePrimary: death or readmission within 90 days 20.3% vs 21.4%, adjusted difference −0.53% (95% CI −1.85 to 0.79); 90-day death 6.9% vs 7.6% (−0.26, −0.95 to 0.43); readmission 15.1% vs 15.4%; dialysis 0.5% vs 0.6%; hospital LOS 165 vs 172 h — all NS, all point estimates favour LR

Notes

TBL critique: huge pragmatic trial covering ED, ward, theatre and ICU with no missing primary data, avoiding the contamination problem of ICU-only fluid trials; ~6 L exposure per patient. Weaknesses: Ontario only; population not very sick (~25% elective surgery); LR adherence only 78% and measured at hospital not patient level; administrative data lose granularity; stopped early with fewer clusters; no economic analysis. TBL verdict: not compelling enough to change individual practice, but given the volumes used any small mortality reduction would matter; also argues for reducing overall fluid use. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/fluid-hospital-wide-lactated-ringers-versus-normal-saline/

pages.title: CARVE-AS

props.v: Carvedilol in new-onset uncomplicated ascites without high-risk varices

pages.html:
Findings

Carvedilol roughly halved ascites-related complications at 1 year and reduced AKI, variceal progression and need for paracentesis; mortality borderline lower

PopulationCirrhosis with new-onset uncomplicated ascites, no/low-risk varices; N=104
InterventionCarvedilol + standard care
ComparatorStandard care
OutcomeComplicated ascites (SBP/HRS-AKI/refractory/severe hyponatraemia) 38.5% vs 67.3% (p=0.03); AKI 34.6% vs 63.4%; 1-yr mortality 9.1% vs 24.2% (p=0.05)

Notes

Khajuria & Jindal, Am J Gastroenterol 2026; single-centre (India), open-label, N=104. Supports NSBB for portal hypertension itself, not just variceal prophylaxis. Small — needs multicentre confirmation. Dose not captured

pages.title: ICRAKI

props.v: Initial RRT modality in critically ill AKI: IHD vs CRRT

pages.html:
Findings

Stopped early: IHD failed to show non-inferiority to CRRT, with higher 90-day mortality. CRRT's advantage on the composite was not statistically significant.

PopulationCritically ill adults needing RRT for AKI, 38 French ICUs; N=554
InterventionInitial intermittent haemodialysis (IHD)
ComparatorInitial continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT)
Outcome90-day death 63.1% vs 53.5% (HR 1.30, 95% CI 1.04-1.63). MAKE90 78.1% vs 71.6%, not significant.

Notes

Stopped early (554 of 1,000 planned) after repeated interim analyses, so effect size may be overestimated. Mortality signal unexplained. CRRT looks safer start if ventilated or on vasopressors.

pages.title: ADVOR (NEJM 2022)

props.v: Acetazolamide added to loop diuretic in acute decompensated HF

pages.html:
Findings

IV acetazolamide improved successful decongestion at day 3; no difference in death/HF readmission at 3 months

Population519 adults hospitalised with acute decompensated HF, clinical fluid overload and raised BNP, not on SGLT2i/acetazolamide, SBP ≥90, eGFR ≥20; 2018–22; double-blind placebo-controlled RCT
InterventionIV acetazolamide 500 mg daily for 3 days (or until decongested) added to IV loop diuretic at double maintenance dose (median maintenance furosemide 60 mg)
ComparatorPlacebo + same loop diuretic protocol
OutcomeSuccessful decongestion at day 3: 42.2% vs 30.5%, RR 1.46 (95% CI 1.17–1.82), persisting to discharge; extra diuresis ~500 mL at 48 h and greater natriuresis on day 2; no difference in mortality, hospital LOS or adverse events; death/HF readmission at 3 months — no difference

Notes

Mullens, NEJM 2022. Basis for the 2026 ESC HF guideline class IIa for sequential nephron blockade (acetazolamide or HCTZ add-on) — see linked practice points. TBL mini-summary (George Walker): acetazolamide improves the surrogate of decongestion (vs ~15% decongested at 72 h across arms in DOSE) but patient-centred benefit is unproven; sits alongside DOSE (furosemide dosing) and ultrafiltration trials (UNLOAD, CARESS-HF) with mixed results. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/tbl-mini-advor/

pages.title: DIGIT-HF
pages.html:
Findings

Digitoxin added to standard care reduced composite of all-cause death or HF hospitalisation

PopulationSymptomatic HFrEF (LVEF ≤40%), NYHA II-IV; N≈1240, international multicentre
InterventionDigitoxin (target level 8-18 ng/mL) plus standard HF therapy
ComparatorPlacebo plus standard HF therapy
OutcomePrimary composite (all-cause death or HF hospitalisation) reduced, HR ~0.82; all-cause mortality alone not significantly different

Notes

Digitoxin is not widely available in the UK (digoxin used instead); Digitoxin is hepatic elimination, longer t1/2, more stable concentrations. Applicability to digoxin unproven.

pages.title: Anbarasan 2026 (magnesium and lactate clearance in sepsis)

props.v: Magnesium for lactate clearance in sepsis

pages.html:
Findings

Daily IV magnesium 2 g for 3 days sped lactate clearance and shortened ICU and hospital stay; no significant 28-day mortality difference

PopulationAdults with sepsis (Sepsis-3) and lactate >2 mmol/L; N=138
InterventionMgSO4 2 g IV over 2 h daily ×3 days
ComparatorSaline placebo
OutcomeTime to 20% lactate clearance 5.7 vs 8.5 h (−2.8 h, −3.7 to −2.0); ICU stay 8 vs 12 days; 28-day mortality — NS

Notes

Anbarasan et al, World J Crit Care Med 2026;15(2). Single-centre (AIIMS Jodhpur), triple-blind, N=138. Surrogate primary outcome; hypothesis-generating rather than practice-changing

pages.title: HALT-IT
pages.html:
Findings

No bleeding mortality benefit; VTE increased

PopulationAcute GI bleed; N=12,009
InterventionTXA
ComparatorPlacebo
OutcomeDeath from bleeding 3.7% vs 3.8%; VTE 0.8% vs 0.4%

Notes

Do not extrapolate CRASH-2 to UGIB

pages.title: HOPE

props.v: ACE inhibitor in high CV risk (Ramipril)

pages.html:
Findings

Ramipril reduced MI, stroke and CV death in high-risk patients without HF or low EF

PopulationAge ≥55 with vascular disease or diabetes + risk factor, no HF; N=9297
InterventionRamipril 10 mg
ComparatorPlacebo
OutcomeMI/stroke/CV death 14.0% vs 17.8%; all-cause death 10.4% vs 12.2%

Notes

Not an HF trial — vascular protection beyond BP lowering. Also cut new-onset diabetes

pages.title: HORIZON-RFT
pages.html:
Findings

Annual zoledronic acid after hip fracture reduced new clinical fractures and all-cause mortality

PopulationRecent hip fracture repair, age ≥50; N=2127
InterventionZoledronic acid 5 mg IV yearly
ComparatorPlacebo
OutcomeNew clinical fracture 8.6% vs 13.9%; all-cause death 9.6% vs 13.3%

Notes

Added Aug 2026; details re-entered from the published paper (Lyles, NEJM 2007) — check against your Word doc

pages.title: Fast vs slow correction of severe hypernatraemia (J Crit Care)
pages.html:
Findings

Early fast correction (>0.5 mmol/L/h) was associated with lower 30-day mortality and better hospital-free survival; no excess neurological harm

PopulationHospitalised adults with Na ≥155 mmol/L corrected within 24 h; N=430
InterventionFast correction >0.5 mmol/L/h
ComparatorSlow correction ≤0.5 mmol/L/h
Outcome30-day mortality HR 0.49; 30-day hospital-free survival HR 1.75

Notes
