Journal of Critical Care 2025, propensity-matched comparative effectiveness study (observational). The ≤0.5 mmol/L/h ceiling is extrapolated from paediatric data. A 2025 J Crit Care meta-analysis (12 studies, N≈10,900) pointed the same way for admission and severe hypernatraemia, OR ~0.5, but low-quality evidence. Source: NEJM Journal Watch (Winawer, Jan 2026) via Conan Liu

pages.title: HYPRESS
pages.html:
Findings

Hydrocortisone in severe sepsis without shock did not prevent progression to shock

PopulationSevere sepsis, not in shock; N=380
InterventionHydrocortisone 200 mg/day ×5 days then taper
ComparatorPlacebo
OutcomeSeptic shock within 14 days 21.2% vs 22.9%, NS

Notes

Keh, JAMA 2016; N=380, German. Steroids are for established shock, not prevention

pages.title: HYVET
pages.html:
Findings

Treating HTN in very elderly reduced death/stroke

PopulationAge >80 HTN; N=3845
InterventionIndapamide ± perindopril
ComparatorPlacebo
OutcomeAll-cause mortality 10.1% vs 12.4%

Notes

Killed nihilism in elderly HTN

pages.title: Meta-analyses: US- vs palpation-guided radial arterial cannulation (Am Heart J 2018; Indian J Anaesth 2025)
pages.html:
Findings

Ultrasound guidance improves first-pass success over palpation; check papers for exact figures

PopulationAdults needing radial arterial catheterisation; pooled RCTs
InterventionUltrasound-guided radial artery cannulation
ComparatorPalpation-guided cannulation
OutcomeHigher first-attempt success with US (pooled RR roughly 1.3-1.4); fewer attempts and less haematoma. Exact figures omitted.

Notes

Screenshot gave no figures. Verify first-pass success and complication data (haematoma, temporary occlusion) in both papers.

pages.title: IMPACT
pages.html:
Findings

Triple therapy reduced exacerbations

PopulationCOPD; N=10,355
InterventionTriple therapy
ComparatorDual therapy
OutcomeExacerbation rate lower

Notes

For frequent exacerbators

pages.title: INCEPTION (NEJM 2023)

props.v: ECPR vs conventional CPR for refractory OHCA

pages.html:
Findings

In a Dutch system with long low-flow times and many low-volume centres, an ECPR strategy did not improve neurologically intact survival over conventional CPR

Population134 adults aged 18–70 with witnessed OHCA, initial shockable rhythm, refractory after >15 min ALS; 10 cardiosurgical centres (8 low-volume) and 12 EMS services in the Netherlands, 2017–21; pragmatic unblinded RCT using local protocols. Only 46/70 (66%) of the ECPR arm were successfully cannulated (13 had ROSC first); median low-flow time 74 min
InterventionExtracorporeal CPR (bifemoral VA-ECMO) per local protocol
ComparatorConventional CPR until ROSC or death (3 crossovers to ECPR, all died)
OutcomePrimary survival with CPC 1–2 at 30 d: 20% (14/70) vs 16% (10/62), OR 1.4 (0.5–3.5), p=0.52. No difference at 3 or 6 months. ECPR: ICU admission 81% vs 36%; major bleeding 16% vs 3%; limb ischaemia 6%; ECMO circuit failure 13%. Survival among those actually cannulated 5/52 (9.6%)

Notes

TBL critique: multicentre, ITT, pre-published SAP, tested a real-world strategy in the intended population. But only 66% of the ECPR arm received it, control survival was double that assumed (16% vs 8%) so underpowered, unblinded teams could withdraw patients and decided on withdrawal of care (ECPR ICU stay median 1 day — detection bias?), no standard protocol, inexperienced centres, 16 min door-to-cannulation and 74 min low-flow (vs ~59 min in ARREST and PRAGUE), and ECPR-recipient survival (9.6%) far below ARREST (46%) or ELSO data. Verdict: ECPR is a systems intervention — this trial doesn't disprove benefit in mature high-volume systems with short low-flow times; the question is which systems can deliver it. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/inception/

pages.title: ISCHEMIA
pages.html:
Findings

Routine invasive strategy did not reduce major CV events

PopulationStable CAD, moderate/severe ischaemia; N=5179
InterventionInitial invasive strategy
ComparatorInitial conservative strategy
OutcomeCV death/MI/unstable angina/HF arrest: no significant reduction

Notes

Symptoms still matter; stable CAD ≠ ACS

pages.title: ISIS-2
pages.html:
Findings

Aspirin reduced vascular mortality after MI

PopulationSuspected MI; N=17,187
InterventionAspirin ± streptokinase
ComparatorPlacebo
OutcomeVascular death 9.4% vs 11.8%

Notes

Historic “give aspirin” trial

pages.title: Rivers EGDT
pages.html:
Findings

EGDT cut mortality in a single centre; MAP ≥65 was one of its targets

PopulationSevere sepsis or septic shock in ED; single centre; N=263
InterventionEGDT protocol (CVP, MAP ≥65, ScvO2 ≥70%)
ComparatorStandard therapy
OutcomeIn-hospital mortality 30.5% vs 46.5%

Notes

Not replicated by ProCESS, ARISE or ProMISe; origin of the MAP 65 convention

pages.title: RSI trial — ketamine vs etomidate, Casey (NEJM 2025)

props.v: Ketamine vs etomidate for emergency intubation

pages.html:
Findings

Ketamine increased peri-intubation cardiovascular collapse vs etomidate, especially in sepsis and APACHE II ≥20; no mortality difference

Population2365 critically ill adults (non-trauma) undergoing emergency intubation, 56% ED / 44% ICU; 46% sepsis, APACHE II 18, 21% on vasopressors; 14 sites at 6 US centres 2022–25; pragmatic open-label RCT under exception from consent, powered for 5.2% mortality difference
InterventionKetamine 1–2 mg/kg actual body weight (median 1.6 mg/kg; 25% exceeded 2 mg/kg)
ComparatorEtomidate 0.2–0.3 mg/kg actual body weight (median 0.28 mg/kg)
OutcomePrimary: in-hospital death by 28 d 28.1% vs 29.1%, ARD −0.8% (95% CI −4.5 to 2.9), p=0.65; sepsis subgroup 38.8% vs 38.2%. CV collapse (SBP <65, new/↑ pressors, arrest) 22.1% vs 17.0%, ARD 5.1 (1.9–8.3), driven by new/increased vasopressors 21.3% vs 15.9%; sepsis 30.6% vs 20.9% (ARD 9.7); APACHE II ≥20 31.4% vs 20.7% (ARD 10.7); SBP drop >30 mmHg 23.9% vs 14.7%; VT 1.0% vs 0.2%; vasopressors at 24 h 38.9% vs 42.3% (NS)

Notes

NEJM 2026;394:1608-20 (online Dec 2025), pragmatic multicentre US RCT. Overall NNH ~20; sepsis or APACHE II ≥20 NNH ~10, driven by new/increased vasopressors; SBP <65 and cardiac arrest not significantly different. Adrenal suppression was not measured — that concern about etomidate comes from older data. Unclear whether reduced-dose ketamine or delayed-sequence intubation is safer. (Merged from three duplicate entries). TBL critique (Chris Nickson, Dec 2025): high methodological rigour, >99% adherence and follow-up, individualised-treatment-effect modelling found no subgroup where either drug was safer. Weaknesses: unblinded (objective outcomes), underpowered for mortality differences <5%, composite driven by hypotension/vasopressor components, US-only and trauma excluded, NRB pre-oxygenation in half. Key dosing criticism: ketamine dosed by actual not ideal body weight in a cohort where half were overweight and a quarter got >2 mg/kg — many experts use ≤1 mg/kg (0.5 mg/kg IBW) in shock; no dose-response analysis. TBL verdict: no mortality difference; collapse more common with ketamine (22% vs 17%, NNH 20; NNH 10 in sepsis/APACHE >20) — reconsider practice, but the trial doesn't say whether low-dose ketamine, etomidate or DSI is safest. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/rsi-ketamine-or-etomidate-for-tracheal-intubation-of-critically-ill-adults/

pages.title: PREPARE II (fluid bolus during intubation) - inferred from The Bottom Line critique

props.v: Fluid bolus to prevent peri-intubation cardiovascular collapse

pages.html:
Findings

Fluid bolus reduced cardiovascular collapse in critically ill adults undergoing intubation

PopulationCritically ill adults undergoing emergency tracheal intubation in ICU; US centres
Intervention500 mL IV crystalloid bolus
ComparatorNo fluid bolus
Outcome

Notes

Unblinded; underpowered for mortality (powered for 5% absolute difference); composite driven by hypotension/vasopressor use; US-only, trauma excluded, mostly NRB pre-oxygenation

pages.title: LIBERATE-D (JAMA 2026)

props.v: Conservative (indication-triggered) vs scheduled thrice-weekly dialysis in AKI-D

pages.html:
Findings

An indication-triggered dialysis strategy in stable AKI-D roughly halved dialysis delivered and shortened time to renal recovery, with a possible (unadjusted-only) increase in recovery by discharge and no excess harm

Population218 haemodynamically stable adults with dialysis-requiring AKI (ATN) on intermittent HD, off vasopressors and ventilation, expected to need outpatient dialysis, baseline eGFR ≥15; 4 US centres, 2020–25; open-label RCT; 81–84% had been in ICU, ~8–11 days from first KRT; stratified by eGFR ≥45 vs <45
InterventionConservative strategy: dialyse only when a trigger is met — urea nitrogen >112 mg/dL (~40 mmol/L urea), K >6.0 (or >5.5 despite treatment), pH <7.15 (or <7.25 with HCO3 <14), hypoxaemia from volume overload (O2 >5 L/min) after diuretics, or clinician judgement
ComparatorScheduled thrice-weekly IHD with extra sessions as indicated; stop when CrCl >20 mL/min or UO >1 L/day (>2 L on diuretics) with falling creatinine
OutcomePrimary kidney recovery by discharge (alive and dialysis-free ≥14 days): 64.2% vs 50.5%, unadjusted OR 1.76 (1.02–3.03), p=0.04 — but prespecified adjusted OR 1.56 (0.86–2.84), p=0.15. Dialysis sessions/week 1.8 vs 3.1; dialysis-free days to day 28: 21 vs 5; time to recovery 2 vs 8.5 d (all p<0.001). 90-d mortality 14.7% vs 18.5% (NS); no difference in LOS or adverse events (hypotension, arrhythmia, arrest, urgent dialysis, electrolyte/acid–base)

Notes

TBL critique: multicentre RCT with clinically relevant outcomes and clear separation in dialysis frequency. But open-label, small (clinician non-equipoise limited recruitment; 909 screened) and underpowered for safety, enrolled only once off pressors/ventilator so not directly an ICU population, most 'conservative' dialysis decisions were clinician judgement rather than protocol triggers, and the primary outcome lost significance after prespecified adjustment. Verdict: adds weight to 'less is more' for KRT in stable AKI-D — fewer sessions and more dialysis-free days with possible better recovery and no excess adverse events — but needs a larger trial, and should not be extrapolated to KRT decisions in unstable ICU patients. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/liberate-d/

pages.title: LOVIT (NEJM 2022)

props.v: High-dose IV vitamin C in sepsis on vasopressors

pages.html:
Findings

High-dose IV vitamin C increased death or persistent organ dysfunction at 28 days in septic patients on vasopressors

Population863 adults with proven/suspected infection on vasopressor infusion, within 24 h of ICU admission; 35 ICUs in Canada, France and New Zealand, 2018–21; blinded placebo-controlled RCT; APACHE II 24, ~58% septic shock, ~46% on steroids
InterventionVitamin C 50 mg/kg IV every 6 h for 96 h (200 mg/kg/day, max 16 doses)
ComparatorMatching placebo (D5W or saline)
OutcomePrimary composite death or persistent organ dysfunction (vasopressors, IMV or new RRT) at day 28: 44.5% vs 38.5%, RR 1.21 (1.04–1.40), p=0.01 — HARM. 6-month death 45.8% vs 43.4%; no difference in organ-dysfunction-free days, SOFA, lactate, QoL, stage 3 AKI, haemolysis or hypoglycaemia

Notes

TBL critique: largest and best-designed trial on the topic — international, blinded, enrolled ~12 h after ICU admission, consistent harm signal across components of the composite and at 6 months. Weaknesses minor: no pathogen/ARDS data, high-income-country ICUs. Verdict: do not use high-dose vitamin C in sepsis on vasopressors; this should end the debate. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/lovit-trial/

pages.title: MacMillan 2015 (DDAVP systematic review)

props.v: Desmopressin to prevent rapid sodium correction in severe hyponatraemia

pages.html:
Findings

Proactive DDAVP (given with hypertonic saline from the start) was associated with the lowest rate of overcorrection; evidence mostly from the Sood series

PopulationSevere hyponatraemia at risk of ODS; observational studies
InterventionDDAVP (proactive / reactive / rescue)
ComparatorHypertonic saline alone
OutcomeOvercorrection lowest with proactive strategy (observational)

Notes

MacMillan, Am J Med 2015. Compared proactive, reactive and rescue strategies; all observational. Guidelines quoted: ≤8 mmol/L/day in high-ODS-risk patients

pages.title: Mark et al (Kaiser) — hyponatraemia correction rate

props.v: Fast vs slow correction of severe hyponatraemia

pages.html:
Findings

Faster 24-h sodium correction was associated with lower 90-day death/neurological events; ODS rare at every rate

PopulationED adults with Na ≤120 mEq/L; N=13,988; median age 74
InterventionMedium (8–12) or fast (>12 mEq/L per 24 h) correction
ComparatorSlow correction (<8 mEq/L per 24 h)
Outcome90-day death or delayed neuro event 21% overall; risk difference vs slow: medium −5.6% (−7.1 to −4.0), fast −9.0% (−11.1 to −6.9)

Notes

Annals of Internal Medicine 2026, retrospective EHR cohort (KP Northern California 2008–23). Challenges the ≤8 mEq/L/24h rule; confounding by indication possible (sicker patients may be corrected slower). Fast group had 1 day shorter LOS. Source: Conan Liu YouTube — 2026 Hospital Medicine Update / NEJM Journal Watch

pages.title: Meduri 2007 (methylprednisolone in early severe ARDS)

props.v: Prolonged low-dose methylprednisolone in early ARDS

pages.html:
Findings

Methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg/day started within 72 h improved lung injury score, reduced ventilation duration and ICU mortality

PopulationEarly (<72 h) severe ARDS; N=91
InterventionMethylprednisolone 1 mg/kg/d infusion, tapered over ~4 weeks
ComparatorPlacebo
OutcomeDay-7 ≥1-point LIS improvement 69.8% vs 35.7%; ICU mortality 20.6% vs 42.9%

Notes

Chest 2007; N=91, single-group of centres, small. Infusion with slow taper; infection surveillance mandatory. Foundation for the 'early, prolonged, low-dose' steroid approach

pages.title: MENDS2

props.v: Dexmedetomidine vs propofol in septic mechanically ventilated adults

pages.html:
Findings

No difference in delirium/coma-free days, ventilator-free days, 90-day mortality or cognition

PopulationSeptic adults on MV needing sedation; N=422
InterventionDexmedetomidine
ComparatorPropofol
OutcomeDelirium/coma-free days 10.7 vs 10.8; 90-day mortality 38% vs 39%, NS

Notes

Hughes, NEJM 2021; N=422. Both light-sedation strategies equivalent in sepsis; choose on haemodynamics/cost

pages.title: MIDAS
pages.html:
Findings

Adding midodrine did not change pressor weaning time, ICU LOS, or readmission

PopulationSeptic shock, weaning off vasopressors
InterventionMidodrine + vasopressor
ComparatorVasopressor alone
OutcomeNo difference in wean time, ICU LOS, or readmission

pages.title: MINT (NEJM 2023)

props.v: Transfusion threshold in MI with anaemia

pages.html:
Findings

A liberal Hb ≥100 g/L transfusion strategy did not significantly reduce 30-day MI or death in anaemic MI patients, but every endpoint trended to benefit and cardiac death was significantly lower — restrictive thresholds may harm after MI

Population3504 adults with STEMI/NSTEMI (56% type 2 MI, 42% type 1) and Hb <100 g/L; mean age 72; 144 sites in 6 countries 2017–23; open-label RCT
InterventionRestrictive: transfuse permitted <80 g/L, strongly recommended <70 g/L or uncontrolled angina (mean day-3 Hb 89; 0.7 units/patient)
ComparatorLiberal: transfuse to keep Hb ≥100 g/L until discharge/30 days (mean day-3 Hb 105; 2.5 units/patient)
OutcomePrimary: MI or death at 30 days 16.9% restrictive vs 14.5% liberal, RR 1.16 (95% CI 1.00–1.35), imputed RR 1.15 (0.99–1.34), p=0.07; cardiac death 5.5% vs 3.2%, RR 1.74 (1.26–2.40); death 9.9% vs 8.3%; MI 8.5% vs 7.2%; heart failure 5.8% vs 6.3% (NS). Subgroups favouring liberal: type 1 MI (18.2% vs 13.8%, RR 1.32) and heart failure/low EF (RR 1.25)

Notes

TBL critique: largest trial on the question (4× all prior trials combined), pragmatic protocols, good separation, 98% follow-up, blinded adjudication of MI. Weaknesses: unblinded, 86% adherence to liberal arm, no screening data, no multiplicity adjustment, counter-intuitive subgroups (type 1 MI and HF benefited most). Fragility index −2 and Bayesian re-analysis (91–99.8% probability restrictive is harmful). TBL verdict: adopt an Hb target of 100 g/L after MI, especially type 1 MI, while individualising for volume status and bleeding. Contrasts with TRICC/TRISS/TRICS-III in non-MI populations. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/mint-restrictive-or-liberal-transfusion-strategy-in-myocardial-infarction/

pages.title: RECOVERY
pages.html:
Findings

Dexamethasone reduced 28-day mortality in ventilated/oxygen-requiring patients, not in those without oxygen. Hydroxychloroquine, lopinavir-ritonavir, azithromycin and convalescent plasma showed no benefit.

PopulationHospitalised COVID-19 patients, UK; dexamethasone comparison N=6425
InterventionDexamethasone 6 mg daily for up to 10 days
ComparatorUsual care
Outcome28-day mortality 22.9% vs 25.7% overall; ventilated 29.3% vs 41.4% (RR 0.64); oxygen only 23.3% vs 26.2%; no oxygen 17.8% vs 14.0% (no benefit)

Notes

Multiple randomised comparisons in one platform trial. Later arms: tocilizumab and baricitinib reduced mortality; Dexamethasone dose and other arms published separately.

pages.title: CRASH-2 / WOMAN pooled analysis (TXA timing)
pages.html:
Findings

TXA benefit is time-dependent; no benefit after 3 hours, and CRASH-2 bleeding deaths rose when given late

PopulationBleeding trauma and postpartum haemorrhage patients; pooled N=40,138
InterventionTranexamic acid, by time since injury or birth
ComparatorPlacebo
OutcomeCRASH-2 bleeding death RR: ≤1h 0.68; 1-3h 0.79; >3h 1.44. ~10% of survival benefit lost per 15 min delay

Notes

Time-to-treatment subgroup finding, not easily retested. Later trials enrolled early, so 3 hours is a ceiling, not a target. Start clock at injury or birth. ESO 2023: within 3h. NICE NG39: not >3h unless hyperfibrinolysis.

pages.title: SUBCUT-HF II

props.v: Home subcutaneous furosemide via wearable pump

pages.html:
Findings

Early discharge with SC furosemide minipump gave more days alive and out of hospital at 30 days than usual IV inpatient care

PopulationHeart failure needing ongoing parenteral diuretics; N=172, 20 UK hospitals
InterventionEarly discharge with wearable minipump delivering SC furosemide at home (n=92)
ComparatorUsual inpatient IV diuretic care (n=80)
Outcome30-day days alive and out of hospital: 4 extra days with early discharge

Notes

UK multicentre, 20 hospitals, published in JACC. Home treatment by patient or carer with clinical review every 3 days. Screenshot cuts off before safety and secondary outcomes.

pages.title: NAVIGATE (BJA 2025)

props.v: Prophylactic intermittent NIV on general wards for mild ARF

pages.html:
Findings

Scheduled 2-hourly NIV cycles on general wards reduced progression of mild ARF to severe ARF but did not change intubation, length of stay or mortality

Population523 adults on non-ICU wards with mild acute respiratory failure (SpO2 <92% on air or P/F <300, new consolidation/atelectasis, mild hypercapnia pH <7.35 or signs of distress; COPD exacerbation and P/F <200 excluded); 11 hospitals in Italy, Greece, Kazakhstan, 2012–2023; open-label RCT; median FiO2 0.30, ~30% on room air
InterventionEarly NIV: 2-h cycles every 8 h on the ward (90% CPAP, median PEEP 7, oronasal mask) for ≥24 h up to 12 d, SpO2 >92% target
ComparatorUsual care (oxygen, diuretics, antibiotics); NIV only once the primary endpoint was reached
OutcomeProgression to severe ARF (P/F <200, pH <7.30, or clinical signs of severe distress on O2) during admission: 18.5% vs 28.3% (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.48–0.90; ARR 9.8%, NNT 11). No difference in hospital LOS (10 vs 9 d), 28-d mortality (11% vs 11%), 90-d mortality, ICU admission (8.3% vs 7.0%) or intubation (6.8% vs 6.2%). Prolonged NIV needed in 11% vs 23%

Notes

Composite primary outcome driven mainly by the subjective 'clinical signs of respiratory distress' in an unblinded trial where usual-care clinicians could only start NIV after declaring the endpoint met (incentive to call it, especially in HF/COPD/COVID patients). Designed before HFNO became routine; 11-year recruitment; monitoring not standardised. TBL verdict: may be safe and feasible with low nurse ratios, but given the soft outcome and no effect on hard endpoints the reviewer is unconvinced of cost-effectiveness and will keep low-/high-flow oxygen first line. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/navigate/

pages.title: NICE-SUGAR
pages.html:
Findings

Tight glucose control increased mortality

PopulationICU patients; N=6104
InterventionTarget 4.5–6.0
ComparatorTarget <10.0
Outcome90-day mortality 27.5% vs 24.9%

Notes

Target ~6–10 mmol/L (≈140–180 mg/dL), not “normal”. Severe hypoglycaemia (≤2.2 mmol/L) 6.8% vs 0.5%. Overturned Van den Berghe (NEJM 2001), a single-centre surgical ICU study that had shown benefit from tight control

pages.title: NICO (JAMA 2023)

props.v: Withholding intubation in comatose acute poisoning (GCS ≤8)

pages.html:
Findings

In uncomplicated poisoning with GCS ≤8, withholding intubation and monitoring closely for up to 4 h was safe and cut ICU admissions and ICU length of stay

Population225 adults with suspected acute poisoning (alcohol/drugs/medication) and GCS ≤8 without immediate need for intubation, respiratory failure, shock, seizure/brain injury or cardiotoxic drug ingestion; 20 EDs + 1 ICU in France; open-label RCT
InterventionConservative airway strategy: intubation withheld for 4 h unless emergency criteria developed (regurgitation, seizure, shock, respiratory distress); GCS every 30 min — 18% intubated
ComparatorUsual care, intubation at physician discretion — 60% intubated
OutcomePrimary hierarchical composite (in-hospital death, ICU LOS, hospital LOS): win ratio 1.85 (95% CI 1.33–2.58, p<0.001). No deaths in either arm. Median ICU LOS 0 vs 24 h; hospital LOS 22 vs 37 h. ICU admission 40% vs 66% (OR 0.23); pneumonia 7% vs 15% (OR 0.43, 0.18–1.05)

Notes

TBL critique: patient-centred outcomes and appropriate hierarchical composite, pragmatic design; but unblinded, result driven by ICU LOS (no deaths, 1 in 5 never admitted to ICU — French ambulances take intubated patients straight to ICU), wide exclusions limit generalisability, 13% first-pass failure in controls. Verdict: GCS <8 from simple poisoning with no other adverse features — close monitoring and delaying intubation for up to 4 h reduces ICU admissions and LOS. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/nico-noninvasive-airway-management-of-comatose-patients-with-acute-poisoning/

pages.title: NIV vs HFNC after extubation in obesity — Hernández (AJRCCM 2025)

props.v: Prophylactic post-extubation support in obese patients

pages.html:
Findings

Prophylactic NIV did not significantly reduce 7-day reintubation versus HFNC in obese patients at intermediate risk of extubation failure, though a Bayesian re-analysis and prior trials suggest probable benefit

Population144 adults with BMI ≥30 ventilated >24 h, passed a 30-min PS 7 SBT, ≤2 high-risk features (PaCO2 >45 at end of SBT excluded); 49/144 had COVID-19; 2 Spanish ICUs 2020–21; open-label RCT powered for a 14% ARR
InterventionHumidified NIV (bilevel, median IPAP 4 above EPAP 8) continuously for 48 h, no HFNC allowed
ComparatorHFNC (median 60 L/min) for 48 h, no NIV rescue allowed
OutcomePrimary: reintubation within 7 days 23.6% vs 33.3%, ARD 9.7% (95% CI −4.9 to 24.4), adjusted OR 0.71 (0.32–1.58) — NS; ICU LOS longer with NIV (11 vs 6.5 days, p=0.02); intolerance 15% vs 4% (p=0.049); no difference in post-extubation respiratory failure, VAP, mortality. Post hoc Bayesian: RR 0.65 (CrI 0.44–0.96), probability of benefit 0.87–0.99

Notes

TBL critique: concealed allocation, 7-day (not 3-day) reintubation endpoint, detailed titration protocols, no crossover. Weaknesses: two Spanish ICUs, a third COVID-19 patients, open-label, baseline imbalances from simple randomisation (NIV group had more COPD, longer ventilation; HFNC group more airway/secretion problems), optimistic 14% ARR assumption so underpowered, only PEEP 8. TBL verdict: given the signal here, in HIGH-WEAN, EXTUB-OBESE and Thille's post-hoc work, continue prophylactic NIV in selected obese patients after extubation. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/niv-vs-hfnc-to-prevent-re-intubation-in-patients-with-obesity/

pages.title: OPTIMA-CC
pages.html:
Findings

Norepinephrine favoured over epinephrine — epinephrine caused more refractory shock, lactic acidosis and tachycardia (trial stopped early)

PopulationCardiogenic shock
InterventionEpinephrine
ComparatorNorepinephrine
OutcomeRefractory shock more common with epinephrine; stopped early

Notes

No MAP/CI difference

pages.title: OSCILLATE
pages.html:
Findings

HFOV increased mortality in moderate-severe ARDS

PopulationModerate-severe ARDS
InterventionHFOV
ComparatorConventional low tidal volume ventilation
OutcomeIn-hospital mortality ↑; stopped early

Notes

Trial stopped early for harm

pages.title: OVISS (JAMA 2025)
pages.html:
Findings

Earlier vasopressin at lower noradrenaline doses (0.2 mcg/kg/min) associated with reduced mortality (OR 0.81)

Population14,453 adults with a first episode of Sepsis-3 septic shock already on noradrenaline, from four US EHR datasets (UCSF derivation n=3608; MIMIC-IV, eICU-CRD and UPMC validation n=10,845); vasopressin started in 20–48% in usual care; retrospective reinforcement-learning study, no prospective arm
InterventionReinforcement-learning policy: initiate vasopressin when the model recommends — typically at noradrenaline ~0.2 mcg/kg/min, SOFA ~7, lactate ~2.5, ~4 h after shock onset
ComparatorObserved clinician practice: vasopressin at noradrenaline ~0.37 mcg/kg/min, SOFA ~9, lactate ~3.6, ~5 h
OutcomeConcordance with the model policy associated with lower in-hospital mortality, aOR 0.81 (95% CI 0.73–0.91), and less RRT (aOR 0.47) but not less ventilation (aOR 1.0); E-value 1.46; model outperformed simple lactate/MAP/noradrenaline thresholds; reward function sensitive to weighting

Notes

TBL critique (Hrishee Vaidya, Jun 2025): open datasets, heterogeneous validation cohorts, thorough sensitivity analyses, mortality-focused evaluation. Major caveats: retrospective observational — needs prospective validation before any causal claim; model lacked echo, fluid responsiveness, CRT; only decision was start/not start, no dosing; Fitted-Q-iteration can pick never-seen actions; weighted importance sampling biases evaluation toward easy cases; arbitrary reward weights (small changes abolished the benefit); 'data available: no'. TBL verdict: supports earlier vasopressin as a hypothesis worth a real-world trial with human oversight, not a practice mandate. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/oviss/

pages.title: PADIS Guidelines
pages.html:
Findings

Recommend dexmedetomidine or propofol over benzodiazepines

PopulationMechanically ventilated ICU patients
InterventionDexmedetomidine/propofol
ComparatorBenzodiazepines
OutcomeDelirium ↓, MV duration ↓

Notes

Society guideline, not a single RCT — better delirium rate & ↓ MV duration

pages.title: PARADIGM-HF
pages.html:
Findings

Sacubitril/valsartan superior to enalapril

PopulationHFrEF; N=8442
InterventionSacubitril/valsartan
ComparatorEnalapril
OutcomeCV death/HF admission 21.8% vs 26.5%

Notes

Major modern HF trial

pages.title: PATCH-Trauma (NEJM 2023)
pages.html:
Findings

More survivors at 28 days but no difference in 6-month survival with favourable functional outcome

Population1310 adults with major trauma at high risk of trauma-induced coagulopathy (COAST score >3), TXA within 3 h of injury; 36 trauma services in Australia, NZ and Germany (advanced trauma systems); ISS 29, 92% blunt, 34% GCS <9; double-blind placebo-controlled RCT
InterventionTXA 1 g IV over 10 min pre-hospital, then 1 g over 8 h
ComparatorMatching placebo bolus and infusion
OutcomePrimary survival with favourable functional outcome (GOS-E ≥5) at 6 months: 53.7% vs 53.5%, RR 1.00 (95% CI 0.90–1.12). Mortality 24 h 9.7% vs 14.1% (RR 0.69, 0.51–0.94); 28 d 17.3% vs 21.8% (RR 0.79, 0.63–0.99); 6 months 19% vs 22.9% (RR 0.83, 0.67–1.03). Vascular occlusive events 23.6% vs 19.7% (RR 1.20, 0.97–1.48), NS

Notes

NEJM 2023; N=1310, Aus/NZ/Germany. Extra survivors often severely disabled; no thrombotic signal. TBL critique (Celia Bradford): blinded, concealed, ITT plus per-protocol, severe-injury cohort in advanced trauma systems with a functional (not just mortality) outcome; weaknesses are ~13% loss to follow-up, a third with protocol deviations (16% open-label TXA in hospital), 6-month follow-up may be too short for neuro recovery, and underpowered subgroups. Verdict: supports CRASH-2 that pre-hospital TXA cuts early haemorrhagic death, at the cost of more survivors with poor neurological outcome — on balance continue pre-hospital TXA in major trauma at risk of coagulopathy. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/patch-2/

pages.title: PEITHO
pages.html:
Findings

Less collapse, more major bleeding/ICH; no mortality benefit at 30 days

PopulationIntermediate-risk PE; N=1005
InterventionTenecteplase + anticoag
ComparatorAnticoag alone
OutcomeDeath/collapse 2.6% vs 5.6%; ICH 2.0% vs 0.2%

Notes

Why thrombolysis is not routine in submassive PE

pages.title: PILOT (NEJM 2022)

props.v: SpO2 targets in mechanically ventilated patients

pages.html:
Findings

Lower, intermediate and higher oxygen-saturation targets in ventilated patients produced no difference in ventilator-free days or mortality

Population2541 ventilated adults (ED/ICU) in a single US centre (Nashville), 2018–21; cluster-randomised cluster-crossover (targets switched every 2 months), unblinded; COVID patients excluded from primary analysis
InterventionLower SpO2 target 90% (88–92%) or intermediate 94% (92–96%)
ComparatorHigher SpO2 target 98% (96–100%)
OutcomeDays alive and ventilator-free at 28 d: 20 vs 21 vs 21 (lower vs intermediate OR 0.95, 0.79–1.13; intermediate vs higher OR 1.00, 0.84–1.19). 28-d in-hospital mortality 34.8% vs 34.0% vs 33.2%, NS. Achieved mean SpO2 93/94/97%, FiO2 0.31/0.37/0.45

Notes

TBL critique: huge single-centre dataset (~8 million SpO2 readings) with excellent separation and adherence; cluster-crossover limits selection bias. But single centre, no surgical patients, respiratory-therapist-delivered; lower-target group never really reached 90% (a third hit FiO2 0.21) so beta error possible; primary outcome can't distinguish death from 28 d of ventilation. Verdict: large benefit from any particular target is very unlikely; author will keep an intermediate target (~94%) and be less aggressive about driving FiO2 down in the absence of hyperoxia. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/pilot-draft/

pages.title: PLATO
pages.html:
Findings

Ticagrelor superior to clopidogrel

PopulationACS; N=18,624
InterventionTicagrelor
ComparatorClopidogrel
OutcomeCV death/MI/stroke 9.8% vs 11.7%

Notes

Modern ACS antiplatelet evidence

pages.title: POISE-3
pages.html:
Findings

TXA reduced major bleeding; non-inferior for cardiovascular events (margin narrowly met)

PopulationNon-cardiac surgery with bleeding/CV risk; N=9535
InterventionTXA 1 g at start and end of surgery
ComparatorPlacebo
OutcomeComposite bleeding 9.1% vs 11.7% (HR 0.76); CV composite 14.2% vs 13.9% (non-inferior)

Notes

Devereaux, NEJM 2022; N=9535. Safety margin was close — not blanket reassurance in very high CV-risk patients

pages.title: PRECIOSA
pages.html:
Findings

Long-term albumin did not significantly improve 1-year transplant-free survival (HR 0.80) but reduced SBP and hepatorenal syndrome

PopulationCirrhosis with ascites and acute decompensation; N=410
InterventionAlbumin 20% 1.5 g/kg every 10 days up to 12 months + standard care
ComparatorStandard care
Outcome1-year transplant-free survival HR 0.80 (0.58–1.10), NS; SBP OR 0.28 (0.09–0.86); HRS OR 0.24 (0.09–0.64)

Notes

Phase III, 14 countries, N=410, EASL 2025 topline. Albutein 20% 1.5 g/kg every 10 days for up to 12 months. Positive secondary outcomes, neutral primary — contrast with ANSWER (positive, open-label) and ATTIRE (negative inpatient)

pages.title: PREOXI (NEJM 2024)
pages.html:
Findings

Preoxygenating with NIV halved peri-intubation hypoxaemia and reduced cardiac arrest compared with an oxygen mask, without increasing aspiration

Population1301 critically ill adults undergoing emergency intubation with sedation and laryngoscopy in 17 ICUs and 7 EDs (USA) 2022–23, not already on positive pressure; pragmatic unblinded RCT; median APACHE II 17, 27% on vasopressors, ~24% on HFNO beforehand
InterventionPreoxygenation with NIV (BiPAP) for ≥3 min: FiO2 1.0, EPAP ≥5, IPAP ≥10, RR ≥10; 88% also received positive-pressure ventilation between induction and laryngoscopy
ComparatorOxygen mask: non-rebreather (88%) or bag-mask without manual ventilation; 31% ventilated between induction and laryngoscopy
OutcomeSpO2 <85% between induction and 2 min after intubation: 9.1% vs 18.5%, difference −9.4% (95% CI −13.2 to −5.6), NNT 11. SpO2 <80%: 6.2% vs 13.2%; <70%: 2.4% vs 5.7%. Peri-intubation cardiac arrest 0.2% vs 1.1% (difference −0.9%, −1.8 to −0.1). Aspiration 0.9% vs 1.4%; new vasopressors 17.2% vs 17.8%. All subgroups favoured NIV (obesity, hypoxaemic failure, high APACHE)

Notes

Pragmatic, concealed, multicentre RCT with near-complete data and independent assessment. Weaknesses: unblinded; hypoxaemia is a surrogate (though it tracks arrest); 20% excluded as already on NIV; the control arm (NRB without ventilation during apnoea) is not usual UK/Australian practice, where BVM with PEEP valve, Mapleson C or HFNO are common — external validity to those settings is unclear; plastic/cost of a BiPAP circuit for minutes. TBL verdict: thought-provoking and practice-challenging; reviewer more likely to use BiPAP for critically ill intubations. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/preoxi-trial-noninvasive-ventilation-for-preoxygenation/

pages.title: Pro-MEDIC (Intensive Care Med 2022)
pages.html:
Findings

Prophylactic melatonin 4 mg nightly did not reduce delirium or improve sleep in ICU patients

Population847 adults with expected ICU stay >72 h, enrolled within 48 h of admission; 12 Australian ICUs, 2016–19; double-blind placebo-controlled RCT; ~81% emergency admissions, ~9% CAM-ICU positive at baseline, PRE-DELIRIC ~44
InterventionEnteral melatonin 4 mg at 21:00 for 14 nights or until ICU discharge
ComparatorIdentical-appearing placebo
OutcomePrimary: delirium-free assessments 79.2% vs 80.0%, p=0.55. Delirium prevalence 35.1% vs 32.7%; delirium/coma-free days 64.2% vs 67.6%; no difference in sleep quantity/quality (>40% poor in both), antipsychotic use (21% vs 19%), ICU/hospital LOS or 90-d mortality (15.5% vs 15.6%). No adverse events; serum melatonin 19.4 vs <0.1 ng/mL confirmed delivery

Notes

TBL critique: the largest and best trial on a widely used drug — multicentre, double-blind, pre-published SAP, local data for power, minimal loss to follow-up, confirmed drug levels, meticulous confounder data. Weaknesses: large exclusions (~10% not expected to be assessable), slightly more missed assessments than planned, single 4 mg immediate-release dose (authors argue 10 mg gives supratherapeutic daytime levels). Verdict: high-quality evidence that 4 mg melatonin, though safe, does not affect delirium and did not even improve sleep — reconsider routine use. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/pro-medic/

pages.title: ProCESS

props.v: Protocolised early goal-directed therapy in septic shock (US)

pages.html:
Findings

Neither EGDT nor a simpler protocol beat usual care for 60-day mortality; usual care had caught up with Rivers' bundle

PopulationED patients with septic shock (refractory hypotension or lactate ≥4) after ≥1 L fluid; N=1341
Intervention6-h EGDT protocol (CVC, ScvO2 ≥70%, transfusion/dobutamine)
ComparatorProtocol-based standard care, or usual care
Outcome60-day in-hospital mortality 21.0% vs 18.2% vs 18.9% (NS); 90-day and 1-year mortality NS; RRT 3.1% vs 6.0% vs 2.8%

Notes

Yealy, NEJM 2014; 31 US EDs, three-arm (EGDT / protocol-based standard care without CVC-ScvO2 targets / usual care). All arms got early antibiotics and ~2 L fluid before randomisation — the real lesson is that early recognition, antibiotics and fluids were already standard. More RRT in the protocol-standard arm. Together with ARISE and ProMISe (same era, MAP 65 target as a marker of modern care) this closed the EGDT chapter

pages.title: PRODEX / MIDEX

props.v: Dexmedetomidine vs propofol / midazolam for ICU sedation

pages.html:
Findings

Dexmedetomidine non-inferior for time at target sedation, with shorter ventilation (vs midazolam) and better arousability/communication

PopulationAdults needing >24 h light–moderate sedation; N=500 (MIDEX) + 498 (PRODEX)
InterventionDexmedetomidine
ComparatorMidazolam (MIDEX) or propofol (PRODEX)
OutcomeTime at target RASS non-inferior; MV duration 123 vs 164 h vs midazolam (p=0.03), NS vs propofol

Notes

Jakob, JAMA 2012; two parallel trials. More hypotension/bradycardia with dexmedetomidine. MENDS2 (2021) now its own entry

pages.title: PROGRESS
pages.html:
Findings

Perindopril-based BP lowering (± indapamide) reduced recurrent stroke; benefit driven by the combination arm

PopulationPrior stroke or TIA, hypertensive or not; N=6105
InterventionPerindopril ± indapamide
ComparatorPlacebo
OutcomeStroke 10% vs 14% over 4 years (RRR 28%)

Notes

Not an HF trial — secondary stroke prevention. Perindopril alone had little effect; combination cut stroke by ~43%

pages.title: ProMISe

props.v: Early goal-directed therapy in septic shock (UK)

pages.html:
Findings

EGDT did not improve 90-day mortality vs usual care in UK EDs, and cost more

PopulationED patients with early septic shock (refractory hypotension or lactate >4) within 6 h; N=1260
Intervention6-h EGDT (CVC, ScvO2 ≥70%, protocolised fluids/pressors/dobutamine/transfusion)
ComparatorUsual resuscitation
Outcome90-day mortality 29.5% vs 29.2% (RR 1.01, 0.85–1.20); ICU admission 88% vs 74%; cost higher

Notes

Mouncey, NEJM 2015; 56 NHS hospitals. Higher baseline mortality (29%) than ARISE/ProCESS. EGDT arm: more ICU admissions, more organ support, worse SOFA at 6 h, higher cost. Completed the trio that showed modern usual care (early antibiotics, fluids, MAP 65) matches the Rivers protocol without CVC-guided targets

pages.title: PROPHY-VAP (Lancet Respir Med 2024)

props.v: Single-dose prophylactic ceftriaxone to prevent early VAP after acute brain injury

pages.html:
Findings

A single early dose of ceftriaxone halved early VAP in ventilated brain-injured patients and was associated with fewer ventilator days, less overall antibiotic exposure and lower mortality

Population319 analysed (345 randomised) brain-injured adults (TBI, stroke, SAH) with GCS ≤12, intubated <12 h and expected to be ventilated >48 h; 9 ICUs in 8 French university hospitals; double-blind placebo-controlled RCT; no SDD used
InterventionSingle dose ceftriaxone 2 g IV within 12 h of intubation
ComparatorPlacebo (saline)
OutcomePrimary early VAP (day 2–7): 14% vs 32%, HR 0.60 (95% CI 0.38–0.95). All VAP by day 28: 20% vs 36%; ventilator-free days 9 vs 5; antibiotic-free days 21 vs 15; 28-d mortality 15% vs 25%. No safety signal (C. difficile 1 vs 2; 1 MRSA and 1 ESBL both in placebo arm)

Notes

TBL critique (Andrew Achilleos): well-executed blinded multicentre RCT, pragmatic criteria, sensible agent (long half-life, broad cover), and total antibiotic exposure fell — the most deliverable form of VAP prevention compared with SDD or AMIKINHAL. Limitations: VAP diagnosis is inaccurate and confounded by neurogenic fever, adjudication committee not independent, blinding done by neighbouring-unit nurses, single country, secondary outcomes (including the 10% mortality difference, implausibly large for the intervention alone) not powered, and resistance outcomes underpowered. Verdict: a short course of prophylactic antibiotic in patients intubated for acute brain injury is beneficial and safe — practice-changing. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/prophy-vap-ceftriaxone-to-prevent-early-ventilator-associated-pneumonia/

pages.title: PROPPR
pages.html:
Findings

1:1:1 (plasma:platelets:RBC) improved haemostasis (86% vs 78%) and reduced exsanguination at 24h vs 1:1:2

PopulationSevere trauma requiring massive transfusion
Intervention1:1:1 ratio
Comparator1:1:2 ratio
OutcomeHaemostasis 86% vs 78%; mortality — no difference

Notes

No 24-hour or 30-day mortality difference; 1:1:1 preferred for massive transfusion

pages.title: PROSEVA
pages.html:
Findings

Proning massively reduced mortality

PopulationSevere ARDS; N=466
InterventionEarly prolonged proning
ComparatorSupine ventilation
Outcome28-day mortality 16.0% vs 32.8%

Notes

One of ICU's best interventions

pages.title: PROTECTION (NEJM 2024)

props.v: Amino acid infusion to prevent AKI after cardiac surgery

pages.html:
Findings

Perioperative IV amino acids reduced biochemical AKI after cardiac surgery with bypass, driven mainly by stage 1 AKI, without changing RRT, mortality or long-term renal function

Population3511 adults undergoing elective cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass (eGFR ≥30, not dialysis-dependent) expected to stay ≥1 night in ICU; 22 centres in Italy, Croatia, Singapore 2019–24; double-blind placebo-controlled RCT (identical bottles)
InterventionBalanced amino acid solution (Isopuramin 10%) 2 g/kg/day (max 100 g/day) from CVC insertion in theatre for up to 72 h or ICU discharge; median 30 h, 126 g
ComparatorRinger's lactate at the same rate (40 mL/h)
OutcomeKDIGO AKI (creatinine criteria) within 7 d: 26.9% vs 31.7%, RR 0.85 (95% CI 0.77–0.94, p=0.002), NNT 21. Stage 1 24.4% vs 28.1% (RR 0.87); stage 3 1.6% vs 3.0% (RR 0.56, 0.35–0.87). RRT 1.4% vs 1.9% (RR 0.73, 0.43–1.22, NS). No difference in ICU/hospital LOS, mortality to 180 d, or creatinine at 30/90/180 d. Benefit also in ≥75-year-olds (39% vs 49%). No excess adverse events

Notes

Large, blinded, well-powered trial with concealed allocation, ITT and minimal loss to follow-up, and a plausible mechanism (afferent arteriolar dilatation, reduced tubuloglomerular feedback). Weaknesses: biomarker primary outcome; most of the effect in stage 1; patient-centred outcomes (RRT, death) not significantly different; no economic analysis; creatinine identical at 30–180 d suggests no lasting renal benefit. TBL verdict: proves amino acids lower creatinine-defined AKI, but without a change in RRT or long-term function the reviewer will not adopt it yet. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/protection-amino-acids-for-kidney-protection/

pages.title: PRORATA
pages.html:
Findings

PCT guidance reduced antibiotic exposure without worsening 28-day mortality; non-inferiority shown

PopulationICU adults with suspected bacterial infection; N=621
InterventionPCT-guided antibiotic start/stop
ComparatorStandard care (guideline-based antibiotics)
OutcomeAntibiotic-free days 14.3 vs 11.6; 28-day mortality 21.2% vs 20.4%; 60-day mortality 30.0% vs 26.1%

Notes

Multicentre French ICUs; 60-day mortality numerically higher with PCT. Open-label; protocol often overridden.

pages.title: Quantitative pupillometry thresholds after OHCA — BOX substudy (Intensive Care Med 2024)
pages.html:
Findings

Automated pupillometry thresholds of qPLR <4% or NPi ≤2 from 24 h onward identify poor neurological outcome after OHCA with no false positives, but miss most poor-outcome patients

Population710 comatose adult OHCA survivors of presumed cardiac cause (91% shockable, mean ROSC 21 min) in 2 Danish cardiac arrest centres 2017–21; prospective diagnostic-accuracy substudy of BOX; clinicians blinded to pupillometry; WLST no earlier than 72 h
InterventionAutomated pupillometry (NPi-200) at admission, 24, 48 and 72 h: quantitative PLR <4% and Neurological Pupil index ≤2 (lowest of two eyes); NSE >60 µg/L at 48 h; combined sequential testing in patients with motor score ≤3 at ≥72 h
ComparatorReference standard: CPC ≥3 at ≥90 days, assessed blinded
OutcomeqPLR <4% from 24–72 h and NPi ≤2 from admission–72 h predicted unfavourable outcome with 0% false-positive rate (PPV 97–100%). Sensitivity poor: 26% (qPLR) and 12% (NPi) at 24 h. NSE >60 µg/L: 2% FPR, 39% sensitivity (0% FPR in persistently comatose); combined with 48-h pupillometry sensitivity rose to 50–55%. 1-year death 93–100% with abnormal pupillometry at 48 h vs ~35%

Notes

Large, blinded, prospectively defined substudy with complete follow-up. Limits: observational, two centres, 82% male, 9% excluded for missing data, no ambient-light control, NPi is proprietary and the algorithm unpublished, sensitivity low even with NSE. TBL verdict: these thresholds give objective support within multimodal neuroprognostication; a normal result does not predict good outcome. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/pupillometry-thresholds-for-neuroprognostication/

pages.title: 65 trial

props.v: Permissive hypotension (MAP 60-65) in vasodilatory shock, age 65+

pages.html:
Findings

Lower MAP target in older patients was not harmful, with less vasopressor exposure. MAP 65 is a target, not a hard threshold.

PopulationICU patients aged 65+ with vasodilatory hypotension
InterventionPermissive hypotension, MAP 60-65 mmHg
ComparatorUsual care (higher MAP target)
Outcome90-day mortality similar between groups; fewer vasopressor-days with permissive target

Notes

Slide cites SSC update (March 2026) supporting ~60 mmHg in age 65+; verify against the guideline. MAP <60 raises kidney/brain dysfunction risk; <50 high ischaemia risk.

pages.title: Quetiapine vs haloperidol for hyperactive delirium — Zakhary (Neurocrit Care 2024)

props.v: Antipsychotic choice in ICU hyperactive delirium

pages.html:
Findings

Low-dose quetiapine and haloperidol produced similar response rates in ICU hyperactive delirium; secondary advantages for quetiapine were small, soft and from a tiny single-centre trial

Population100 adult ICU patients with hyperactive delirium (CAM-ICU + RASS), mean APACHE II 24, at a single Egyptian centre (Alexandria) April–July 2023; AKI, liver failure, prior antipsychotics, stroke and head injury excluded; double-blind (over-encapsulated) RCT, no placebo arm
InterventionQuetiapine 25–50 mg/day PO/NG titrated to agitation
ComparatorHaloperidol 1–2 mg/day PO/NG titrated to agitation
OutcomeResponse (≥50% fall in DRS-R-98 to ≤12 without relapse): 96% vs 88% (p=0.61). Quetiapine: shorter ICU stay (10.1 vs 11.7 d, p=0.018), lower day-7 DRS-R-98 (5 vs 9), more 'sleep hours' (nurse-estimated). No difference in hospital LOS, ventilation (36% vs 40%), ICU mortality (16% vs 28%) or in-hospital mortality (16% vs 32%). QT prolongation 3 vs 1; EPS 3 in haloperidol arm

Notes

Double-blind, ITT, clinically relevant question. Major weaknesses: n=100, single centre, no placebo despite ~90% response in both arms, very low haloperidol dose (1–2 mg/day vs median 8.3 mg/day in AID-ICU), opaque power calculation designed to detect a large effect (a null result is not equivalence), unclear handling and scoring of ventilated patients, DRS-R-98 only on days 3 and 7, AKI/liver failure excluded, thin adverse-event reporting. TBL verdict: either drug is a reasonable option; haloperidol stays first line (AID-ICU signal of benefit), quetiapine for those with contraindications such as parkinsonism. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/quetiapine-versus-haloperidol-for-delirium/

pages.title: RACE II

props.v: Lenient vs strict AF rate control

pages.html:
Findings

Lenient rate control non-inferior

PopulationPermanent AF; N=614
InterventionLenient HR <110
ComparatorStrict HR <80 rest
OutcomeComposite CV outcome 12.9% vs 14.9%

Notes

Supports HR <110 if stable/asymptomatic

pages.title: Rafat 2014 (reactive DDAVP)

props.v: Desmopressin given once sodium is rising too fast

pages.html:
Findings

DDAVP cut urine output, raised urine osmolality and halted the correction rate — but about half of patients had already overcorrected by the time it was given

PopulationHyponatraemia with rapid correction in ICU
InterventionDDAVP after overcorrection detected
ComparatorBefore DDAVP (within-patient)
OutcomeNa correction rate ~1 → 0 mmol/L/h (p<0.001); urine output 700 → <100 ml/h; ~50% still overcorrected

Notes

Rafat, Crit Care Med 2014; observational. Shows reactive DDAVP works physiologically but needs vigilance to catch the water diuresis in time — the argument for a proactive clamp in high-risk patients

pages.title: RALES
pages.html:
Findings

Spironolactone reduced mortality

PopulationSevere HFrEF; N=1663
InterventionSpironolactone
ComparatorPlacebo
OutcomeMortality 35% vs 46%

Notes

Landmark MRA trial

pages.title: RE-LY
pages.html:
Findings

Dabigatran 150mg reduced stroke vs warfarin

PopulationAF; N=18,113
InterventionDabigatran
ComparatorWarfarin
OutcomeStroke/SEE lower with 150mg

Notes

110mg had less bleeding

pages.title: RECOVERY
pages.html:
Findings

Dexamethasone reduced mortality in hypoxic COVID

PopulationHospitalised COVID; N=6425
InterventionDexamethasone
ComparatorUsual care
OutcomeMortality 22.9% vs 25.7%; ventilated 29.3% vs 41.4%

Notes

Harm/no benefit if no oxygen

pages.title: REDUCE
pages.html:
Findings

5 days steroids non-inferior to 14 days

PopulationAECOPD; N=314
InterventionPrednisolone 5 days
ComparatorPrednisolone 14 days
OutcomeRe-exacerbation similar

Notes

Supports short courses

pages.title: REMAP-CAP corticosteroid domain (Intensive Care Med 2025)
pages.html:
Findings

7-day hydrocortisone did not improve 90-day mortality in severe CAP needing organ support; signal towards harm

Population658 adults (536 hydrocortisone, 122 control) in ICU within 48 h of presentation with severe CAP needing respiratory (IMV 40%, NIV 15%, HFNC ≥30 L/min 36%) or vasopressor support; COVID-19 and chronic steroid users excluded; 101 sites in 18 countries (57% Australia) 2018–23; open-label Bayesian adaptive platform trial, 3045 further platform patients informed covariate adjustment
InterventionHydrocortisone 50 mg IV 6-hourly for 7 days, no taper (99% received; median 7 days)
ComparatorNo corticosteroid (23% received steroids for clinical indications, median 4 days)
OutcomePrimary: 90-day mortality 15.0% vs 9.8%, adjusted OR 1.56 (95% CrI 0.80–3.31), probability of benefit 10%; consistent across shock/influenza strata (ORs 1.52–1.63); ICU mortality 9.3% vs 5.7%; cardiovascular support 2 vs 3 days (shorter); organ-support-free days 24 vs 22.5 (probability of superiority 85%); SAEs 1.3% vs 0.8%

Notes

Contrasts with CAPE COD. Imbalanced randomisation (536 vs 122). Influenza strata: OR ~1.5 with wide intervals — too few patients to answer the steroids-in-flu question (your 13/09 query). TBL critique (Louise Connell, Sep 2025): robust adaptive design, international, 97.7% follow-up, 99% fidelity. Weaknesses: open-label; randomisation imbalance from a data-coding error and sites without a control arm; 23% control contamination with steroids; hydrocortisone group slightly older/sicker (lower P/F, more diabetes); tiny influenza strata. TBL verdict: routine 7-day hydrocortisone does not improve and may worsen mortality in ICU-level severe CAP, challenging current guideline recommendations. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/remap-cap-corticosteroids/

pages.title: REMAP-CAP (influenza antiviral domain)
pages.html:
Findings

Oseltamivir met the predefined threshold for inferiority vs no antiviral in critically ill influenza; signal of harm

PopulationCritically ill adults with influenza; N≈442
InterventionOseltamivir (5 or 10 days)
ComparatorNo antiviral
Outcome90-day mortality higher with oseltamivir (>19% vs ~14%); probability of harm >96%

Notes

From your to-add list (13/09). Preprint, not yet peer-reviewed; only ~124 true no-antiviral controls. Steroids-in-influenza question still open

pages.title: RENOVATE (JAMA 2024)

props.v: HFNO vs NIV in acute respiratory failure

pages.html:
Findings

HFNO was non-inferior to NIV for intubation or death at 7 days across most causes of ARF, with better comfort; data remain thin for COPD, immunocompromised and ACPO patients

Population1766 adults with ARF (SpO2 <90%/PaO2 <60 on air + distress or RR >25) in 33 Brazilian hospitals 2019–23, in 5 groups: non-immunocompromised hypoxaemic (n=485), immunocompromised (50), COPD with respiratory acidosis (77), acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (272), COVID-19 (882); Bayesian adaptive non-inferiority RCT (margin OR 1.55 ≈ 10% absolute) with dynamic borrowing across groups
InterventionHigh-flow nasal oxygen: 45 L/min (30 in COPD) titrated to 60, FiO2 from 0.5; NIV rescue allowed in COPD/ACPO
ComparatorNIV via face mask: IPAP 12–16/EPAP 4 (COPD) or IPAP 12–14/EPAP 8 (others), up to 20/12; 24-h use encouraged
OutcomeIntubation or death within 7 days: 39.0% vs 38.1% overall. Non-inferiority met in non-immunocompromised, COPD, ACPO and COVID-19 groups; futility stopped the immunocompromised group early. No difference in 28/90-d mortality, ventilator-free or ICU-free days; comfort better with HFNO. Crossover HFNO→NIV 23% in COPD

Notes

Large pragmatic trial with clear protocols and low crossover overall. Weaknesses: unblinded with clinician-decided intubation; generous 10% non-inferiority margin that includes death; small COPD and immunocompromised groups with wide intervals; 23% COPD crossover to NIV; NIV delivered only 10–13 h/day; sensitivity analysis without borrowing gave different results in small groups. TBL verdict: HFNO is a reasonable first-line option in selected ARF, especially when NIV tolerance is poor, while the trajectory is established. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/renovate-high-flow-vs-niv/

pages.title: REVISE (NEJM 2024)

props.v: Stress ulcer prophylaxis in ventilated patients

pages.html:
Findings

Daily IV pantoprazole reduced clinically important upper GI bleeding in ventilated patients by 2.5 percentage points with no effect on mortality, VAP or C. difficile

Population4821 adults ventilated in ICU and expected to remain ventilated beyond the next day (ventilated <72 h; excluded if on acid suppression for bleeding risk or on DAPT/anticoagulant+antiplatelet); 68 hospitals in 8 countries 2019–23; double-blind placebo-controlled RCT; ~70% on vasopressors, ~90% enterally fed, ~50% steroid-exposed
InterventionIV pantoprazole 40 mg daily until extubation (median 5 d)
ComparatorMatched IV saline placebo
OutcomeClinically important upper GI bleeding by 90 d: 1.0% vs 3.5%, absolute difference 2.5% (95% CI 1.6–3.3), HR 0.30 (0.19–0.47), NNT 40. 90-d mortality 29.1% vs 30.9% (HR 0.94, 0.85–1.04). Patient-important bleeding 1.5% vs 4.2%. VAP 23.2% vs 23.8%, C. difficile 1.2% vs 0.7%, new RRT 6.1% vs 6.0% — all NS. No subgroup effect (incl. APACHE II ≥25)

Notes

Large, blinded, well-powered RCT with excellent internal validity, pragmatic criteria and concordant patient-important secondary outcome; benefit seen despite 90% enteral feeding. Weaknesses: efficacy was not contentious after SUP-ICU/PEPTIC (a harm-powered design might have been more useful); ~50% steroid exposure; silent on non-ventilated patients and oral PPI. TBL verdict: prescribe IV pantoprazole for all ventilated patients unless contraindicated, even when fed, for the duration of ventilation — safe, no mortality or infective signal. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/revise-stress-ulcer-prophylaxis-during-invasive-mechanical-ventilation/

pages.title: Rivers EGDT
pages.html:
Findings

Protocolised sepsis resuscitation reduced mortality

PopulationSevere sepsis/septic shock; N=263
InterventionEGDT
ComparatorStandard care
OutcomeIn-hospital mortality 30.5% vs 46.5%

Notes

Historically important, now superseded

pages.title: ROCKET-AF
pages.html:
Findings

Rivaroxaban non-inferior to warfarin

PopulationAF; N=14,264
InterventionRivaroxaban
ComparatorWarfarin
OutcomeStroke/SEE non-inferior

Notes

Higher-risk AF cohort

pages.title: ROSE
pages.html:
Findings

No mortality difference with early NMB in moderate-severe ARDS; stopped for futility

PopulationModerate-severe ARDS
InterventionEarly NMB (cisatracurium)
ComparatorUsual care ± NMB as needed
OutcomeMortality — no difference; stopped for futility

Notes

Conflicts with ACURASYS — usual-care sedation had become lighter

pages.title: SAFE
pages.html:
Findings

Albumin no better than saline overall

PopulationICU patients; N=6997
Intervention4% albumin
ComparatorSaline
Outcome28-day mortality 20.9% vs 21.1%

Notes

Subgroups debated

pages.title: SALSA

props.v: Rapid intermittent bolus vs slow continuous infusion of 3% saline in symptomatic hyponatraemia

pages.html:
Findings

Both strategies were effective and safe; boluses gave faster initial correction with fewer patients needing re-lowering of sodium; no difference in the primary overcorrection outcome

PopulationSymptomatic hyponatraemia, Na ≤125 mmol/L; N=178
InterventionRapid intermittent bolus 3% saline
ComparatorSlow continuous infusion 3% saline
OutcomeOvercorrection 17.2% vs 24.2% (ARD −6.9%, −18.8 to 4.9; p=0.26); relowering treatment needed less often with bolus

Notes

Baek, JAMA Intern Med 2020; 3 Korean hospitals, open-label, mean age 73, Na ≤125. Bolus 2 ml/kg over 20 min q6h PRN vs infusion 0.5–1 ml/kg/h. Overcorrection = >12 mmol/24 h or >18/48 h. No DDAVP used. Supports the fixed small-bolus approach in the European guideline

pages.title: SAVE
pages.html:
Findings

No difference between supraglottic airway and ETT for ROSC

PopulationOut-of-hospital cardiac arrest
InterventionSupraglottic airway
ComparatorEndotracheal intubation
OutcomeROSC — no significant difference

pages.title: Thille 2022 (PS vs T-piece SBT, high-risk)

props.v: Spontaneous breathing trial method in high-risk extubation

pages.html:
Findings

Pressure-support SBT led to more successful extubations than T-piece in patients at high risk of reintubation; no difference in reintubation

PopulationVentilated >24 h, high reintubation risk (age >65 or chronic cardiac/lung disease); N=969
Intervention30-min pressure-support SBT (PS 8, PEEP 0)
Comparator1-h T-piece SBT
OutcomeSuccessful extubation 77.7% vs 72.9%; reintubation at 7 days 14.9% vs 13.6%, NS

Notes

JAMA 2022; N=969. Pairs with Subirà 2019 (own entry) — together they favour an easier (PS) SBT

pages.title: SEPSISPAM
pages.html:
Findings

No mortality difference between higher (80–85) and lower (65–70) MAP targets

PopulationSeptic shock
InterventionMAP target 80–85
ComparatorMAP target 65–70
OutcomeMortality — no difference; AFib ↑ with higher target

Notes

Higher target increased AFib; chronic-HTN subgroup needed less RRT with higher target

pages.title: SETPOINT2 (JAMA 2022)

props.v: Early vs standard tracheostomy in severe stroke

pages.html:
Findings

Early tracheostomy in severe stroke did not improve 6-month survival without severe disability, and a third of the standard-timing group never needed one

Population382 ventilated adults with severe non-traumatic stroke (AIS 28%, ICH 41%, SAH 31%), SETscore >10 and clinician-judged need for tracheostomy; 26 neuro-ICUs in Germany and USA, 2015–20; RCT with blinded outcome assessment; ~50% decompressive craniectomy, median GCS 6–7
InterventionEarly percutaneous tracheostomy within 5 days of intubation (median day 4; 95% received it)
ComparatorStandard timing — tracheostomy from day 10 (median day 11; only 67% received it: 22% extubated, 11% died)
OutcomePrimary mRS 0–4 at 6 months: 43.5% vs 47.1%, difference −3.6% (−14.3 to 7.2), aOR 0.93 (0.60–1.42). mRS 0–3: 24.3% vs 19.6% (aOR 1.48, 0.89–2.48); 6-month death 35.0% vs 29.6%; ICU discharge 17 vs 19 d; end of ventilation 14 vs 11 d — all NS. Tracheostomy-related adverse events ~17% in both

Notes

TBL critique: multicentre, ITT, good separation and adherence, 3.4% loss to follow-up. But mRS 0–4 is a very wide 'good' outcome (mRS 4 = dependent), no weaning protocol, 49% of patients from 4 centres, a poor-prognosis cohort (only ~10% reached mRS 0–2), and mixed stroke types with differing trajectories; 1 in 3 standard-arm patients avoided a procedure with ~20% complication rate. Verdict: no evidence early tracheostomy beats standard timing in severe stroke, and it may subject patients to an unnecessary procedure. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/setpoint2/

pages.title: Shared decision-making in code status discussions — Becker (NEJM Evidence 2025)

props.v: Structured shared decision-making for DNACPR discussions

pages.html:
Findings

A structured shared decision-making approach with prognostic information and a decision aid increased DNR preferences and reduced decisional conflict without increasing patient distress

Population2663 general medical inpatients needing a code-status discussion (cognitive impairment and predicted futility — GO-FAR ≥14 or CFS ≥7 — excluded), under 206 residents; 6 Swiss teaching hospitals 2019–23; cluster RCT randomising residents
Intervention1-h SDM workshop (CPR survival <20%, 40% neurological deficit), CLEAR checklist (engage, learn/inform, explore preferences, assess/document, review advance directives), visual decision aid, ≥3 supervised discussions
Comparator1-h generic communication-skills session, no checklist or decision aid
OutcomePrimary: DNR preference after discussion 50.0% vs 37.2%, adjusted RR 1.37 (95% CI 1.25–1.50); 30-day DNR status 48.0% vs 36.7%; decisional conflict score 14.4 vs 21.8 (adjusted difference −7.06, −9.43 to −4.68); patient involvement (SDM-Q-9) 76.6 vs 58.6; fewer chose ventilation (65.7% vs 72.0%) or ICU (79.1% vs 82.5%); no difference in distress, LOS or 30-day mortality

Notes

TBL critique: pragmatic cluster RCT in real-world wards, randomised residents to avoid contamination, co-designed with patients, fidelity checks, 30-day data. Limitations: Swiss teaching hospitals and three languages only; open-label with possible Hawthorne effect; sanitised images; no data on actual CPR attempts or survival; questionnaire within 24 h; unclear durability of resident behaviour. TBL verdict: an adaptable model for ward and ICU — a short workshop plus visual aids may improve goals-of-care conversations, especially for junior clinicians. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/shared-decision-making-in-resuscitation-decisions/

pages.title: SMART

props.v: Balanced crystalloids vs saline in ICU

pages.html:
Findings

Balanced crystalloids reduced major adverse kidney events at 30 days

PopulationICU adults; N=15,802
InterventionBalanced crystalloid (LR / Plasma-Lyte)
Comparator0.9% saline
OutcomeMAKE30 14.3% vs 15.4% (OR 0.91, 0.84–0.99)

Notes

Semler, NEJM 2018; N=15,802, single-centre cluster-crossover. Small absolute difference; biggest in sepsis. Drove the shift to balanced fluids

pages.title: SOLVD
pages.html:
Findings

Enalapril reduced mortality

PopulationSymptomatic HFrEF; N=2569
InterventionEnalapril
ComparatorPlacebo
OutcomeMortality 35.2% vs 39.7%

Notes

Foundation of HFrEF therapy

pages.title: Sood 2013 (DDAVP + hypertonic saline)

props.v: Proactive desmopressin with 3% saline for severe hyponatraemia

pages.html:
Findings

Combining DDAVP with a hypertonic saline infusion from the outset achieved a mean 5.8 mmol/L rise in 24 h with no overcorrection in any patient

PopulationSevere hyponatraemia, Na <120 mmol/L; N=24
InterventionDDAVP 2 mcg IV q8h + 3% saline infusion
ComparatorNone (case series)
OutcomeMean Na rise 5.8 mmol/L at 24 h; overcorrection 0/24

Notes

Sood, Sterns et al, Am J Kidney Dis 2013; uncontrolled case series from Rochester, NY. Target <6 mmol/L in first 24 h. Adrogué-Madias predicted the change well once the kidneys were clamped. One pulmonary oedema requiring diuresis. Basis of the 'proactive DDAVP' strategy

pages.title: SPRINT
pages.html:
Findings

SBP <120 reduced CV events and mortality

PopulationHigh-risk HTN, no diabetes; N=9361
InterventionSBP target <120
ComparatorSBP target <140
OutcomePrimary CV outcome 5.2% vs 6.8%; all-cause death 3.3% vs 4.5%

Notes

More hypotension/syncope/AKI

pages.title: ALONE-AF
pages.html:
Findings

Stopping OAC ≥1 year after a first successful ablation reduced the stroke/embolism/major-bleeding composite, driven by less bleeding; stroke rates were low in both arms

PopulationNo atrial arrhythmia ≥1 year after first ablation, ≥2 Holters; N=840
InterventionStop oral anticoagulation
ComparatorContinue standard-dose DOAC
OutcomeStroke/SE/major bleeding at 2 years 0.3% vs 2.2% (p=0.02); stroke/SE 0.3% vs 0.8%, NS; major bleeding 0% vs 1.4%

Notes

JAMA 2025 (ESC Hot Line); 18 Korean sites, open-label, N=840, mean 3.6 years post-ablation, median CHA2DS2-VASc 2. AF-freedom judged on two Holters only (low sensitivity). Editorial: keep anticoagulating if CHA2DS2-VASc >3 or prior stroke

pages.title: STAAMP
pages.html:
Findings

Pre-hospital TXA did not reduce 30-day mortality overall; benefit in severe shock and when given within 1 h

PopulationTrauma at risk of haemorrhage, pre-hospital; N=927
InterventionTXA 1 g pre-hospital (± further in-hospital dosing)
ComparatorPlacebo
Outcome30-day mortality 8.1% vs 9.9%, NS; SBP <70: 18.5% vs 35.5%

Notes

Guyette, JAMA Surg 2020; N=927, US air-medical. Supports early, pre-hospital dosing in the sickest

pages.title: STARRT-AKI
pages.html:
Findings

Early RRT did not improve mortality

PopulationSevere AKI ICU; N=3019
InterventionAccelerated RRT
ComparatorStandard/delayed RRT
Outcome90-day mortality 43.9% vs 43.7%

Notes

Largest AKI timing trial

pages.title: Sterns 2010 (controlled correction, Na 96)

props.v: Controlled correction of profound hyponatraemia with DDAVP and hypertonic saline

pages.html:
Findings

Alcoholic patient with Na 96 (thiazide, SSRI, beer potomania, hypovolaemia) corrected safely and gradually using DDAVP to block water diuresis plus hypertonic saline

PopulationSingle patient, Na 96 mmol/L, multifactorial hyponatraemia
InterventionDDAVP + hypertonic saline
Comparator—
OutcomeControlled correction without ODS

Notes

Sterns, Am J Kidney Dis 2010; case report that seeded the Rochester strategy. Shows the approach works even at extreme sodium values

pages.title: STOP-IT
pages.html:
Findings

Short-course antibiotics non-inferior after source control

PopulationIntra-abdominal infection; N=518
InterventionFixed ~4 days
ComparatorLonger course
OutcomeComposite outcome 21.8% vs 22.3%

Notes

Stewardship classic

pages.title: STRESS-L (JAMA 2023)

props.v: Landiolol (ultra-short β1-blocker) for tachycardia in septic shock on noradrenaline

pages.html:
Findings

Landiolol did not improve organ function in tachycardic septic shock and showed a signal of harm (more SAEs, higher pressor need, trend to higher mortality) — trial stopped early

Population126 adults in ICU with septic shock (Sepsis-3), noradrenaline >0.1 mcg/kg/min for 24–72 h and HR ≥95; 40 UK NHS ICUs; open-label phase 2b RCT, stopped early by DMC (planned n=340)
InterventionLandiolol infusion from 1 mcg/kg/min, titrated every 15 min to HR 80–94 within 6 h, weaned once off vasopressors >12 h (median 2 days)
ComparatorStandard care, no β-blockade
OutcomePrimary mean SOFA over 14 days: 8.8 vs 8.1, MD 0.75 (95% CI −0.49 to 2.0, p=0.24). 28-d mortality 37.1% vs 25.4% (OR 1.76, 0.77–4.03); 90-d mortality 43.5% vs 28.6% (OR 2.04, 0.91–4.57). Serious adverse events 25.4% vs 6.4% (p=0.006); higher noradrenaline dose with landiolol (0.34 vs 0.24 mcg/kg/min)

Notes

TBL critique (George Walker): well-run pragmatic RCT with high adherence and a sick cohort (mean noradrenaline 0.37, SOFA 10), but open-label, non-patient-centred primary outcome, no mandated cardiac monitoring to identify who might benefit/harm (e.g. RV dysfunction), and early cessation limits power. Verdict: will not use ultra-short β-blockade in septic shock patients on noradrenaline with tachycardia; confine to trials. Contrasts with Morelli 2013 esmolol single-centre data. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/stress-l/

pages.title: SUBCUT-HF II

props.v: Early discharge with wearable subcutaneous furosemide pump in acute HF

pages.html:
Findings

Early discharge on a patient-operated SC furosemide minipump gave 4 more days alive and out of hospital at 30 days and a 5.5-day shorter admission, with similar serious adverse events

PopulationHospitalised with HF and congestion still needing parenteral diuretics; N=172 (92 vs 80)
InterventionEarly discharge with SC furosemide via wearable minipump + home reviews
ComparatorUsual inpatient IV diuresis
OutcomeDays alive and out of hospital to day 30: 25.9 vs 21.9 (+4.0, 2.1–5.8, p<0.001); index stay 5.5 days shorter (3.6–7.4); SAE 25% vs 23%; HF hospitalisation 60d 14% vs 6% (NS); CV death 2% vs 4%

Notes

Campbell RT et al, JACC 2026;88(15):1781–1793; 20 UK hospitals, open-label. Home review every 3 days. HF readmission at 60 days numerically higher (14% vs 6%, OR 2.45, 0.81–7.43) — not significant but the signal to watch. Device problems in 3% of 1054 applications, none serious. Needs community services to deliver it. Source: 'What You Missed In Medicine This Week'

pages.title: Subirà 2019 (PS vs T-piece SBT)
pages.html:
Findings

30-min pressure-support SBT led to more successful extubations than 2-h T-piece, with no difference in reintubation

PopulationVentilated ≥24 h, ready for SBT; N=1153
Intervention30-min PS 8 cmH2O SBT
Comparator2-h T-piece SBT
OutcomeSuccessful extubation 82.3% vs 74.0%; reintubation 11.1% vs 11.9%, NS

Notes

JAMA 2019; N=1153, Spain. An easier SBT gets more people off the ventilator without more failures

pages.title: TAME (NEJM 2023)

props.v: Targeted mild hypercapnia vs normocapnia after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest

pages.html:
Findings

Targeted mild hypercapnia for 24 h after OHCA did not improve 6-month neurological outcome compared with normocapnia

Population1700 comatose adults after OHCA of presumed cardiac/unknown cause, within 180 min of sustained ROSC (70% shockable, 88% witnessed); 63 ICUs in 17 countries; open-label RCT with blinded outcome assessment, co-enrolment with TTM2
InterventionMild hypercapnia: PaCO2 50–55 mmHg (6.7–7.3 kPa) for 24 h, then normocapnia restored over 24–48 h
ComparatorNormocapnia: PaCO2 35–45 mmHg for 24 h
OutcomePrimary favourable neurological outcome (GOS-E ≥5) at 6 months: 43.5% vs 44.6%, adjusted RR 0.98 (95% CI 0.87–1.11). Death by 6 months 48.2% vs 45.9%; poor functional outcome (mRS 4–6) 53.4% vs 51.3%; no subgroup or adverse-event differences. Good separation (time-weighted PaCO2 49.8 vs 40.8 mmHg)

Notes

TBL critique (George Walker): large international RCT, rapid and well-maintained PaCO2 separation, standardised WLST and blinded prognostication, pre-published SAP; weaknesses are unblinded clinicians, CO2 target abandoned in 8% vs 3%, and 7% missing primary outcome data. Verdict: no benefit or harm from mild hypercapnia — continue to target normocapnia unless ventilatory constraints dictate otherwise. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/blog/ebm/tame/

pages.title: TARGET Protein (JAMA 2025)

props.v: Augmented enteral protein in critical illness

pages.html:
Findings

Augmenting enteral protein to ~1.1 g/kg/day did not increase hospital-free days alive at 90 days and may harm ventilated patients and those with new AKI — consistent with EFFORT Protein and PRECISe

Population3397 ICU patients >16 y prescribed enteral nutrition (82% ventilated, 55% on vasopressors, APACHE II 19); 8 ANZ ICUs 2022–23; cluster-randomised crossover (3-month blocks), open-label
InterventionNutrison Protein Intense (100 g protein/L): delivered 1.12 g/kg IBW/day protein, 14 kcal/kg/day; median 87 h
ComparatorNutrison Protein Plus (63 g/L): 0.69 g/kg IBW/day, isocaloric 14 kcal/kg/day; median 84 h
OutcomePrimary: days alive and free of index hospital at day 90 median 62 vs 64, difference −1.97 days (95% CI −7.24 to 3.30), p=0.46; alive at day 90 72.6% vs 74.0%; ICU LOS longer with augmented protein 6.6 vs 6.2 days (p=0.04); harm signal in ventilated (p-interaction 0.02) and new-RRT (p<0.001) subgroups, both favouring usual protein; urea higher at day 5 and 10

Notes

TBL critique: large pragmatic trial, patient-centred outcome, no loss to follow-up, clear protein separation, and importantly tested a lower 'augmented' dose than EFFORT (1.7) or PRECISe (1.9 g/kg). Weaknesses: ANZ tertiary centres (90% Australia), open-label, short exposure (~3.5 days) relative to a 90-day outcome, no continuation after ICU, index-hospital readmissions only, crossover temporal drift. TBL verdict: no evidence for augmented protein in ICU and some groups (AKI) may be harmed; future work should look at later-phase feeding or low-muscle-mass subgroups. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/target-protein/

pages.title: CHEST Antithrombotic Therapy for VTE Disease: Compendium and Review of CHEST Guidelines 2012-2021 (DVT treatment)

props.v: DVT treatment guidance (proximal, isolated superficial, isolated distal)

pages.html:
Findings

Proximal DVT: 3 months DOAC over VKA; anticoagulation alone over interventional therapy; home treatment if circumstances adequate

PopulationAdults with acute DVT: proximal/deep, isolated superficial vein thrombosis, isolated distal DVT
InterventionDOAC for 3 months (proximal); fondaparinux 2.5 mg daily for 45 days or rivaroxaban 10 mg daily (superficial); anticoagulation if extension or high risk (distal)
ComparatorVKA; no anticoagulation; serial imaging; interventional therapy; IVC filter plus anticoagulation
OutcomeGuideline recommendations only; no trial outcome data given. Superficial: fondaparinux 2.5 mg daily for 45 days if high risk of progression.

Notes

IVC filter only if anticoagulation contraindicated; recommend against routine filter plus anticoagulation. Isolated distal DVT: serial imaging for 2 weeks if no severe symptoms or extension risk; if anticoagulated, duration as for proximal DVT.

pages.title: TGC-Fast (NEJM 2023)

props.v: Tight vs liberal glucose control in ICU without early parenteral nutrition

pages.html:
Findings

With early PN withheld, computer-guided tight glucose control avoided the hypoglycaemia seen in NICE-SUGAR but did not shorten ICU stay or reduce mortality

Population9230 adults admitted to 11 ICUs at 3 Belgian hospitals (median APACHE II 21, 20% diabetic), not receiving early PN; excluded DKA/HHS; RCT, clinicians unblinded, patients/assessors blinded
InterventionTight glucose control 4.4–6.1 mmol/L (80–110 mg/dL) via the LOGIC-Insulin computer algorithm
ComparatorLiberal control: insulin only if glucose >11.9 mmol/L on two readings, then target 10.0–11.9 mmol/L
OutcomePrimary time to ICU discharge readiness: HR 1.00 (95% CI 0.96–1.04, p=0.94). 90-d mortality 10.5% vs 10.1%, RR 1.04 (0.92–1.17). Severe hypoglycaemia 1.0% vs 0.7% (RR 1.53, 0.97–2.39). Tight group: less severe AKI 7.2% vs 8.6% (RR 0.84, 0.73–0.97), less new RRT 4.7% vs 5.8% (RR 0.82, 0.68–0.98), lower peak GGT/ALP — not corrected for multiplicity

Notes

TBL critique (Daniel Chung): large real-world RCT, LOGIC algorithm effectively prevented hypoglycaemia so the glucose target itself could be tested; but median glucose in the tight arm was above target, single country/3 centres, no multiplicity correction so renal/hepatic secondary signals are hypothesis-generating, and the protocol adds nursing workload. Verdict: no convincing clinical benefit — continue to target <10 mmol/L (180 mg/dL) with strict avoidance of hypoglycaemia, per guidelines. Reconciles Leuven 2001/2006 vs NICE-SUGAR: the earlier harm was likely hypoglycaemia plus early PN-driven hyperglycaemia. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/tgc-fast-tight-blood-glucose-control-without-early-parenteral-nutrition-in-the-icu/

pages.title: Smit et al — CRP predicts steroid benefit in CAP (IPD meta-analysis)

props.v: Who benefits from corticosteroids in hospitalised CAP

pages.html:
Findings

Steroids cut 30-day mortality overall (OR 0.72), but the benefit was confined to patients with CRP >204 mg/L

PopulationHospitalised adults with CAP in placebo-controlled steroid RCTs; N=3224
InterventionAdjunctive corticosteroids
ComparatorPlacebo
Outcome30-day mortality 6.6% vs 8.7% (OR 0.72); CRP >204: 6.1% vs 13.0% (OR 0.43, 0.25–0.76); CRP ≤204: OR 0.98

Notes

Lancet Respir Med 2025; individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 8 RCTs, N=3224. CRP threshold from the two most recent trials (n=1355). No heterogeneity by PSI class. More hyperglycaemia (24.8% vs 12.8%) and readmission (7.0% vs 3.7%). Your note read '204' — that is the threshold

pages.title: TICH-2
pages.html:
Findings

TXA reduced haematoma expansion and early deaths but did not improve 90-day functional outcome

PopulationSpontaneous ICH within 8 h; N=2325
InterventionTXA 1 g bolus + 1 g over 8 h
ComparatorPlacebo
OutcomemRS at 90 days — no difference (OR 0.88, 0.76–1.03); day-7 deaths 9% vs 11%

Notes

Sprigg, Lancet 2018; N=2325, UK-led. Why TXA is not routine in ICH

pages.title: TIGHT K (JAMA 2024)

props.v: Potassium targets to prevent AF after cardiac surgery

pages.html:
Findings

Replacing potassium only when it falls to ≤3.5 mmol/L is non-inferior to chasing >4.5 mmol/L for post-CABG atrial fibrillation, at a fraction of the cost

Population1690 adults after isolated CABG without prior AF, high-grade AV block, rhythm drugs or dialysis; 23 centres (21 UK, 2 Germany) 2020–23; open-label non-inferiority RCT (margin 10% absolute), blinded event adjudication, ambulatory monitors
InterventionRelaxed: supplement potassium only when serum K+ ≤3.5 mmol/L (mean K+ 4.4→4.1; median 0 supplements)
ComparatorTight: supplement when K+ ≤4.5 mmol/L (mean 4.6→4.3; median 7 supplements)
OutcomeNew-onset AF/atrial tachyarrhythmia >30 s within 120 h: 27.8% vs 26.2%, risk difference 1.7% (95% CI −2.6 to 5.9) — non-inferior; consistent in all subgroups and per-protocol. Other dysrhythmias 19.1% vs 21.1%, inpatient mortality, ICU and hospital LOS (2 and 6 d) all NS. Mean supplementation cost $39 vs $151

Notes

Multicentre RCT with blinded adjudication, ambulatory AF detection, achieved separation in supplementation frequency and a cost analysis. Limits: open-label, CABG only, more protocol non-adherence in the tight arm, serum K+ stayed >4 in both arms (so says little about K+ <4), diuretic use not reported, costs Barts-specific. TBL verdict: high-quality answer to a daily cardiac ICU question — stop aggressively targeting K+ >4.5 after CABG; cost and environmental savings. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/tight-k/

ComparatorPlacebo

Notes
