pages.title: TRAIN (JAMA 2024)

props.v: Transfusion threshold in acute brain injury

pages.html:
Findings

In anaemic patients with acute brain injury, a liberal transfusion threshold of 9 g/dL improved 6-month neurological outcome compared with 7 g/dL

Population820 adults (18–80) in ICU with TBI, SAH or ICH, GCS ≤13, expected ICU stay >72 h and Hb ≤9 g/dL within 10 days of injury; 72 ICUs in 22 countries 2017–22; open-label RCT with blinded outcome assessment
InterventionLiberal: transfuse 1 unit RBC when Hb <9 g/dL (for up to 28 days)
ComparatorRestrictive: transfuse when Hb <7 g/dL
OutcomeUnfavourable neurological outcome at 180 d (GOS-E 1–5): 62.6% vs 72.6%, RR 0.86 (95% CI 0.78–0.95). 28-d mortality 20.7% vs 22.5% (NS); organ failure and ICU LOS NS. Cerebral ischaemic events 8.8% vs 13.5% (RR 0.65, 0.44–0.97); no excess thrombotic events

Notes

Large pragmatic multinational RCT with concealed allocation, blinded assessors, good separation and few violations. Limits: two sample-size amendments; unblinded ICU staff with non-protocolised prognostication/WLST; pre-randomisation transfusions unknown; broad pathology mix; cerebral ischaemia detection open to bias; mortality higher than similar trials. TBL verdict: with HEMOTION, target a more liberal threshold (~9 g/dL) in acute brain injury. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/train-transfusion-strategies-in-acute-brain-injured-patients/

pages.title: TRAUMOX2 (JAMA 2024)

props.v: Oxygen targets in early trauma care

pages.html:
Findings

An 8-hour restrictive oxygen strategy targeting SpO2 94% in trauma did not reduce death or major respiratory complications compared with liberal high-flow oxygen

Population1457 adults with blunt (89%) or penetrating trauma triggering full trauma-team activation, randomised pre-hospital (41%) or on arrival; 15 pre-hospital bases + 5 major trauma centres in Denmark, Netherlands, Switzerland 2021–23; open-label RCT, blinded outcome assessment; median ISS 14, 24% intubated
InterventionRestrictive oxygen for 8 h: lowest FiO2 to keep SpO2 94% (PaO2 ~85 mmHg)
ComparatorLiberal oxygen for 8 h: 15 L/min or FiO2 1.0 pre-hospital/trauma bay, ≥12 L/min or FiO2 ≥0.6 thereafter (PaO2 280→230 mmHg)
OutcomeDeath and/or major respiratory complication (pneumonia, ARDS) within 30 d: 16.1% vs 16.7%, risk difference 0.56% (95% CI −2.7 to 3.82), OR 1.01 (0.75–1.37). Death 8.6% vs 7.3% (OR 1.28, 0.85–1.92); major respiratory complications 8.9% vs 10.8% (OR 0.84, 0.59–1.19). More hypoxaemic episodes, fewer surgical-site infections with restrictive (exploratory). No subgroup effect

Notes

Impressive pre-hospital randomisation with concealment, early intervention (~50 min from injury), clear separation and minimal loss to follow-up. Limits: 233/236 post-randomisation exclusions (possible bias toward liberal arm), open-label, event rate lower than powered for, components of the composite pointed in opposite directions, only 8 h of intervention and 60% randomised in hospital after some oxygen exposure, moderate-severity cohort. TBL verdict: targeting normoxia (SpO2 94–98%) early in moderate–severe trauma is reasonable. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/traumox2/

pages.title: TRICC
pages.html:
Findings

Restrictive transfusion safe in stable ICU patients

PopulationICU patients; N=838
InterventionHb trigger 70
ComparatorHb trigger 100
Outcome30-day mortality 18.7% vs 23.3%

Notes

In-hospital mortality 22.2% vs 28.1% (p=0.05); 30-day difference not significant overall but lower with restrictive in the less sick (APACHE II ≤20: 8.7% vs 16.1%) and under-55s (5.7% vs 13.0%) — hypothesis-generating subgroups. Restrictive group received ~54% fewer units. TRISS (septic shock, 2014) gave the same answer; MINT (acute MI, 2023) is the exception where liberal looked better

pages.title: TTM2
pages.html:
Findings

Hypothermia (33°C) not superior to normothermia (≤37.5°C) after cardiac arrest

PopulationComatose adults after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest; N=1900
InterventionTargeted 33°C
ComparatorNormothermia with early treatment of fever (≥37.8°C), target ≤37.5°C
Outcome6-month mortality 50% vs 48% (NS); poor functional outcome (mRS 4–6) 55% vs 55%; arrhythmia with haemodynamic compromise 24% vs 17%

Notes

Dankiewicz, NEJM 2021. No mortality or functional difference at 6 months; cooling to 33°C not required. More arrhythmias with haemodynamic compromise in the hypothermia arm (24% vs 17%). Normothermia arm still had active fever treatment (device cooling if ≥37.8°C) — the message is prevent fever, not 'do nothing'

pages.title: Burnett et al.

props.v: Saline vs ultrasound gel for acoustic coupling

pages.html:
Findings

Saline gave adequate acoustic coupling in simulation; clinical equivalence not established

PopulationOperators performing ultrasound-guided regional anaesthesia (simulation setting)
InterventionNormal saline as acoustic coupling medium
ComparatorUltrasound gel
OutcomeSaline can couple acoustically; no evidence of equivalent cannulation success or infection outcomes

Notes

Saline runs off easily, so image quality is harder to maintain. Sterile single-use gel remains the UKHSA-recommended standard for invasive procedures. Published in Anesthesia & Analgesia.

pages.title: UK-ROX (JAMA 2025)

props.v: Conservative oxygen targets in ventilated ICU patients

pages.html:
Findings

Targeting SpO2 90% in ventilated ICU patients did not reduce 90-day mortality compared with usual oxygen therapy

Population16,500 adults within 12 h of invasive ventilation after unplanned ICU admission, FiO2 >0.21 (ECMO excluded); 97 NHS ICUs 2021–24; median age 60, APACHE II 16, 33% sepsis, 9% HIE; registry-embedded pragmatic RCT powered for 2.5% ARR
InterventionConservative oxygen: lowest FiO2 to keep SpO2 90% (alarms 88–92%) until ICU discharge/90 days
ComparatorUsual care: clinician-directed oxygen, no SpO2 upper limit
OutcomePrimary: 90-day all-cause mortality 35.4% vs 34.9%, adjusted risk difference 0.7% (95% CI −0.6 to 2.1), p=0.28; no difference in ICU/hospital LOS, organ-support-free days, ICU/hospital/1-year mortality, or in HIE, sepsis or brain-injury subgroups. Good separation: mean SpO2 93.3% vs 95.1%; 62.6 vs 27.2 h in 88–92%

Notes

TBL critique: largest trial on this question, strong internal validity (allocation concealment, ITT, near-complete follow-up), clear separation, generalisable. Unblinded but mortality endpoint; pre-randomisation oxygen exposure unaccounted; powered only for a 2.5% difference so a smaller but important effect is not excluded. TBL verdict: adds substantially to the evidence (OXYGEN-ICU, HOT-ICU, ICU-ROX, PILOT) that conservative targets don't improve survival; MEGA-ROX (n=40,000) will add to this. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/icm/uk-rox-trial/

pages.title: BICAR-ICU

props.v: Bicarbonate for severe metabolic acidaemia with AKI

pages.html:
Findings

Bicarbonate did not improve day-28 mortality/organ failure overall; reduced need for RRT; mortality benefit in the pre-specified AKIN 2–3 stratum

PopulationICU, severe metabolic acidaemia (pH ≤7.20), moderate-severe AKI (AKIN 2-3); N=640
Intervention4.2% IV sodium bicarbonate to target pH >7.30
ComparatorNo bicarbonate (standard care)
OutcomeDay-60 mortality 62.1% vs 71.5% (p=0.046) in AKIN 2-3 stratum; overall primary outcome not significant; RRT use 35% vs 52%

Notes

pages.title: WATERFALL (NEJM 2022)
pages.html:
Findings

Aggressive fluids caused more fluid overload with no improvement in pancreatitis severity; stopped early for harm

Population249 adults with acute pancreatitis (Revised Atlanta) presenting <24 h from pain onset, without moderately severe/severe disease, heart failure, CKD, decompensated liver disease or electrolyte derangement at baseline; 18 centres in Spain (86%), India, Italy, Mexico, 2020–21; open-label RCT stopped early by DSMB for harm; ~60% gallstone, ~25% SIRS, ~52% hypovolaemic
InterventionAggressive: lactated Ringer's 20 mL/kg bolus then 3 mL/kg/h for 48 h; further 20 mL/kg boluses for UO <0.5 mL/kg/h or SBP <90
ComparatorModerate: 10 mL/kg bolus only if hypovolaemic, then 1.5 mL/kg/h for 20 h; 10 mL/kg boluses as needed
OutcomePrimary moderately severe or severe pancreatitis: 22.1% vs 17.3%, RR 1.28 (0.77–2.12). Fluid overload 20.5% vs 6.3% (significant). Severe AP, local complications, ICU admission, persistent organ failure, persistent SIRS and death all NS but trended towards moderate. Cumulative LR at 48 h 7.8 vs 5.5 L

Notes

From your to-add list (13/09). Supports moderate fluids in acute pancreatitis. TBL critique: multicentre RCT, no loss to follow-up, ITT, clear protocol and pre-specified overload definitions, strong safety focus. But 86% Spanish, unblinded, stopped early (trend to benefit of moderate might have reached significance), mild disease with low comorbidity only, unclear accounting of pre-randomisation fluid, and 20% vs 8% discontinued the intervention (bias to null). Verdict: robust evidence that high-volume fluid causes overload in mild AP — no hard clinical sequelae here, but positive balance is linked to worse outcomes in the critically ill, so it matters. Source: https://www.thebottomline.org.uk/summaries/aggressive-or-moderate-fluid-resuscitation-in-acute-pancreatitis/

pages.title: WOMAN-2

props.v: TXA to prevent PPH in anaemic women

pages.html:

PopulationVaginal birth with Hb <100 g/L; N≈15,000
InterventionTXA 1 g IV after cord clamping
ComparatorPlacebo
OutcomePPH (≥500 mL or shock) 7.0% vs 7.4%, NS

Notes

pages.title: ZODIAC

props.v: Head position (0° vs 30°) while awaiting thrombectomy in LVO stroke

pages.html:
Findings

Lying flat at 0° almost eliminated early neurological deterioration before thrombectomy and was associated with fewer deaths at 3 months; stopped early for efficacy

PopulationAdults with CT-confirmed LVO and viable penumbra awaiting thrombectomy; N=92 (45 vs 47)
InterventionHead of bed 0° (flat)
ComparatorHead of bed 30°
OutcomeEarly neuro deterioration ≥2 NIHSS points 1/45 vs 26/47 (HR 24.4, 4.65–254.4); ≥4 points 1 vs 20; 3-month death 4.4% vs 21.7%

Notes

Alexandrov et al, JAMA Neurology 2025; US multicentre 2018–2023; tiny (N=92) and stopped early, so the effect size is unstable and the CI enormous. Position checked every 10 min until cath lab. Mechanism: gravity augments penumbral perfusion. Source: 'What You Missed In Medicine This Week' newsletter

pages.title: Shock isn't an automatic contraindication to enteral feeding: consider early low-dose EN if norepinephrine <0.3 mcg/kg/min
pages.html:
If you can safely use the gut, use the gut: enteral nutrition supports gut integrity and microbiome, and is protective against upper GI bleeding (REVISE). In the acute phase aim for trophic feeds at 10-20 ml/hour; more isn't always better, so avoid aggressive full-dose nutrition.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Albumin in cirrhosis: 20–25% at 6–8 g per litre after paracentesis >5 L, plus SBP, AKI and HRS-AKI
pages.html:
Paracentesis >5 L: 6–8 g/L removed (whole tap), e.g. 8 L = 48–64 g; rounding to 12.5/25 g vials limits waste. SBP: 1.5 g/kg at diagnosis, 1 g/kg day 3. AKI >stage 1A: 1 g/kg/day for 2 days (max 100 g). HRS-AKI: 20–40 g/day with terpressin. ADQI–ICA 2024 drops the mandatory 48-h albumin challenge, but EASL data show ~40% of responders had not responded by 24 h. Terpressin plus albumin risks respiratory failure (CONFIRM), so reassess volume daily and stop at first sign of overload.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Patient must fall ~400-500 times a year before ICH risk outweighs stroke prevention from AF anticoagulation
pages.html:
Falls risk alone is rarely a valid reason to withhold anticoagulation in AF. The stroke prevention benefit outweighs intracranial haemorrhage risk unless falls are extremely frequent.

Source: SHM 2026

pages.title: Severe ARDS still poorly oxygenated despite lung-protective ventilation: consider APRV where appropriate
pages.html:
If oxygenation remains poor despite lung-protective ventilation in severe ARDS, consider alternative strategies such as APRV. Use it where appropriate and according to local expertise.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Work up MINOCA

props.v: Parlati et al. – ANOCA, INOCA, MINOCA review

pages.html:
Parlati et al. – ANOCA, INOCA, MINOCA review (2025): Narrative review: ANOCA/INOCA/MINOCA are not benign; linked to serious CV events and long-term disability

Trial: Parlati et al. – ANOCA, INOCA, MINOCA review

Source: Parlati et al. – ANOCA, INOCA, MINOCA review

pages.title: Norepinephrine is first-line pressor in almost all shock
pages.html: Alpha > beta agonism; dose 0.01-0.50 mcg/kg/min. Risks are limb/digital ischaemia at higher doses and a small arrhythmia risk from beta agonism. The author considers central access at around 0.10 to reduce ischaemia risk, though peripheral use at higher doses is sometimes seen without harm; evidence is unclear.

pages.title: Start an alpha blocker (e.g. Flomax) at least 3 days before a voiding trial in BPH-related retention
pages.html:
Don't attempt a trial of void without an alpha blocker in BPH-related acute urinary retention. If it fails, consider CIC (preferred, every 4-6h, target <500 mL) to avoid detrusor damage from a distended bladder; aim for PVR <100-150 before weaning. Use an indwelling Foley if initial PVR >1000-1500 mL, or if the patient is unable/unwilling to do CIC. Guidelines say Foley after the 2nd-3rd failed trial, but it can be considered after the 1st. Consider Bactrim prophylaxis at catheter removal if in >7 days in higher-risk patients; usually omit in young, healthy patients.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Angiotensin II and methylene blue are rare, late-line rescue pressors
pages.html: They are considered for 4th or 5th line use. If a patient needs them, the prognosis is usually already very poor.

pages.title: TXA adult IV dosing varies by indication: usually 1 g, given IV only
pages.html:
Trauma/TBI: 1 g over 10 min then 1 g over 8 h (or single 2 g per ATLS 11th), within 3 h. Military TCCC: 2 g slow IV/IO over 1 min. Postpartum: 1 g over 10 min, repeat if bleeding continues after 30 min or restarts within 24 h. POISE-3: 1 g at start and end of noncardiac surgery. ATACAS: 50 mg/kg over 30 min after induction in coronary surgery. IV only, never near spinal/epidural drugs. Check kidneys: keep the loading dose, reduce repeat and infusion doses. Local protocols vary.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Decompensated HF: check diuretic response within 2 and 6 hours, not next morning
pages.html:
Loop-naive: furosemide 40 mg IV; already on a loop: twice the usual oral dose IV. At 2 h spot urine sodium ≥70 mmol/L is adequate, otherwise double the IV dose. At 6 h urine output ≥100 mL/h is adequate, otherwise double again. Ceiling furosemide 600 mg/day (1,000 mg in severe renal impairment). PUSH-AHF: sodium-guided escalation raised natriuresis but not death or readmission. 2026 ESC: class IIb.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: If expiratory flow doesn't return to zero before the next breath, think auto-PEEP (air trapping)
pages.html:
Check the expiratory flow waveform: normally it returns to zero before the next breath. Failure to do so means air trapping, dynamic hyperinflation and intrinsic PEEP. Fix by lengthening expiratory time: raise inspiratory flow, lower VT, lower RR if possible. If necessary, measure intrinsic PEEP with an end-expiratory hold/occlusion. In selected patients, apply external PEEP below intrinsic PEEP to reduce inspiratory threshold load.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: 25% albumin moves water, it doesn't add it: borrowed from the interstitium
pages.html:
25 g albumin gives ~500 mL plasma gain either way: 5% (500 mL) is all from the bag, 25% (100 mL) recruits ~400 mL from interstitium. No benefit in the dry patient, as there is nothing to borrow. Never dilute 25% with sterile water (hypotonic, fatal haemolysis); use 0.9% saline or 5% dextrose. Doses are in grams, not volumes.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Ketamine gives sedation and analgesia with minimal respiratory depression
pages.html: Rate 8-25 mg/hr. Can cause emergence reactions or hallucinations and a transient rise in HR and BP.

pages.title: CRRT mode follows the goal: SCUF fluid, CVVH convection, CVVHD diffusion, CVVHDF both
pages.html:
SCUF: UF only, no dialysate or replacement, fluid removal with little solute clearance. CVVH: replacement fluid (pre- or post-filter), convection, good middle-molecule clearance. CVVHD: counter-current dialysate, diffusion, excellent small-solute clearance (urea, K+). CVVHDF: dialysate plus replacement fluid, broadest clearance. Pre-dilution gives longer filter life but lower clearance; post-dilution is more efficient, so keep filtration fraction <20-25% to avoid clotting.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: N-acetylcysteine as a mucolytic: smells like rotten eggs, sticky, and never shown to beat 3% saline inhaled
pages.html:
Teaching reel (drddo, 'Lesson 40: Mucolytics') lists the downsides of nebulised n-acetylcysteine: sulphurous rotten-egg smell, sticky residue, and respiratory therapists dislike using it. The presenter states it has never been shown to be better than 3% inhaled saline. Caption also flags a risk of use (cut off in screenshot), likely bronchospasm.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: 25% albumin moves water, it doesn't add it: 100 mL of 25% recruits interstitial fluid to match 500 mL of 5%
pages.html:
25 g of albumin expands plasma by about the same amount either way. With 5% all the volume comes from the bag; with 25% the gain beyond the infused volume is drawn from the interstitium, so it needs oedematous patients and does little in the dry. Never dilute 25% with sterile water (hypotonic, fatal haemolysis); use 0.9% saline or 5% dextrose.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Dexmedetomidine: useful in delirium and for weaning, but causes bradycardia
pages.html: Second-line sedative at 0.2-1.4 mcg/kg/hr; lighter sedation than propofol and sometimes hypotension. It has less respiratory depression, so it can be used in extubated patients and when preparing for extubation.

pages.title: Urea is an effective treatment for SIADH
pages.html:
Doctor's note from 2025–2026 teaching: oral urea raises serum sodium in SIADH via osmotic diuresis. Study name not captured; to confirm.

Source: quick

pages.title: Glomerular disease: endothelial/GBM injury gives haematuria; podocyte injury gives nephrotic syndrome
pages.html:
Filtration barrier: fenestrated endothelium (~70–100 nm), GBM, podocyte foot processes with slit diaphragm (~25–40 nm). Endothelial ± GBM injury: haematuria, proteinuria, hypertension (nephritic). Podocyte injury: heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, hyperlipidaemia, ± hypercoagulability (nephrotic). Biopsy shows which layer is damaged.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Aim for I:E ratio ≥1:2; if shorter, lengthen expiration to avoid dynamic hyperinflation
pages.html:
If I:E becomes shorter than 1:2, increase inspiratory flow, reduce tidal volume, and reduce RR if clinically possible. This gives adequate expiratory time and reduces dynamic hyperinflation (breath stacking/auto-PEEP).

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Reserve 7% hypertonic saline for bronchiectasis (e.g. CF, PCD), not routine mucolytic use
pages.html:
Instagram reel (drdo, Lesson 40: Mucolytics) caption text: 'Really only should use 7% saline in bronchiectasis, ex: cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, etc'. The caption is cut off at 'Don't forget the risk of…', so the risk mentioned is not visible (hypertonic saline can cause bronchospasm, so check the full video).

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Many conditions cause false-positive procalcitonin
pages.html: Causes include trauma, burns, fungal infection, ARDS, paraneoplastic syndromes, medullary thyroid cancer, falciparum malaria, AKI and CKD.

pages.title: Albumin is more than an oncotic agent: low albumin hides anion gap, misleads total phenytoin and calcium
pages.html:
Albumin carries, buffers and scavenges, so low levels raise free drug/calcium fraction and speed clearance of highly bound antibiotics (ceftriaxone, ertapenem). Add ~2.5 to the anion gap per 1 g/dL albumin below 4 (e.g. albumin 2 turns gap 12 into 17). Mechanism is not indication: ALBIOS, ARISS and ATTIRE showed no survival benefit from targeting albumin, so measure free phenytoin or ionised calcium rather than infusing albumin to fix a total level.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Propofol is first-line sedation but beware hypotension and propofol infusion syndrome
pages.html: Quick on, quick off; 5-50 mcg/kg/min. Propofol infusion syndrome features acidosis, rhabdomyolysis and bradycardia, with high mortality. Check triglycerides every 3 days and consider switching at about 400-500 mg/dL (or if hypotension limits use). Green urine is harmless and does not signal PRIS.

pages.title: ARDSnet PEEP/FiO2 tables: titrate PEEP upward in step with rising FiO2
Saline can be used as US coupling instead of gel.
pages.html:
Easier drying than gel.

Expect run-off and image degradation.

Use in emergencies/non-invasive procedures.

Trial: Burnett et al.

Source: Burnett et al.

pages.title: Procalcitonin may be more useful in paediatric meningitis
pages.html: In meningitis, PCT may have more value in children than in adults.

pages.title: Suzetrigine: new non-opioid analgesic, selective peripheral nerve sodium channel blocker
pages.html:
Suzetrigine blocks the voltage-gated sodium channel NaV1.8 in peripheral pain-sensing nerves, offering analgesia without opioid receptor effects.

Source: quick

pages.title: TXA protects formed clot; it does not build clot or replace factors
pages.html:
Tranexamic acid occupies lysine-binding sites so plasminogen cannot dock on fibrin, slowing clot breakdown. Works best when fibrinolysis is high (early after injury, birth, bypass); later fibrinolysis shuts down and TXA may add clot risk. Not a hemostatic agent: a bleeding vessel still needs surgery, embolisation or endoscopy. Half-life ~2h after IV dose; renally cleared mostly unchanged, so accumulates in kidney impairment; never intrathecal.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: ANOCA, INOCA, MINOCA: non-obstructive CAD (<50% stenosis) classified by troponin, documented ischaemia and symptoms
pages.html:
All have non-obstructive CAD (<50% in any major epicardial artery on CCTA/invasive angiogram). MINOCA: troponin rise + documented ischaemia + angina. INOCA: no troponin rise, ischaemia documented, angina. ANOCA: angina/symptoms only, no troponin rise and no documented ischaemia. Source: Ya'qoub et al, Am J Med 2021;134:1321-1329.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Default PEEP for bag-mask ventilation is 5 cm H2O
pages.html:
Physiologic end-expiratory pressure; limits alveolar collapse during preoxygenation and apnoea, with lower risk of hypotension, gastric insufflation and excessive airway pressure. PreVent trial bag-mask protocol used PEEP 5–10 cm H2O; ventilation during apnoea reduced severe hypoxaemia.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Avoid midazolam: it worsens delirium and accumulates in fat
pages.html: If needed, use boluses rather than an infusion (2-20 mg/hr). It greatly increases ICU delirium, and after several days it can take days to clear and for the patient to wake. Neutral effect on BP.

pages.title: New-onset AF in ICU: approach and rate/rhythm control choices
pages.html:
No rigid algorithm. Assess symptoms and haemodynamics, and whether AF is cause or consequence of critical illness. New-onset AF carries worse outcomes: treat as a severity marker and look for triggers (sepsis, electrolyte disturbance, hypovolaemia, catecholamines).

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Mucolytics carry a risk of precipitating an asthma attack (bronchospasm) in susceptible patients
pages.html:
Instagram reel (drddo, 'Lesson 40: Mucolytics'): the caption reads 'Don't forget the risk of…' and the on-screen subtitle completes it as 'an asthma attack'. Caution with mucolytics in asthma or airway hyperreactivity, as thinned secretions and irritant effects can provoke bronchospasm. Only the caption and one subtitle are visible, so mechanism and specific drugs are not shown.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Rocuronium boluses can help refractory ventilator dyssynchrony
pages.html: Cisatracurium, rocuronium and vecuronium are the main agents; take care not to confuse vecuronium with Versed (midazolam). The author recalls PRN rocuronium pushes of about 50-100 mg once or twice, but is unsure of exact dosing, so check local guidance.

pages.title: Amyloid biopsy: organ beats fat pad
pages.html:
Heart, kidney or liver biopsy is more sensitive for amyloidosis than abdominal fat pad aspirate.

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: Amyloidosis causes acquired factor X deficiency
pages.html:
Factor X is sequestered on amyloid fibrils → bleeding tendency.

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: Anal cancer: HIV is a very common association
pages.html:
HPV-driven; think of it in people living with HIV (and MSM) presenting with anal symptoms.

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: Apixaban is absorbed in the proximal small bowel
pages.html:
Caution after proximal small-bowel resection or short gut — absorption may be unreliable.

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: Autonomic dysreflexia in spinal cord injury: GTN paste
pages.html:
Sit up, remove the trigger (bladder/bowel), and use topical nitrate for the hypertension — easy to wipe off if BP drops.

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: Set tidal volume by predicted body weight, not actual: start 8 mL/kg, titrate to 6 mL/kg, keep Pplat ≤30
pages.html:
PBW (kg): male = 50 + 2.3 × (height in inches − 60); female = 45.5 + 2.3 × (height in inches − 60). Start VT 8 mL/kg PBW, reduce by 1 mL/kg every 2 h to target 6 mL/kg. Keep plateau pressure ≤30 cmH2O; if above, reduce VT in 1 mL/kg steps to a minimum of about 4 mL/kg PBW. Low VT + Pplat ≤30 = lung protection.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Early vs late pressors have similar outcomes; excess fluid comes with risk
pages.html:
Beginner instinct is to give 4-6L of fluids before starting vasopressors. The data show early vs late pressors have similar outcomes, while excess fluid carries risk (e.g. oedema, organ congestion), so don't delay pressors purely to complete a large fluid load.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Bartonella endocarditis mimics ANCA vasculitis
pages.html:
Culture-negative endocarditis → RPGN with low complement. Looks like ANCA vasculitis (can even be ANCA-positive) — don't give immunosuppression before excluding it.

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: Rapid hs-cTn rule-out excludes acute myocardial injury only, not significant coronary artery disease
pages.html:
Rapid hs-cTn algorithms rule out acute myocardial injury, NOT significant CAD. Depending on pretest probability, subsequent imaging remains mandatory to achieve the low event rates published in clinical trials.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Behçet's: acneiform rash on the back
pages.html:
Papulopustular lesions on the trunk are a recognised cutaneous feature (plus pathergy).

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: Only one third of CVID presents with active infection
pages.html:
CVID can also present with pulmonary involvement or autoimmune disease. Do not wait for recurrent infections to consider it.

Source: SHM 2026

pages.title: Titrate sedation to a RASS target of 0 to -1
pages.html: RASS runs from -5 (unarousable) to +4 (combative), and nurses titrate sedation to it. Aim deeper (-4 to -5) before paralysis. Sedation and analgesia are separate goals.

pages.title: Burkholderia granulomas
pages.html:
Burkholderia behaves like TB and like Pseudomonas; melioidosis (B. pseudomallei) gives acute granulomas.

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: Metformin on admission: hold or continue? Recent (2025/26) evidence – study name to confirm
pages.html:
Doctor's note records a 2025/26 study comparing holding versus continuing metformin at the start of admission. Study name and result not captured; check the source before acting on it.

Source: quick

pages.title: Castleman disease
pages.html:
Rare lymphoproliferative disorder driven by IL-6: unicentric (one node group, surgical cure) vs multicentric (systemic symptoms; HHV-8/HIV-associated or idiopathic; treat with anti-IL-6 e.g. siltuximab). Your note was the question — this is the one-liner answer.

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: Paralysis in ARDS: ACURASYS benefit not confirmed by ROSE
pages.html: ACURASYS (2010) showed a mortality benefit from 48 hours of paralysis in ARDS with P:F <150; ROSE (2019) found none. Practice may move away from routine use.

pages.title: Antihistamines and steroids don't work in bradykinin-mediated angioedema; only useful if mast cell-mediated
pages.html:
Reserve H1 antihistamines and glucocorticoids for suspected allergic (mast cell) aetiology. For recurrent idiopathic angioedema, trial a non-sedating antihistamine BID (cetirizine 10mg or desloratadine 5mg gave significant improvement in 86%; can go up to 20mg BID before calling it unresponsive). Hydroxyzine added no benefit.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Confusion: separate altered level of consciousness from focal deficit
pages.html:
Drowsy/reduced GCS is a different problem from 'can't get words out' (dysphasia). Decide which you are looking at before working it up.

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: 'Coughing up blood' has three sources
pages.html:
Haemoptysis, haematemesis, or epistaxis that has been swallowed/coughed back up. Clarify before you label it.

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: Cronkhite–Canada syndrome
pages.html:
Non-hereditary GI polyposis with protein-losing enteropathy; alopecia, nail dystrophy and hyperpigmentation.

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: Cryptococcus gattii infects the immunocompetent
pages.html:
Unlike C. neoformans, gattii causes disease in immunocompetent hosts and forms solid masses (cryptococcomas) in lung/brain.

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: CVID: diagnose by vaccine response; can mimic sarcoid
pages.html:
Test with a vaccine challenge (poor antibody response). CVID can cause a sarcoid-like syndrome with lung involvement and lymphadenopathy.

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: Cystic lung disease: apical cysts + micronodules + smoker = Langerhans cell histiocytosis
pages.html:
Upper-zone predominant, bizarre-shaped cysts in a young smoker.

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: Cystic lung disease: basal cysts + renal tumours = Birt–Hogg–Dubé
pages.html:
Also fibrofolliculomas and pneumothorax. (Already in Anki.)

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: Cystic lung disease: diffuse cysts in a premenopausal woman = LAM
pages.html:
Lymphangioleiomyomatosis — round thin-walled cysts throughout; associated with tuberous sclerosis.

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: Wellens and de Winter signs are OMI/STEMI equivalents pointing to critical proximal LAD stenosis
pages.html: Wellens syndrome: biphasic (type A) or deeply inverted (type B) T waves in V2–V3, seen in pain-free intervals after transient or subacute LAD occlusion, with a risk of imminent anterior MI. De Winter sign: upsloping ST depression with tall, symmetrical T waves in the precordial leads during acute chest pain, seen in roughly 2% of acute LAD occlusions. Both warrant urgent angiography rather than stress testing. Avoid exercise stress testing in Wellens.

pages.title: Procalcitonin-guided duration for CAP is off-label and gives little gain
pages.html: Schuetz et al 2018 looked at antibiotic duration in CAP. The ADAPT-Sepsis study showed only a 1-day difference.

pages.title: Procalcitonin does not identify bacterial superinfection in COVID-19
pages.html: Schouten et al 2021 found it unhelpful for detecting superimposed bacterial infection in COVID-19.

pages.title: Default post-intubation drips: norepinephrine, propofol and fentanyl, then adjust
pages.html: These are the first-line pressor, sedative and analgesic. Know the progression of pressors with maximum rates, sedative side effects, and RASS titration.

pages.title: Lambda > kappa free light chain in renal impairment is suspicious
pages.html: Kappa is normally cleared more than lambda in renal impairment, so the ratio shifts towards kappa. A lambda excess is therefore not explained by renal impairment alone and should raise suspicion of a clonal process.

pages.title: 25% albumin moves water, it doesn't add it: 25 g gives similar plasma expansion to 5% only if interstitial water exists
pages.html:
25 g albumin is 500 mL of 5% (iso-oncotic, all volume from the bag) or 100 mL of 25% (hyperoncotic, recruits interstitial water). 5% carries ~5x the sodium load; rate ceiling 5 vs 1-2 mL/min. Useless in the dry patient with nothing to borrow. Never dilute 25% with sterile water: hypotonic, fatal haemolysis. Use 0.9% saline or 5% dextrose.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Dose ketamine for RSI on actual bodyweight, not ideal bodyweight, including in obesity
pages.html:
Actual bodyweight dosing is better supported by pharmacokinetic principles (Erstad and Barletta 2020) and expert consensus (Morgan et al 2021). Relevant as half of trial patients were overweight and over a quarter had obesity. 25% received more than the nomogram maximum (2 mg/kg actual body weight); many experts use <1 mg/kg in the critically ill.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Phenylephrine is a pure alpha agonist: useful if arrhythmias limit beta-agonist pressors
pages.html: It can cause reflex bradycardia. Avoid in obstructive shock.

pages.title: Procalcitonin can be falsely negative in early, localised or subacute infection
pages.html: Early infections, localised infections and subacute endocarditis may not raise PCT. A negative result should not rule out infection.

pages.title: Early low-dose enteral nutrition is reasonable in shock on norepinephrine <0.3 mcg/kg/min
pages.html:
If you can safely use the gut, use the gut: enteral nutrition supports gut integrity and microbiome and is protective against upper GI bleeding (REVISE). More isn't always better: in the acute phase aim for trophic feeds at 10-20 ml/hour and avoid aggressive full-dose nutrition.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Consider MAP ~60 in age 65+
pages.html:
Consider a MAP target of ~60 mmHg in patients aged 65+ with vasodilatory shock.

Trial: 65 trial

Source: 65 trial

pages.title: Procalcitonin has poor sensitivity and specificity, so it is unreliable for starting or stopping antibiotics
pages.html: Kamat et al (Clin Infect Dis) found poor diagnostic performance. About 1 in 6 infections have a negative PCT, so it is bad for both starting and stopping decisions.

pages.title: Urgent RRT indications: AEIOU. Oliguria or a high creatinine alone is not an indication.
pages.html:
A: severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.1) not responding to medical therapy. E: refractory hyperkalaemia (K+ >6.5 mEq/L) or ECG changes. I: dialyzable toxins (lithium, methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylates, metformin/MALA, valproate). O: diuretic-resistant fluid overload or pulmonary oedema. U: uraemic pericarditis, encephalopathy, neuropathy or bleeding (traditionally BUN >100 mg/dL).

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Dobutamine and milrinone are inotropes that vasodilate and can lower BP
pages.html: Used mainly in cardiogenic shock. Dobutamine (B1 > B2, 'fast on, fast off') suits a relatively normal SVR but is highly arrhythmogenic. Milrinone, a PDE inhibitor, takes about 6 hours to work, suits high SVR, has less arrhythmia risk, but is renally cleared so avoid in renal failure.

pages.title: Hypercalcaemia causes polyuria via acquired nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, driving severe volume depletion
pages.html:
High calcium impairs aquaporin-2 function in the collecting duct, causing ADH resistance and large dilute urine losses with marked hypovolaemia. Rehydrate with IV fluids first.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: GI bleed + thrombocytopenia: think cirrhosis / portal hypertension
pages.html:
Low platelets in a GI bleeder points to portal hypertension and varices. Anaemia on arrival suggests a longer-term bleed rather than an acute one.

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: RRT replaces filtration only, not endocrine kidney functions (EPO, vitamin D activation, renin)
pages.html:
Renal replacement therapy is artificial support taking over excretory functions: solute clearance, fluid removal and correction of acid-base and electrolyte imbalance. Blood and dialysate/effluent are separated by a semipermeable membrane (urea, K+, creatinine, water move across). Acute (AKI in ICU): IHD, SLED, CRRT, PD. Chronic (ESRD): HD, PD, with transplant as definitive treatment. Endocrine functions need separate treatment, e.g. ESAs and vitamin D analogues.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Choose the preload responsiveness test by ventilation status and CO monitoring, not habit
pages.html:
Ask three questions: is the patient intubated with spontaneous breathing, is haemodynamic monitoring in place, and are the test's validity conditions met? A fluid bolus raises CO, not BP, so tests need CO or a surrogate (PPV, VTI, EtCO2). With no CO monitor on a ventilated patient without spontaneous breathing, options include PLR with PPV/EtCO2, EEOT, EEOT+EIOT or the TVC. Mini-fluid challenge and PLR (CO rise ≥10%) are the main options otherwise. Lai & Monnet, Expert Opinion: Hemodynamics.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Avoid steroids without oxygen need
pages.html:
RECOVERY (2020): Dexamethasone reduced 28-day mortality in ventilated/oxygen-requiring patients, not in those without oxygen. Hydroxychloroquine, lopinavir-ritonavir, azithromycin and convalescent plasma showed no benefit.

Trial: RECOVERY

Source: RECOVERY

pages.title: HFpEF: first decompensation typically in the late 70s
pages.html:
Age of first exacerbation is a clue to phenotype.

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: Agitation on the ventilator may be pain: increase analgesia, not just sedation
pages.html: Analgesia and sedation are separate entities. When nursing asks for more sedation because the patient is not tolerating the vent, inadequate analgesia is often the cause.

pages.title: Early enteral feeding helps ventilated patients; continue tube feeds on moderate pressors
pages.html: Feeding within 24-48 hours improves outcomes, yet feeds are often cut to trophic rates when pressor needs are high, for fear of bowel ischaemia. Literature suggests feeds are relatively safe up to norepinephrine 0.30 mcg/kg/min; back off for vomiting or unexplained rising lactate, though lactate source is hard to interpret. The author's own threshold is about >0.15.

pages.title: Consider stress-dose steroids by the third or fourth pressor
pages.html: IV hydrocortisone 50 mg q6h or 100 mg q8h for 5-7 days. Studies are controversial: shock resolves faster but there is minimal to no mortality effect.

pages.title: SCLC, metastatic NSCLC, metastatic melanoma: consider MRI brain even without neurological features
pages.html:
These cancers carry a high risk of cerebral metastases, which may be asymptomatic at diagnosis.

Source: SHM 2026

pages.title: Infectious causes of vasculitis
pages.html:
Secondary syphilis (and aortitis), TB and endemic mycoses can all cause vasculitis — exclude before immunosuppressing.

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: IV magnesium over 20 minutes for bronchodilation
pages.html:
Acute severe asthma: 2 g IV MgSO4 over 20 min.

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: Fentanyl is first-line ICU analgesic but has a long context-sensitive half-life
pages.html: 25-200 mcg/hr with neutral BP effect. Its half-life lengthens the longer it is infused, so clearance can be slow after prolonged use.

pages.title: Biopsy a metastasis rather than the suspected primary
pages.html:
A metastasis gives the most advanced stage and may be more accessible than the primary site.

Source: SHM 2026

pages.title: Low protein gap (total protein minus albumin) suggests a process such as CVID
pages.html:
A low globulin fraction points to hypogammaglobulinaemia. Consider immunoglobulin measurement when the gap is low.

Source: SHM 2026

pages.title: PEEP pearls: titrate, be patient, never disconnect
pages.html:
Too little PEEP loses recruitment; too much over-stretches the lung. Oxygenation response to PEEP is slow, and PEEP is lost fast on disconnection. High-flow oxygen gives ~1 cmH2O PEEP per 10 L/min.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: QTc with wide QRS: subtract (QRS - 100) from the QT, then enter into MDCalc
pages.html:
Wide QRS inflates the measured QT. Correct with QT - (QRS - 100), then calculate the QTc using MDCalc.

Source: SHM 2026

pages.title: Low serum albumin is mostly redistribution, not loss: infused albumin joins the same leaking pool
pages.html:
In septic shock albumin escapes the circulation at up to ~15%/h (about 3× normal 5%/h) as inflammation speeds transcapillary leak. Capillaries filter and do not reabsorb, and the revised Starling principle makes subglycocalyx π(sg) the key opposing force. Textbook albumin:crystalloid replacement is 1:3-5, but in SAFE it was about 1:1.4, and correcting the number has not changed outcomes.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Interpret early-stopped trials cautiously
pages.html:
Stopped at 554 of 1,000 planned after repeated interim analyses, so effect size may be overestimated.

Trial: ICRAKI

Source: ICRAKI

pages.title: RRT clearance: diffusion for small solutes, convection for middle molecules, UF removes fluid, adsorption for cytokines
pages.html:
Diffusion moves solutes down a concentration gradient (urea, K+); counter-current flow raises efficiency. Convection drags solutes with water under pressure and needs replacement fluid; better for middle molecules. Ultrafiltration pushes plasma water across the membrane by hydrostatic gradient (TMP), driving fluid removal. Adsorption binds solutes (e.g. cytokines) to the membrane or resin (AN69, oXiris, CytoSorb). Rule of thumb: diffusion for small solutes, convection for middle molecules.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Dopamine is arrhythmogenic, which is why norepinephrine replaced it as first-line
pages.html: Doses: <3 'renal', 3-10 beta, >10 alpha. Renal-dose dopamine has poor evidence, giving only mild diuresis with no outcome benefit and possible harm. SOAP II (2010) showed similar mortality versus norepinephrine but far more arrhythmias with dopamine.

pages.title: Avoid albumin in brain injury: SAFE-TBI showed higher mortality, concentrated in severe injury (GCS 3-8)
pages.html:
SAFE-TBI (2007): 24-month death 33.2% with albumin vs 20.4% with saline. Albumin also gave no benefit in cardiac surgery (ALBICS, ALBICS-AKI: AKI 48.9% vs 43.4%), with more bleeding and AKI signals. No benefit for low serum albumin, with furosemide, dialysis hypotension, or non-SBP infection in cirrhosis. 20-25% albumin in brain injury is untested.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: In decompensated HF, ask two questions: is the patient congested, and is the patient perfused?
pages.html:
Warm-wet is the usual admission: IV loop diuretic without delay, then measure the response. Cold-wet is shock: stage it, call the shock team, plan inotrope or mechanical support. Cold-dry is uncommon: assess filling before giving or removing volume. Warm-dry: look for another cause of symptoms before diuresing. Name precipitants in the first hour: ACS, arrhythmia (often rapid AF), infection, missed doses/salt/fluid load, hypertensive emergency, PE, acute valve lesion or tamponade, NSAIDs/steroids/negative inotropes.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Carbapenems plus valproate raise seizure risk
pages.html: Carbapenems substantially reduce serum valproate levels, which can precipitate breakthrough seizures. Avoid the combination where possible, or choose an alternative antibiotic.

pages.title: Long-acting naltrexone in opioid misuse: overdose risk when it wears off
pages.html:
Addiction specialists avoid it for opioids (unlike alcohol): tolerance is completely lost, then the person uses their old dose and overdoses.

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: Low ALP: zinc deficiency or Wilson's disease
pages.html:
ALP is a zinc-dependent enzyme. In Wilson's, high copper drives zinc low. (Also hypophosphatasia, hypothyroidism.)

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: Lupus vulgaris
pages.html:
Cutaneous TB: reddish-brown plaques on head and neck; 'apple-jelly' nodules on diascopy.

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: In ARDS, the role of corticosteroids depends on the underlying cause, not the ARDS label
pages.html:
Severe CAP: hydrocortisone 200 mg/day cut 28-day mortality (CAPE COD, NEJM 2023). Septic shock ± ARDS: hydrocortisone 200 mg/day established for vasopressor-dependent shock (APROCCHSS/ADRENAL). Influenza-associated ARDS: no routine steroids (FLUDEX ongoing). Non-HIV Pneumocystis pneumonia: severity-guided use, not universal (PIC trial, NEJM 2025).

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Docusate is no better than placebo for constipation
pages.html:
Evidence shows no meaningful benefit over placebo. Prefer osmotic or stimulant laxatives where a laxative is needed.

Source: SHM 2026

pages.title: Head-up 30° in FASTHUG has weak evidence for preventing VAP, despite the physiological rationale
pages.html:
Supine posture increased aspiration of radiolabelled colloid about fivefold vs semirecumbent (Torres 1992), but this has not translated into proven VAP reduction. Niël-Weise 2011 meta-analysis (3 trials, N=337) found insufficient evidence, though experts still prefer it. Head elevation remains essential when ICP is raised.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Never paralyse without adequate sedation, and limit paralysis to about 48 hours
pages.html: Inadequate sedation risks awareness while paralysed, with severe psychological trauma. BIS can monitor brain activity and train-of-four the depth of paralysis. Paralysis carries a high risk of ICU myopathy, so avoid prolonged use.

pages.title: Start PEEP at 5–8 cmH2O; increase if oxygenation inadequate or FiO2 >60% needed
pages.html:
Initial PEEP is 5–8 cmH2O. Increase when oxygenation remains inadequate or a high FiO2 (>60%) is required. Higher PEEP improves oxygenation via alveolar recruitment. Balance against haemodynamic compromise and overdistension.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Non-purulent cellulitis: ~5% fail and progress to abscess
pages.html:
Warn patients and safety-net for fluctuance.

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: Add vasopressin as second-line when norepinephrine needs keep escalating
pages.html: Acts on V1 receptors to vasoconstrict; given at a fixed 0.03-0.04 units/min, not titrated, because titration was linked to mesenteric ischaemia. It may spare norepinephrine but has not been shown to improve outcomes. Claims that it is less pH-dependent in acidaemia lack strong evidence.

pages.title: Set ventilator inspiratory flow ~60 L/min if passive, ≥80 L/min in respiratory distress
pages.html:
Quiet/no spontaneous breathing: ~60 L/min. Respiratory distress or high minute ventilation: ≥80 L/min. Higher flow shortens inspiratory time (Ti), leaving more time for expiration, which matters in air trapping.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Don't correct calcium for hypoalbuminaemia
pages.html:
Doctor's note (2025–2026 teaching): albumin-adjusted calcium is not reliable; the formula is unvalidated and can mislead. Consider ionised calcium where it matters. Source to confirm.

Source: quick

pages.title: Occlusion MI, not just STEMI: the ECG equivalents
pages.html:
ST elevation, ST depression (posterior MI), hyperacute T waves, de Winter T waves, Wellens' pattern, Aslanger pattern, South African Flag Sign, New onset Bifascicular block, Terminal QRS distortion, Precordial Swirl, Northern OMI. All indicate occlusion MI. Also called false negative STEMI.

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy illness script: Adolescent male with mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation and spastic weakness plus Addison's biochemistry
pages.html: Mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation with progressive spastic weakness, hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia in an adolescent male suggests X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (ABCD1 mutation) causing adrenal insufficiency and CNS demyelination. Peroxisomal beta-oxidation failure raises very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFA), so check plasma VLCFA, morning cortisol/ACTH and MRI brain.

pages.title: Start ventilation in Assist-Control (AC); consider SIMV only for excessive spontaneous RR causing alkalosis or significant auto-PEEP
pages.html:
Initial setup: set 5 parameters - mode, tidal volume, RR, PEEP, FiO2 (example shown: VT 450, RR 14, PEEP 5, FiO2 0.4). Default mode is AC. Consider SIMV if excessive spontaneous respiratory rate causes respiratory alkalosis, or if there is significant auto-PEEP.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: MAP 65 is a target, not a threshold
pages.html:
MAP = (1/3)SBP + (2/3)DBP = SVR x CO. 65 derives from the autoregulation floor and early sepsis trials.

Trial: 65 trial

Source: 65 trial

pages.title: Paracentesis: go left lower quadrant
pages.html:
Thinner abdominal wall and no caecum on the left.

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: APRV needs high intrathoracic pressure, so patients need a lot of fluid volume, unlike the dry-lung ARDS strategy
pages.html:
Sustained high intrathoracic pressure markedly decreases preload, so APRV usually needs more vasopressors or more fluid, both unsatisfactory. This runs contrary to the FACTT conservative-fluid approach in ARDS. It is also unfamiliar, which is a safety issue for staff troubleshooting overnight.

Source: Screenshot

pages.title: Platelets and thrombosis
pages.html:
Thrombosis with thrombocytopenia: think HIT, APS, TTP, DIC. Thrombocytosis is usually reactive — chronic infection/inflammation.

Source: Teaching notes 16/09/2026 (Conan Liu)

pages.title: 20% albumin after cardiac surgery increases AKI — don't give it for renal protection
pages.html:
15-h infusion of 300 mL 20% albumin after high-risk on-pump surgery raised KDIGO AKI (48.9% vs 43.4%, RR 1.12), worst in eGFR <60 (RR 1.14), and increased transfusion (38% vs 30%). No benefit on MAKE, RRT or mortality.

Trial: ALBICS-AKI

Source: The Bottom Line — ALBICS-AKI review

pages.title: 3% saline does not need a central line
pages.html:
Widespread dogma, no good evidence; safe peripherally for boluses and short infusions (PulmCrit).

Source: PulmCrit hyponatraemia series (Farkas) + SGEM/RebelEM/AJKD blog — screenshots 19/10/2026

pages.title: 5 days of prednisolone is enough for a COPD exacerbation
pages.html:
Non-inferior to 14 days for re-exacerbation (REDUCE).

Trial: REDUCE

Source: REDUCE

pages.title: 8.4% bicarbonate ≈ 6% saline — twice as strong as 3%
pages.html:
2000 mOsm/L. One 50-ml ampoule = 100 ml of 3% NaCl. Trainees happily push two amps of bicarb but balk at 200 ml of 3% — same osmotherapy.

Source: PulmCrit hyponatraemia series (Farkas) + SGEM/RebelEM/AJKD blog — screenshots 19/10/2026

pages.title: ACE inhibitors reduce mortality in symptomatic HFrEF
pages.html:
Enalapril is the foundation of HFrEF therapy (SOLVD).

Trial: SOLVD

Source: SOLVD

pages.title: Acute brain injury is the exception to Hb 70 — transfuse at Hb <9 g/dL
pages.html:
In TBI/SAH/ICH with GCS ≤13, a 9 g/dL threshold vs 7 g/dL reduced unfavourable 6-month GOS-E (62.6% vs 72.6%, RR 0.86) and cerebral ischaemic events (8.8% vs 13.5%) without excess thrombosis. Mortality unchanged. Consistent with HEMOTION.

Trial: TRAIN

Source: The Bottom Line — TRAIN review

pages.title: Acute pancreatitis: moderate, not aggressive, fluids
pages.html:
Aggressive resuscitation caused fluid overload without reducing severity; stopped for harm (WATERFALL).

Trial: WATERFALL

Source: WATERFALL

pages.title: Add clopidogrel to aspirin in NSTE-ACS
pages.html:
Fewer CV events at the price of more bleeding — the origin of DAPT (CURE).

Trial: CURE

Source: CURE

pages.title: Adrogué-Madias predicts the immediate effect of a fluid, not what happens next
pages.html:
It ignores renal water handling, so it fails as soon as the kidneys start excreting water. Under a DDAVP clamp it becomes reliable.

Source: PulmCrit hyponatraemia series (Farkas) + SGEM/RebelEM/AJKD blog — screenshots 19/10/2026

pages.title: After a hip fracture, give IV zoledronic acid
pages.html:
Annual 5 mg cut new fractures (8.6% vs 13.9%) and all-cause death; give ≥2 weeks post-op with vitamin D replete (HORIZON-RFT).

Trial: HORIZON-RFT

Source: HORIZON-RFT

pages.title: After CABG, only replace potassium when K+ ≤3.5 — chasing >4.5 doesn't prevent AF
pages.html:
Relaxed (≤3.5) vs tight (≤4.5) replacement: new AF 27.8% vs 26.2%, non-inferior, no difference in other arrhythmias, mortality or LOS; a quarter of the cost and a median of 0 vs 7 supplements. Both arms stayed >4.0 mmol/L, so it doesn't licence ignoring genuine hypokalaemia.

Trial: TIGHT K

Source: The Bottom Line — TIGHT K review

pages.title: After cardiac arrest, prevent fever — don't cool to 33°C
pages.html:
Normothermia (≤37.5°C) matched hypothermia for death and function (TTM2).

Trial: TTM2

Source: TTM2

pages.title: After initial resuscitation, restricting fluid in septic shock is safe but doesn't save lives
pages.html:
No 90-day mortality difference (CLASSIC); give fluid for a reason.

Trial: CLASSIC

Source: CLASSIC

pages.title: After OHCA, MAP ≥65 is enough — no need to push to 77
pages.html:
BOX BP arm (n=789, double-blind): MAP 77 vs 63 mmHg gave the same death/poor-neurology rate at 90 days and the same bleeding/infection. Higher targets just mean more noradrenaline.

Trial: BOX (BP)

Source: The Bottom Line — BOX (blood pressure) review

pages.title: After OHCA, PaO2 9–10 vs 13–14 kPa makes no difference — just avoid hypoxia and extreme hyperoxia
pages.html:
BOX oxygen arm (n=789): restrictive and liberal targets had identical 90-day death/CPC 3–4 (32% vs 34%). Together with PILOT and EXACT, moderate normoxia is the pragmatic target.

Trial: BOX (oxygen)

Source: The Bottom Line — BOX (oxygen) review

pages.title: After OHCA, qPLR <4% or NPi ≤2 at ≥24 h predicts poor outcome with 0% false positives
pages.html:
Automated pupillometry thresholds (BOX substudy, n=710) had PPV 97–100% for CPC ≥3 but sensitivity only 12–26%; adding NSE >60 µg/L at 48 h raised sensitivity to ~50%. Use as one objective element of multimodal prognostication, never alone, and never before 24 h for qPLR.

Trial: BOX pupillometry substudy

Source: The Bottom Line — BOX pupillometry substudy review

pages.title: After OHCA target normocapnia — mild hypercapnia adds nothing
pages.html:
TAME (n=1700): PaCO2 50–55 mmHg (6.7–7.3 kPa) for 24 h vs 35–45 mmHg gave identical 6-month favourable neurological outcome (43.5% vs 44.6%, RR 0.98) and mortality. Ventilate post-arrest patients to PaCO2 4.7–6.0 kPa; don't deliberately run them hypercapnic for cerebral vasodilatation.

Trial: TAME

Source: The Bottom Line — TAME review

pages.title: After stroke/TIA, lower BP even if 'normotensive'
pages.html:
Perindopril + indapamide cut recurrent stroke by ~43%; perindopril alone did little (PROGRESS).

Trial: PROGRESS

Source: PROGRESS

pages.title: AF-free ≥1 year after first ablation with CHA2DS2-VASc ≤3: stopping OAC is reasonable
pages.html:
Composite 0.3% vs 2.2%, driven by less bleeding; stroke rare either way. Keep anticoagulating if CHA2DS2-VASc >3 or prior stroke (ALONE-AF, Korean, open-label).

Trial: ALONE-AF

Source: ALONE-AF

pages.title: Aim lower for BP in high-risk non-diabetics if they tolerate it
pages.html:
SBP <120 cut CV events and death vs <140, at the cost of more hypotension, syncope and AKI — pick patients and monitor.

Trial: SPRINT

Source: SPRINT

pages.title: Albumin and saline are equivalent for ICU resuscitation
pages.html:
No mortality difference overall; avoid albumin in TBI (SAFE).

Trial: SAFE

Source: SAFE

pages.title: Albumin in cirrhosis — the practical position
pages.html:
Use albumin for SBP, HRS-AKI and large-volume paracentesis. Don't target >30 g/L in hospital (ATTIRE) and don't give routine long-term outpatient albumin (ICTMG 2024); some European centres differ.

Source: ICTMG 2024 (from your notes)

pages.title: Albumin in sepsis: safe but not superior
pages.html:
Targeting ≥30 g/L didn't change mortality (ALBIOS); septic-shock subgroup is a hypothesis only.

Trial: ALBIOS

Source: ALBIOS

pages.title: Albumin in sepsis — where guidelines sit
pages.html:
SAFE, ALBIOS and ARISS: safe, not superior. SSC 2026 and ICTMG 2024 suggest against routine albumin; consider only after large crystalloid volumes.

Source: SSC 2026 / ICTMG 2024 (from your notes)

pages.title: Albumin in septic shock: still unproven
pages.html:
Stopped early, underpowered, many never reached target (ARISS) — don't read as a definitive negative.

Trial: ARISS

Source: ARISS

pages.title: Anaemia after MI: transfuse to Hb 100 g/L, not 70–80
pages.html:
MINT (n=3504): restrictive vs liberal gave 30-day MI/death 16.9% vs 14.5% (RR 1.16, just missed significance) and cardiac death 5.5% vs 3.2% (RR 1.74). The restrictive Hb 70 rule from TRICC/TRISS does not apply to acute MI, particularly type 1 MI or heart failure — target Hb ≥100 while watching for TACO.

Trial: MINT

Source: The Bottom Line — MINT review

pages.title: Andexanet for factor Xa-inhibitor ICH: smaller haematomas, more strokes, no functional gain — stick with 4-factor PCC
pages.html:
Haemostatic efficacy 67% vs 53% at 12 h but thrombotic events 10.3% vs 5.6% (ischaemic stroke 6.5% vs 1.5%), mRS 0–3 at 30 d 28% vs 31%. Trial stopped early on a surrogate, industry-sponsored, excluded GCS <7. TBL: insufficient evidence to use andexanet.

Trial: ANNEXA-I

Source: The Bottom Line — ANNEXA-I review

pages.title: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK 2: CRT-guided resuscitation shortens organ support, not death
pages.html:
Win ratio 1.16 was driven by ~1 fewer day of vasopressors/ventilation/CRRT; 28-d mortality identical (26.5% vs 26.6%). Benefit concentrated in APACHE II >19. Likely a bundle effect (hourly expert reassessment, fluid-responsiveness testing before every bolus, echo, MAP and dobutamine trials) rather than CRT alone — so use CRT alongside lactate, MAP and urine output, not instead of them. SSC 2026 adopts CRT as an adjunct.

Trial: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK 2

Source: The Bottom Line — ANDROMEDA-SHOCK 2 review (Tim Law, Dec 2025)

pages.title: Angiotensin II is an option in refractory vasodilatory shock
pages.html:
Raised MAP and spared catecholamines in ~70%; no mortality data (ATHOS-3).

Trial: ATHOS-3

Source: ATHOS-3

pages.title: Apixaban: the DOAC with the cleanest bleeding record
pages.html:
Better than warfarin on stroke, major bleeding and all-cause death (ARISTOTLE) — why it is the default in many AF patients.

Trial: ARISTOTLE

Source: ARISTOTLE

pages.title: Avoid aggressive recruitment manoeuvres in ARDS
pages.html:
High-PEEP recruitment increased 28-day mortality and barotrauma (ART).

Trial: ART

Source: ART

pages.title: Balanced crystalloids or saline in DKA — either is acceptable

props.v: Soliman et al. — balanced crystalloids vs saline in DKA (SR/MA)

pages.html:
No difference in time to DKA resolution in pooled RCTs; evidence base weak (Soliman SR/MA).

Trial: Soliman et al. — balanced crystalloids vs saline in DKA (SR/MA)

Source: Soliman et al. — balanced crystalloids vs saline in DKA (SR/MA)

pages.title: Balanced crystalloids by default — but saline in traumatic brain injury
pages.html:
SMART (small MAKE30 benefit), PLUS and BaSICS (no mortality difference) together: balanced fluids are a reasonable default and SSC 2026 suggests them over saline. The exception is TBI — in BaSICS the TBI subgroup had higher 90-day mortality with balanced fluid (31.3% vs 21.1%), PLUS excluded TBI, and the lower tonicity of balanced solutions can worsen cerebral oedema. Use 0.9% saline in brain injury.

Trial: BaSICS

Source: BaSICS

pages.title: Benzodiazepine-refractory status: levetiracetam, fosphenytoin or valproate — all equal
pages.html:
~50% seizure cessation with each; pick on side-effect profile and availability (ESETT).

Trial: ESETT

Source: ESETT

pages.title: Bicarbonate for severe acidaemia with AKI didn't change mortality
pages.html:
BICARICU-2 tested the BICAR-ICU subgroup prospectively and was largely neutral; may still reduce RRT.

Trial: BICARICU-2

Source: BICARICU-2

pages.title: Bicarbonate in severe acidaemia with AKI: no survival gain, but KRT fell from 50% to 35%
pages.html:
BICARICU-2 (n=640, pH ≤7.20, KDIGO 2–3 AKI): 90-day mortality 62% vs 62%, but 4.2% bicarbonate targeting pH ≥7.30 (max 1 L/24 h) delayed KRT (31 vs 16 h) and reduced its use by day 28 — at the cost of more fluid balance (+0.6 L) and slightly more vasopressor use. Reasonable to use bicarbonate to defer dialysis in this group; don't expect it to save lives.

Trial: BICARICU-2

Source: The Bottom Line — BICARICU-2 review

pages.title: Bleeding trauma: TXA 1 g over 10 min then 1 g over 8 h, within 3 hours
pages.html:
Reduced all-cause and bleeding deaths; harmful if given late (CRASH-2).

Trial: CRASH-2

Source: CRASH-2

pages.title: Canagliflozin reduces CV events; note the amputation signal
pages.html:
MACE reduced in high-risk T2DM; amputation risk ~doubled (CANVAS).

Trial: CANVAS

Source: CANVAS

pages.title: Cancer-associated VTE beyond 6 months: apixaban 2.5 mg BD
pages.html:
Reduced dose non-inferior for recurrence with less bleeding (API-CAT).

Trial: API-CAT

Source: API-CAT

pages.title: CAPE COD steroid benefit: start early, no shock, not influenza, taper by response
pages.html:
The CAPE COD mortality effect (6.2% vs 11.9%) came from hydrocortisone 200 mg/day started within ~20 h of admission in severe CAP without vasopressor-dependent shock or influenza, continued 8 or 14 days with taper depending on day-4 response (P/F >200, breathing spontaneously, SOFA not worse). Also fewer intubations (19.5% vs 27.7%) and vasopressor starts. Only 72 deaths (fragility index 6) and ~45% culture-negative — those trended to benefit most.

Trial: CAPE COD

Source: The Bottom Line — CAPE COD review

pages.title: Cardiogenic shock: noradrenaline, not adrenaline
pages.html:
Adrenaline caused more refractory shock, lactic acidosis and tachycardia; stopped early (OPTIMA-CC).

Trial: OPTIMA-CC

Source: OPTIMA-CC

pages.title: Clamp-bolus technique: plot a 6 mmol/day line, check Na 4–6-hourly, bolus back onto it
pages.html:
Calculate the full 3% saline (or D5W if too high) volume to return to target, give it over ~2 h, recheck only after the whole bolus is in. ≤250 ml 3% per bolus. MDCalc 'Sodium correction rate' does the maths.

Source: PulmCrit hyponatraemia series (Farkas) + SGEM/RebelEM/AJKD blog — screenshots 19/10/2026

pages.title: CLASSIC's null result reflects already-restrictive usual care, not a licence for liberal fluid
pages.html:
Both arms got ~3 L before randomisation and differed by only ~2 L by day 5 (8.8 vs 10.8 L). The message is 'give boluses for a defined reason, then de-escalate', not 'fluid volume doesn't matter'.

Trial: CLASSIC

Source: The Bottom Line — CLASSIC review

pages.title: Colloids didn't beat crystalloids in hypovolaemic shock
pages.html:
Secondary 90-day signal never confirmed; stick with crystalloids (CRISTAL).

Trial: CRISTAL

Source: CRISTAL

pages.title: Consider finerenone in HFpEF/HFmrEF
pages.html:
Reduced worsening HF events + CV death in LVEF ≥40%; monitor K+ and eGFR (FINEARTS-HF).

Trial: FINEARTS-HF

Source: FINEARTS-HF

pages.title: Cryopreserved platelets are not non-inferior to liquid-stored — keep liquid-stored first line
pages.html:
CLIP-II: cryopreserved platelets in bleeding cardiac surgery gave 13% more 24-h chest-drain loss (CI crossed the 20% margin), 31% more total blood loss, more BARC-4 bleeding (32% vs 12%), more transfusion and longer ICU stay. Reserve cryopreserved units for settings with no liquid-stored supply.

Trial: CLIP-II

Source: The Bottom Line — CLIP-II review

pages.title: Dabigatran 150 mg beats warfarin for stroke; 110 mg bleeds less
pages.html:
Choose dose by bleeding risk and renal function (RE-LY).

Trial: RE-LY

Source: RE-LY

pages.title: Dapagliflozin in T2DM cuts HF admissions more than MACE
pages.html:
CV death/HF admission 4.9% vs 5.8%; MACE neutral (DECLARE-TIMI 58).

Trial: DECLARE-TIMI 58

Source: DECLARE-TIMI 58

pages.title: DDAVP clamp vs clamp-bolus: either works; bolus just gives tighter control
pages.html:
Clamp + slow 3% infusion is fine. 3% has sluggish kinetics (effect seen at 5–10 h) so infusions drift and get forgotten; PRN boluses give a closed feedback loop, like PRN labetalol vs an infusion. No patient-centred outcome data for either.

Source: PulmCrit hyponatraemia series (Farkas) + SGEM/RebelEM/AJKD blog — screenshots 19/10/2026

pages.title: Default to balanced crystalloids in ICU
pages.html:
Fewer major adverse kidney events than saline, especially in sepsis (SMART).

Trial: SMART

Source: SMART

pages.title: Default to videolaryngoscopy for emergency intubation in ED/ICU
pages.html:
DEVICE (n=1417, stopped early for efficacy): first-pass success 85.1% with VL vs 70.8% with DL (+14.3%, 95% CI 9.9–18.7), no difference in severe peri-intubation complications. Effect largest for operators with <100 intubations and trended to null in the most experienced — so for trainees and non-anaesthetists, VL (Macintosh-style or hyperangulated by patient) should be the first-attempt device.

Trial: DEVICE

Source: The Bottom Line — DEVICE review

pages.title: Dexamethasone 6 mg for hypoxic COVID; none if no oxygen
pages.html:
Mortality cut most in ventilated patients; possible harm without hypoxia (RECOVERY).

Trial: RECOVERY

Source: RECOVERY

pages.title: Dexmedetomidine sedates to target as well as propofol/midazolam with better arousability
pages.html:
Shorter ventilation vs midazolam; more hypotension/bradycardia (PRODEX/MIDEX).

Trial: PRODEX / MIDEX

Source: PRODEX / MIDEX

pages.title: Digitoxin reduced death/HF admission in HFrEF — but it isn't digoxin
pages.html:
Hepatic elimination, long half-life, stable levels; UK uses digoxin, and DECISION didn't replicate the benefit (DIGIT-HF).

Trial: DIGIT-HF

Source: DIGIT-HF

pages.title: Diuretic-resistant acute HF: add acetazolamide (or thiazide) to the loop
pages.html:
Sequential nephron blockade speeds decongestion (ADVOR) without changing hard outcomes. 2026 ESC: class IIa.

Trial: ADVOR

Source: ADVOR

pages.title: DNACPR discussions: give the CPR outcome numbers and use a structured checklist
pages.html:
Becker 2025 cluster RCT: a 1-h SDM workshop, CLEAR checklist and visual aid stating in-hospital CPR survival <20% with ~40% neurological deficit raised DNR choice from 37% to 50% (RR 1.37) and cut decisional conflict, with no extra distress. Patients overestimate CPR benefit — tell them the numbers.

Trial: Becker 2025 (SDM code status)

Source: The Bottom Line — Shared decision making in resuscitation review

pages.title: Do the ABCDEF bundle every day
pages.html:
Higher compliance → less delirium, shorter stay, lower mortality in >15,000 patients (Pun 2019).

Trial: ABCDEF Bundle

Source: ABCDEF Bundle

pages.title: Don't chase HbA1c <6% in high-CV-risk T2DM
pages.html:
Intensive control increased mortality (ACCORD) — individualise targets.

Trial: ACCORD

Source: ACCORD

pages.title: Don't fast ventilated patients before extubation — keep the feed running
pages.html:
Continuing enteral nutrition until extubation was non-inferior to 6 h fasting + gastric suction for reintubation/death at 7 days (17.2% vs 17.5%), with faster SBT-to-extubation (2 h vs 17.6 h) and fewer glucose swings. Be cautious with ileus, high aspirates, prolonged ventilation or likely post-extubation dysphagia.

Trial: Ambroisie (feed until extubation)

Source: The Bottom Line — Ambroisie (feed until extubation) review

pages.title: Don't give routine bicarbonate for mild–moderate acidosis in shock
pages.html:
No renal or mortality benefit at pH <7.30 (SODa-BIC); huge exclusion rate limits generalisability.

Trial: SODa-BIC

Source: SODa-BIC

pages.title: Don't paralyse routinely in moderate–severe ARDS
pages.html:
No mortality benefit with early NMB vs light sedation; stopped for futility (ROSE).

Trial: ROSE

Source: ROSE

pages.title: Don't push enteral protein above ~0.7–1 g/kg/day in the acute phase of critical illness
pages.html:
TARGET Protein (n=3397): 1.12 vs 0.69 g/kg IBW/day made no difference to days alive out of hospital at 90 days, lengthened ICU stay, and showed harm signals in ventilated and new-RRT patients. With EFFORT Protein and PRECISe, three RCTs now say higher protein does not help and may harm, especially in AKI.

Trial: TARGET Protein

Source: The Bottom Line — TARGET Protein review

pages.title: Don't start antifungals on a β-D-glucan alone in sepsis
pages.html:
CandiSep: BDG ≥80 pg/mL-triggered antifungals doubled antifungal exposure and cost with no mortality benefit. Use clinical risk (septic shock + MOF + multisite colonisation) and cultures; BDG at best supports stopping, not starting.

Trial: CandiSep

Source: The Bottom Line — CandiSep review

pages.title: Don't start RRT early in AKI without a hard indication
pages.html:
Accelerated RRT gave no mortality benefit and more dialysis dependence (STARRT-AKI).

Trial: STARRT-AKI

Source: STARRT-AKI

pages.title: Don't start steroids for ARDS after day 14
pages.html:
Late methylprednisolone gave no mortality benefit and higher death when begun >14 days; taper slowly to avoid rebound (ARDSNet LaSRS).

Trial: ARDSNet LaSRS (late steroids)

Source: ARDSNet LaSRS (late steroids)

pages.title: Don't target albumin ≥30 g/L in hospitalised decompensated cirrhosis
pages.html:
No reduction in infection, renal dysfunction or death; more pulmonary oedema (ATTIRE).

Trial: ATTIRE

Source: ATTIRE

pages.title: Don't thrombolyse intermediate-risk PE routinely
pages.html:
Less haemodynamic collapse but ICH 2% vs 0.2% and no mortality benefit (PEITHO); reserve for deterioration.

Trial: PEITHO

Source: PEITHO

pages.title: Don't use a corticotropin test to pick who gets steroids
pages.html:
Response status didn't predict benefit; no mortality gain in a less-sick cohort (CORTICUS).

Trial: CORTICUS

Source: CORTICUS

pages.title: Don't push protein above ~1.3 g/kg/day in ICU — especially with AKI or high SOFA
pages.html:
EFFORT Protein (n=1301, nutritional-risk ventilated patients): ≥2.2 vs ≤1.2 g/kg/day prescribed (1.6 vs 0.9 delivered) — no improvement in discharge alive by 60 d (46% vs 50%) or mortality, and worse outcomes with baseline AKI (60-d mortality HR 1.4) or SOFA ≥9. Follow ESPEN: build progressively to ~1.3 g/kg/day; avoid high-dose protein in the sickest or those with AKI.

Trial: EFFORT Protein

Source: The Bottom Line — EFFORT Protein review

pages.title: Doxapram is a bridge, not a substitute for NIV, in hypercapnic COPD

props.v: Cochrane: doxapram for ventilatory failure in COPD exacerbations

pages.html:
Marginal blood-gas benefit over placebo in the first hours, no mortality benefit, conflicting data vs NIV (Cochrane 1997, 4 trials, n=176). Use only when NIV is unavailable, declined or not tolerated.

Trial: Cochrane: doxapram for ventilatory failure in COPD exacerbations

Source: Cochrane: doxapram for ventilatory failure in COPD exacerbations

pages.title: Early cisatracurium in severe ARDS — once standard, now selective
pages.html:
Improved 90-day survival in 2010 (ACURASYS) but ROSE (2019) found no benefit with lighter sedation; use for ventilator dyssynchrony, not routinely.

Trial: ACURASYS

Source: ACURASYS

pages.title: Early, prolonged, low-dose steroids in ARDS are the regimen that works
pages.html:
1 mg/kg/d methylprednisolone within 72 h with slow taper; needs infection surveillance (Meduri 2007).

Trial: Meduri 2007 (methylprednisolone in early severe ARDS)

Source: Meduri 2007 (methylprednisolone in early severe ARDS)

pages.title: Early tight glycaemic control in new T2DM pays off for decades
pages.html:
Microvascular benefit, with a legacy effect on MI and death (UKPDS).

Trial: UKPDS

Source: UKPDS

pages.title: Early tracheostomy (<10 days) may shorten ICU stay and reduce mortality
pages.html:
Cochrane 2015: low-quality evidence; TracMan found no mortality difference — decide case by case.

Trial: Cochrane: early vs late tracheostomy

Source: Cochrane: early vs late tracheostomy

pages.title: Early vasopressin reduces RRT need but not kidney injury
pages.html:
Add vasopressin to spare noradrenaline; don't expect renal protection (VANISH).

Trial: VANISH

Source: VANISH

pages.title: Early vasopressors with less fluid is as good as liberal fluid in sepsis
pages.html:
No mortality difference in the first 24 h (CLOVERS) — tailor to the patient.

Trial: CLOVERS

Source: CLOVERS

pages.title: ECPR only works as a system — INCEPTION failed with 74-min low-flow times and low-volume centres
pages.html:
Multicentre Dutch RCT: ECPR 20% vs CCPR 16% CPC 1–2 at 30 d (NS), with only 66% of the ECPR arm cannulated. Contrast ARREST (single high-volume centre, ~59 min low-flow, 43% survival). Refer for ECPR only where a mature pathway can get flow on within ~60 min.

Trial: INCEPTION

Source: The Bottom Line — INCEPTION review

pages.title: Edoxaban is a reasonable DOAC in AF
pages.html:
Non-inferior to warfarin for stroke with less major bleeding (ENGAGE AF).

Trial: ENGAGE AF

Source: ENGAGE AF

pages.title: EGDT not better than usual care
pages.html:
Mortality 18.6% vs 18.8% (ARISE).

Trial: ARISE

Source: ARISE

pages.title: EGDT, protocolised standard care and usual care all equal
pages.html:
Modern early antibiotics and fluids had caught up (ProCESS).

Trial: ProCESS

Source: ProCESS

pages.title: Sepsis resuscitation: basics beat invasive monitoring
pages.html:
Early antibiotics, sensible fluid, noradrenaline to MAP 65 and lactate/CRT-guided reassessment are what matter. ProCESS, ARISE and ProMISe (2014–15, >4,000 patients) found no mortality benefit from CVC-ScvO2-driven EGDT over that usual care. Keep Rivers' urgency, drop his targets.

Trial: ProCESS

Source: ProCESS / ARISE / ProMISe

pages.title: ELAIN's early-RRT benefit hasn't held up
pages.html:
Single-centre surgical ICU; outweighed by AKIKI and STARRT-AKI.

Trial: ELAIN

Source: ELAIN

pages.title: Empagliflozin in HFrEF: class effect confirmed
pages.html:
Fewer HF admissions/CV deaths, slower eGFR decline, with or without diabetes (EMPEROR-Reduced).

Trial: EMPEROR-Reduced

Source: EMPEROR-Reduced

pages.title: Eplerenone benefits even mild (NYHA II) HFrEF
pages.html:
MRA is for all symptomatic HFrEF, not just severe (EMPHASIS-HF).

Trial: EMPHASIS-HF

Source: EMPHASIS-HF

pages.title: European 2014: 150 ml 3% over 20 min, check Na, repeat to a 5 mmol/L rise
pages.html:
Up to three boluses (≥4 ml/kg total). Simpler in practice: a single 4 ml/kg 3% bolus then check — a 100 ml bolus only raises Na ~0.9 mmol/L and lab rounding (±0.5) hides it.

Source: PulmCrit hyponatraemia series (Farkas) + SGEM/RebelEM/AJKD blog — screenshots 19/10/2026

pages.title: Even a sodium of 96 can be corrected in a controlled way
pages.html:
DDAVP to block water diuresis plus hypertonic saline — the extreme case that launched the Rochester strategy (Sterns 2010).

Trial: Sterns 2010 (controlled correction, Na 96)

Source: Sterns 2010 (controlled correction, Na 96)

pages.title: Family-recorded re-orientation messages are a cheap, low-risk delirium adjunct — weak evidence
pages.html:
FAVoR RCT (n=178): hourly 2-min scripted family voice recordings for 5 days gave ~1% more delirium-free days, significant only after adjustment. Reasonable to offer alongside the ABCDEF bundle; don't expect a large effect.

Trial: FAVoR

Source: The Bottom Line — FAVoR review

pages.title: Fentanyl with ketamine RSI doubles post-induction hypotension — use it only when blunting hypertension matters
pages.html:
FAKT: SBP <100 in 29% vs 16% with fentanyl (1 mcg:1 mg ketamine), though hypertension and tachycardia fell. In shock/sepsis skip or minimise fentanyl; in ICH/aortic dissection the pressor-response blunting may be worth it.

Trial: FAKT

Source: The Bottom Line — FAKT review

pages.title: Fluid bolus before intubation didn't reliably prevent collapse

props.v: PREPARE II (fluid bolus during intubation) - inferred from The Bottom Line critique

pages.html:
PREPARE II was neutral overall; have vasopressors drawn up instead. Check entry — details inferred from a Bottom Line critique.

Trial: PREPARE II (fluid bolus during intubation) - inferred from The Bottom Line critique

Source: PREPARE II (fluid bolus during intubation) - inferred from The Bottom Line critique

pages.title: Frequent COPD exacerbators: triple therapy
pages.html:
Fewer exacerbations and a mortality signal vs dual therapy (ETHOS).

Trial: ETHOS

Source: ETHOS

pages.title: Furosemide in acute HF: bolus or infusion, high or low — outcomes similar
pages.html:
Higher dose relieves symptoms faster with transient creatinine rise (DOSE).

Trial: DOSE

Source: DOSE

pages.title: GCS ≤8 from simple poisoning: watch, don't tube, for up to 4 h
pages.html:
NICO: withholding intubation (18% vs 60% intubated) with 30-min GCS checks and clear rescue triggers (regurgitation, seizure, shock, respiratory distress) cut ICU admission (40% vs 66%) and ICU LOS with no deaths and no excess pneumonia. Applies only to alcohol/benzodiazepine/GHB-type coma without hypoxia, shock, seizure, brain injury or cardiotoxic drugs. GCS alone is not an indication to intubate.

Trial: NICO

Source: The Bottom Line — NICO review

pages.title: Give 3% saline as repeated small boluses, not a slow infusion
pages.html:
2 ml/kg over 20 min, repeated as needed: faster initial correction, fewer patients needing sodium re-lowered, overcorrection no worse (SALSA). No calculations needed.

Trial: SALSA

Source: SALSA

pages.html:

pages.html:
Continuous vs 30-min intermittent: 90-d mortality 24.9% vs 26.8% (OR 0.91, p=0.08; adjusted OR 0.89, p=0.04), clinical cure 55.7% vs 50.0%, no excess resistant organisms or C. diff. Needs a loading bolus and a dedicated line; revert to intermittent dosing on the ward.

pages.title: Give TXA in non-cardiac surgery with bleeding risk

pages.title: Haloperidol for ICU delirium: symptom control only, no proven outcome benefit
pages.html:
AID-ICU (n=1000, blinded): haloperidol 2.5 mg TDS (max 20 mg/day) vs placebo — days alive and out of hospital at 90 d 35.8 vs 32.9 (NS); days free of delirium/coma NS. The 90-day mortality signal (36% vs 43%) is secondary with fragility index 4 and more missing data than that, so don't treat it as proven. Reserve haloperidol for distressing hyperactive delirium; don't give it to hypoactive delirium expecting benefit; watch QTc.

pages.title: Hb 70 is the transfusion trigger in septic shock
pages.html:

pages.html:
ARiE: adding rifaximin 550 mg BD to broad-spectrum antibiotics (all on lactulose) did not speed resolution of overt HE in ICU cirrhotics (47% vs 45%, ~4 days). Possible mortality benefit only in decompensated cirrhosis without ACLF (subgroup, weak). Use rifaximin when lactulose is not tolerated or HE is refractory, and for secondary prevention — not as an acute accelerator.

pages.html:
